dram.picks.0.group: The big three — a bet on a structural shortage
dram.picks.0.note: The same hands decide how many wafers go to HBM and how many to DDR5. They are cheap (a P/E of 4–8) because the market expects a collapse; they win if the shortage is structural.
dram.picks.0.rows.0.exposure: DRAM + HBM; the only large pure play on a US exchange
dram.picks.0.rows.0.priced: Valued like a commodity business ahead of a collapse — upside if the shortage is structural.
dram.picks.0.rows.0.why: Direct exposure to both the structural DDR5 shortage and HBM growth. Record revenue on a forward P/E below the market.
dram.picks.0.rows.1.exposure: the HBM leader plus large DRAM; listed in Korea
dram.picks.0.rows.1.priced: A cheap multiple; the Korean listing and the cyclicality are in the price.
dram.picks.0.rows.1.why: First in HBM and one of three in DRAM — a direct beneficiary of both shortages. It warns of a shortage past 2030 itself.
dram.picks.0.rows.2.exposure: the largest memory maker; DRAM + HBM + NAND
dram.picks.0.rows.2.priced: The valuation is diluted by the conglomerate; less pure exposure than Micron.
dram.picks.0.rows.2.why: The most diversified of the three. It is chasing HBM4 leadership; scale and the balance sheet smooth the cycle.
dram.picks.1.note: The calmer way to play the theme is through equipment for the new fabs. And the main bearish catalyst is CXMT.
dram.picks.1.rows.0.exposure: etch and deposition equipment for memory; a direct beneficiary of the 2027–2028 fab build-out
dram.picks.1.rows.0.risk: Orders are cyclical; export restrictions to China; a capex pause hits revenue.
dram.picks.1.rows.0.why: It earns on any memory capacity build-out regardless of which of the three wins. Less commodity risk than the makers themselves.
dram.picks.1.rows.1.exposure: equipment for memory manufacturing and advanced packaging
dram.picks.1.rows.1.risk: Capex cyclicality; export restrictions to China.
dram.picks.1.rows.1.why: A broad beneficiary of both new memory fabs and HBM packaging. Diversified across the whole industry.
dram.picks.1.rows.2.exposure: a Chinese DRAM maker, ramping cheap DDR5 output fast
dram.picks.1.rows.2.risk: A direct threat to the structural-shortage thesis; the listing is an event in its own right.
dram.picks.1.rows.2.why: Not an investment idea but the key risk: CXMT is the leading candidate to flood the market and break the price. Watch its output ramp.
dram.picksTakeaway: The pure play is Micron (DRAM + HBM on a US exchange): upside if the shortage is structural rather than cyclical. SK hynix and Samsung are the same theme, more diversified and cheaper on the multiple. Equipment (Lam Research, Applied Materials) is the calmer way to play the new fab construction. The main risk for all of them is China's CXMT: keep the position small and watch its cheap-DDR5 output.
dram.problems.items.0.gap: The main contender, China's CXMT, is 1.5–2 generations behind and cut off from EUV tools by the US ban — and without them a finer node and more bits per wafer are unreachable. Its share rose from ~4% to ~8% in a year, but it runs straight into the equipment. Any new memory fab takes 18–36 months from decision to product, so there is nothing left to relieve the 2026–2027 shortage with, and CXMT's capacity (from 320K to 420K wafers a month) only reaches the market by 2027–2028.
dram.problems.items.0.note: one caveat here: the product is standard and a customer can change supplier more easily than in HBM — so the same restraint that creates the shortage turns into a price collapse at the first sign of surplus.
dram.problems.items.0.problem: Growth in ordinary memory is constrained by a shortage of silicon wafers, and there is physically nothing with which to relieve it quickly. Almost no new fabs are being built: industry investment rose only 14% in a year (to $61B) and goes not to volume but to HBM (the stacked memory used in AI accelerators) and the move to a new process. Meanwhile every wafer switched to HBM consumes the area of three ordinary-memory wafers. The result: bit output grows only ~16% in 2026 against a historical norm of 20–30%, while data-centre demand is several times higher and the price per bit added +93–98% in a single quarter.
dram.problems.items.0.solution: With no new fabs, the only way to add bits is moving to a finer process (the 1α → 1β → 1γ nodes — successive generations of ever-smaller memory cell): the finer the cell, the more bits per wafer. At leading-edge nodes that requires EUV lithography (printing ultra-fine structures on the wafer; the machines come from the world's only supplier), made only by ASML (AMS: ASML). Micron was first to run the 1-gamma node on EUV, with SK Hynix and Samsung catching up. So the industry expands by shrinking the cell rather than by building — and the next scarce link shifts to the supply of EUV machines.
dram.problems.items.0.winners: Micron (NASDAQ: MU) — the most advanced process (the 1-gamma node on EUV lithography) and a record 84.9% gross margin; more bits per wafer on the same equipment. SK Hynix (KRX: 000660) — the cost leader, which overtook Samsung on operating profit for full-year 2025. Both win because, with the wafer count fixed, the winner is whoever squeezes more bits out of each one more cheaply. ASML takes its share: without its machines the move to a finer node is impossible.
dram.problems.takeaway: Relieving it strengthens the same three: the winner is whoever moves output to a finer node first (Micron, SK Hynix), while entry for China is closed by the EUV ban. But the protection is weaker than in HBM: the product is a commodity, so the leadership holds exactly until the first surplus.
dram.risks.0.note: The defining risk. The pattern has always repeated: a 4–7 quarter upswing, then a 4–8 quarter downturn, revenue falling 25–40%, margins from 50%+ to the low 20s or negative, and the shares losing 50–60% and falling 1–2 quarters ahead of the results. Examples: Micron −56% in 2018–19, −50% in 2022–23, −77% in the 2008 crisis.
dram.risks.1.note: The largest structural threat. It targets the cheap segment the three leaders are ceding themselves. For now it is held back by its technological lag and the US ban on lithography tools, but after 2028 this is a real variable. Even Apple has reportedly been looking at buying from CXMT.
dram.risks.2.note: The classic «shortage → surplus» pattern. Warehouses are empty now (a plus), but if AI spending pauses the turn will be sharp because of the extreme operating leverage.
dram.risks.2.risk: The cycle turns and inventories build
dram.risks.3.note: Computers and phones are falling, so all the demand rests on data centres. It was precisely that fear that knocked the shares down in July 2026. Michael Burry opened a short position against Micron on 1 July.
dram.risks.3.risk: The whole bet hangs on the giants' AI spending
dram.risks.4.note: A double effect. The US ban on supplying advanced equipment to China holds CXMT back — a plus for the three leaders. The minus: Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron face price-fixing suits amid record prices.
dram.roadmap.disruption.0.angle: The most realistic architectural change, but the net effect is close to zero. The controllers for it are made by Astera Labs (NASDAQ: ALAB) and Rambus (NASDAQ: RMBS).
dram.roadmap.disruption.0.detail: The technology lets several servers' memory be gathered into a shared pool and used more efficiently. In theory that reduces the need for new memory, but it simultaneously creates demand for separate expansion modules.
dram.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: It does not abolish the market but extends its growth. The main beneficiaries are the equipment suppliers: ASML (NASDAQ: ASML), Applied Materials (NASDAQ: AMAT), Lam (NASDAQ: LRCX).
dram.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: Memory dies will start being grown vertically, as flash memory already has been. That allows density to keep rising once ordinary transistor shrinking hits its limit. Timing: 2027–2030 and beyond.
dram.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: No effect within the decision horizon. There is no replacement for ordinary memory in 2026–2028.
dram.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: Alternative storage principles that have been discussed for decades. None has come close to ordinary memory's economics on cost per gigabyte.
dram.roadmap.generations.0.note: The three leaders are discontinuing it, and by end-2026 volume could fall to 20–25% of the 2024 level. Hence the shortage and prices that in places exceed the newer generation — Nanya and Winbond win.
dram.roadmap.generations.1.note: It stays the main standard for several more years. The main source of volume growth is not new fabs but the move to a finer process.
dram.roadmap.generations.2.note: A new direction: compact modules for AI servers (SOCAMM) — a third the size of the usual kind and a third more efficient. Micron ships first.
dram.roadmap.generations.3.note: The next architectural revolution — by analogy with how flash memory went 3D. It will need new equipment: ASML, Applied Materials and Lam win.
dram.roadmap.generations.3.spec: a move to 8–9 nm, dies stacked on dies
dram.roadmap.generations.4.note: Far beyond the decision horizon. It does not affect the current investment.
dram.roadmap.takeaway: There is no technological threat to the product itself — nothing can replace ordinary memory. The risk here is different: the technology is itself the source of volume growth (the move to finer nodes), which means a glut can arrive without a single new fab, simply because the same area starts yielding more memory.
dram.scenarios.cases.0.name: Bear
dram.scenarios.cases.0.note: spot turns, CXMT dumps, inventories build — the precedents are Micron −56% (2018–19) and −50% (2022–23)
dram.scenarios.cases.1.name: Base
dram.scenarios.cases.1.note: the shortage holds through 2027 and floor-priced contracts prop up the trough, but peak rate of price growth has already passed
dram.scenarios.cases.2.name: Bull
dram.scenarios.cases.2.note: SK Hynix's chief is right — the shortage runs past 2030, CXMT stalls without EUV, and the giants' AI demand does not slow
dram.scenarios.expectedReturn: ~0…+5%/yr (Micron, probability-weighted) — the asymmetry is skewed downward
dram.scenarios.takeaway: The asymmetry here is dangerous: the downside is a genuine halving (the precedents are Micron −56%, −50% and −77% in 2008), while the upside is capped because the entry is late and peak rate of price growth has already passed. This is a trade on the duration of the shortage with a hand on the exit, not a buy-and-hold position.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.0.detail: Almost no new ordinary-memory fabs are being built: investment rose only 14% and goes to HBM and the process transition rather than to volume.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.1.detail: The Idaho fab will not run before 2027, with meaningful volume only from mid-2027.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.2.detail: The new M15X building will not add meaningful volume before mid-2027 either.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.3.detail: The P5 fab only arrives in 2028.
dram.supply.capacityAdds.4.detail: The world's main source of new supply: from 320K to 420K wafers a month by 2027, doubling by 2030 and tripling by 2035 — on IPO money.
dram.supply.crowdingOut: The older memory generation (DDR4) is a separate story. The three leaders are discontinuing it and a shortage has appeared: in places the price has passed the newer DDR5, lead times have reached 30–40 weeks, and individual parts have risen several-fold. That is a distinct source of profit for Nanya and Winbond.
dram.supply.leadTime: A new memory fab takes 18–36 months from decision to product. So everything being laid down now will only affect the market by 2028: there is nothing left to relieve the 2026–2027 shortage with.
dram.supply.takeaway: The shortage is guaranteed through 2027 — there is physically nothing to relieve it with, and that is the most reliable part of the thesis. The argument is about 2028: some expect a shortage past 2030, others (Bloomberg Intelligence) think the worst has already passed in the first half of 2026 and that 2028 brings a surplus. The exit signal is spot prices turning and CXMT's output rising.
dram.supply.utilization: The fabs are fully loaded, with no spare space in the industry. Volume growth comes almost entirely from moving to a finer process: on IDC's estimate, bit output grows only ~16% in 2026 against a historical norm of 20–30%.
dram.thesis.bigIdea: DRAM looks like an ordinary memory cycle about to collapse — and the market prices the makers cheaply (a forward P/E of 4–8). But this time the cycle is broken the other way: [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] for AI is eating the wafers (the same cell takes three times the area in HBM), and the big three — Samsung, SK hynix and Micron — have shifted ~93% of output to HBM. Ordinary DDR5 quadrupled in price over autumn 2025 and rose another +90% in a single quarter of 2026, and there will be no new fabs until mid-2027. The conclusion: the shortage is structural rather than cyclical; the pure play is Micron, and the main risk is China's CXMT.
dram.thesis.stream.0.t: What it is, and why the price took off
dram.thesis.stream.1.t: DRAM is working memory (DDR5 in servers and PCs), what the processor is operating on right now. In 2026 its price took off not from ordinary demand but because [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] for AI is taking its wafers: the same capacity occupies three times the silicon area in HBM, and the big three have shifted around 93% of their combined output to HBM. As a result ordinary DDR5 went from $6.84 to $27.20 a gigabyte over autumn 2025 and rose another +90% in the first quarter of 2026.
dram.thesis.stream.10.items.0.n: like a commodity ahead of a collapse
dram.thesis.stream.10.items.1.n: but the market gives no credit for it
dram.thesis.stream.10.items.2.n: the leading candidate to break the price
dram.thesis.stream.11.t: Where we differ from the market
dram.thesis.stream.12.t: The market is right that DRAM is a commodity cycle, but it underrates how long this shortage lasts. While HBM takes the wafers and there are no new fabs until 2027–2028, ordinary memory stays structurally starved — prices and margins hold longer than the familiar cyclical model assumes. The bear side is real too: the product is standard, the customer has no reason to stay with a supplier, and China's CXMT is scaling output and could flood the market with cheap memory — at which point the cycle turns sharply.
dram.thesis.stream.14.t: DRAM's cheapness is the price of the fear of a collapse. At a P/E of 4–8 the market embeds an imminent turn. If the structural shortage holds (HBM eats the wafers, the fabs run late), the makers are cheap; if CXMT floods the market or AI demand weakens, the collapse arrives as usual. The bet comes down to one question: is this shortage structural, or just another cycle peak?
dram.thesis.stream.15.t: Where it is going, and what would break the thesis
dram.thesis.stream.16.rows.0.1: a commodity collapse comes closer — bearish for the three
dram.thesis.stream.16.rows.1.0: HBM keeps taking wafers and DDR5 stays short
dram.thesis.stream.16.rows.2.0: The new fabs (M15X, Micron, Samsung P5) arrive on schedule
dram.thesis.stream.16.rows.3.1: HBM and all memory fall together — the cycle turns
dram.thesis.stream.18.t: DRAM offers the highest growth in the chain with the worst resilience to the cycle. This time the shortage is structural: HBM has taken ~93% of output, DDR5 has risen several-fold, and the fabs run late to 2027–2028. But the product remains a commodity, and the turn will be sharp.
dram.thesis.stream.19.t: The pure play is Micron (the only large DRAM and HBM maker on a US exchange). SK hynix and Samsung are the same theme but more diversified. Equipment (Lam Research, Applied Materials) is a calmer way to play the new fab construction. The main risk for all of them is China's CXMT: keep the position small and watch its output.
dram.thesis.stream.2.items.2.l: of the big three's output goes to HBM
dram.thesis.stream.3.t: Why this is not an ordinary cycle
dram.thesis.stream.4.t: Memory usually lives by a brutal commodity cycle: boom → fab build-out → glut → price collapse. This time the constraint is different — structural. HBM gives a maker 5–10x the margin (an HBM module is $60–100 against $5–10 for comparable DDR5), so with wafers short it is rational to push HBM and keep ordinary memory starved. There is no new capacity until mid-2027: SK hynix's M15X fab and Micron's first wafers arrive mid-2027, Samsung's P5 in late 2028. SK hynix warns the shortage could run past 2030.
dram.thesis.stream.5.items.1.n: M15X and Micron in 2027, Samsung's P5 in 2028
dram.thesis.stream.5.items.2.l: how far out SK hynix sees the shortage
dram.thesis.stream.5.items.2.n: this is no longer a typical short cycle
dram.thesis.stream.7.t: The market is a tight three: Samsung, SK hynix and Micron split almost all DRAM output. They are the same three that make [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]], so the decision «this wafer to HBM or to DDR5» is taken by the same hands. Among the listed names, Micron offers the pure play on a US exchange; SK hynix and Samsung trade in Korea and are more diversified.
dram.thesis.stream.9.t: The market prices DRAM makers cheaply — a forward P/E of 4–8, like a commodity business ahead of a collapse. The logic is familiar: prices are at a peak, so a downturn and falling profits lie ahead. That is why the multiples stay low even on record revenue — the market refuses to pay for profit it considers temporary.
dram.tldr.0: The sharpest upswing in memory's history: contract prices +93–98% in a single quarter (a record), with record margins (Micron's gross margin at 84.9%, SK Hynix's operating margin at 72%). The cause is not demand but wafers being diverted to HBM (the stacked memory used in AI accelerators).
dram.tldr.1: The pivotal fact: in Q1 2026 ordinary DDR5 memory (the current working-memory standard) overtook HBM on profit per wafer. The most profitable product in a fab is now ordinary memory, not HBM.
dram.tldr.2: Prices are set by a lack of supply rather than by demand: the fabs are switching wafers from ordinary memory to HBM, and every gigabyte of HBM consumes three times the silicon. Almost no new fabs are being built (capex +14% in a year).
dram.unitEconomics.costCurve: The cheapest producers are Micron (the 1-gamma process with EUV lithography) and SK Hynix. The most expensive, with the most scrap, is CXMT: it has a large die and no access to EUV. That is the only thing currently restraining Chinese price pressure.
dram.unitEconomics.grossMargin: The cycle's key turning point: in Q1 2026 ordinary DDR5 memory (a 64 GB module) overtook HBM on both revenue and profit per wafer. HBM used to be four times more valuable. The consequence is twofold: it stopped paying for fabs to keep converting area to HBM, and the makers gained an argument for raising HBM prices sharply in 2027 — otherwise ordinary memory is the better product to make.
dram.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: Micron's average memory price has reached a 10-year high — roughly three times the early-2024 trough. Concretely: a 32 GB memory kit cost less than $80 in mid-2025, and by June 2026 nothing below $375 will buy one. Spot prices rose roughly 700% in a year.
dram.unitEconomics.takeaway: The key fact for the decision: ordinary memory is now more profitable than HBM per wafer — it is no longer the poor relation but a fab's most valuable product. But the operating leverage cuts both ways: when prices turn, the profit will fold as fast as it grew.
dram.unitEconomics.yields.0.label: Operating leverage
dram.unitEconomics.yields.0.value: At its limit: Micron's unit cost rose 10% while revenue rose 346% — nearly the whole price increase fell to profit. It works just as harshly in reverse.
dram.unitEconomics.yields.1.label: Where the industry's profit sits now
dram.unitEconomics.yields.1.value: Ordinary memory has become the main source of profit for all three: Samsung's memory division delivered ~94% of the company's entire Q1 2026 profit.
dram.unitEconomics.yields.2.label: Where margins will return to
dram.unitEconomics.yields.2.value: The historical mid-cycle norm is 35–45% gross, around 20% and below at the trough. Today's 80%+ is not a new reality but a peak.
dram.universe.0.exposure: memory is ~77–79% of revenue, mostly ordinary
dram.universe.0.note: The purest American play. A record 84.9% margin, with ~$100B contracted through 2030. Maximum leverage to a cycle turn — in both directions. Reports 22 September 2026.
dram.universe.1.note: The HBM leader, so its share in ordinary memory is smaller. Its chief is the loudest optimist on the shortage («and past 2030»).
dram.universe.2.exposure: memory is one part of the conglomerate
dram.universe.2.note: No. 1 by share in ordinary memory, but the exposure is diluted by phones and contract chipmaking. Memory delivered ~94% of Q1 2026 profit.
dram.universe.3.note: The purest bet on ordinary memory specifically, based on the older generations. Maximum leverage but maximum risk too, plus low liquidity. Cisco and Solidigm took equity stakes for supply.
dram.universe.4.note: A direct beneficiary of the older-generation memory shortage. Up nearly 9x in a year.
dram.universe.5.note: The lower-risk way to play the theme: paid regardless of which maker wins share, and it falls markedly less in a downturn. For the first time it earned more from memory than from processors.
dram.universe.6.exposure: equipment, memory is part of the business
dram.universe.6.note: It wins from the move to finer nodes and, in future, from vertical memory. The exposure is diluted, but the cyclicality is milder.
dram.universe.7.note: The highest memory exposure among the large equipment makers.
dram.universe.8.note: Less an idea to buy than the main risk to everyone else. Asia's largest IPO of 2026, with the retail tranche 244 times oversubscribed.
dram.universe.9.exposure: a basket: Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron ~73%
dram.universe.9.note: A simple way to take the whole theme as a basket without picking an individual name. The first pure memory fund, launched in April 2026.
dram.update.bottomLine: The bottom line: the shortage is real and physically irreducible before 2027 — the new fabs cannot arrive in time. But this is the most cyclical and most commoditised part of memory, where every previous upswing ended with the shares falling 50–60%, and the market has already begun pricing a top. The sensible decision is to take this as a 12–18 month bet on the cycle rather than a long-term position: size it to survive a halving, and set the exit conditions in advance. The main exit signal is spot prices turning and CXMT's output rising sharply.
dram.update.headline: Record prices — and a 20% fall in the shares: the market is pricing a cycle top
dram.update.stories.0.detail: Asia's largest IPO of 2026: 57.9B yuan (~$8.55B), with the retail tranche 244 times oversubscribed and a debut on 27 July. The money goes toward tripling production by 2035. CXMT's share has already risen from ~4% to ~8% in a year, with quarterly revenue up 719%. It targets exactly the cheap segment the three leaders are vacating for HBM.
dram.update.stories.0.title: China's CXMT lists with $8.55B
dram.update.stories.1.detail: On 1 July Michael Burry opened a position against Micron. Three weeks later Morgan Stanley called the same sell-off «an attractive entry point». SK Hynix's chief said (10 July) that 2027 will be «the worst year for supply in the industry's history» and that demand will exceed supply even past 2030. Meanwhile Bloomberg Intelligence thinks the worst of the shortage has already passed and that a glut is possible by 2028.
dram.update.stories.1.title: The professionals disagree
dram.update.stories.1.verdict: there is no consensus on the top
dram.update.stories.2.detail: From their late-June highs, Micron, Samsung, SK Hynix and the memory fund have lost more than 20% (Micron 28–40% in places). The cause is not the current numbers but the fear that the peak is already in view: a forward P/E of 4–8 says outright that the market expects profits to fall. The historical pattern is on their side — memory shares turn 1–2 quarters before the results do.
dram.update.stories.2.title: The shares fell more than 20% on record results
dram.update.stories.2.verdict: the market is pricing not the profit but its duration
dram.update.stories.3.detail: Contract prices added 93–98% in Q1 2026 — the largest single-quarter rise on record. But then: +58–63% in Q2, with +40–50% expected in Q3. The growth is still enormous, but it is slowing, and that is the classic sign of a cycle passing its top. Analyst forecasts have started to diverge: for Q3, Jefferies guides +40–50% while TrendForce guides just +15–18%.
dram.update.stories.3.title: Prices rose at a record rate, but the growth is slowing
dram.update.stories.4.detail: TrendForce (2 June 2026) confirmed it: in Q1 2026 ordinary DDR5 memory (a 64 GB module) overtook HBM on both revenue and profit per wafer. A year ago HBM was four times more valuable. The consequences matter: it stopped paying for fabs to keep converting area to HBM, and the makers gained an argument for raising HBM prices sharply in 2027.
dram.update.stories.4.title: Ordinary memory overtook HBM on profitability
dram.update.summary: July 2026 produced a rare picture: the best results in memory's history alongside falling shares. Here is what sits behind that, and what it means for the decision.
dram.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Next the constraint becomes the move to a finer process — currently the main source of volume growth in place of new fabs. That requires EUV lithography tools, made only by ASML: the binding constraint shifts to it.
dram.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: The binding constraint is the silicon wafers themselves: they are short because the fabs are giving ever more area over to HBM. Almost no new fabs are being built, so there is physically nothing with which to expand output quickly.
dram.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Industry investment rose only 14% in a year (to $61B) — against 30–50% in previous expansion phases. And it is directed not at new ordinary-memory fabs but at HBM and the move to a new process. It is precisely that restraint that creates the shortage.
dram.valueCapture.margins.3.margin: 35–45% gross, around 20% and below at the trough
dram.valueCapture.takeaway: Right now the makers take almost everything: at Micron, ~98 cents of every additional revenue dollar falls to gross profit. But this is the peak — the historical mid-cycle norm is three times lower (35–45%), and that is where profits will return to. Equipment (ASML) earns less at the peak but earns it steadily.
dram.verdict.bear.0: China (CXMT — a new Chinese memory maker) is flooding the market with cheap memory: its share rose from ~4% to ~8% in a year, an $8.55B IPO funds a tripling of production, and it is aiming precisely at the cheap segment the three leaders are ceding.
dram.verdict.bear.1: The cycle turns — as it always does: every previous shortage ended in a glut, with revenue falling 25–40% and the shares 50–60%. The current price spike is three times stronger than the 2017–18 upswing, so the fall could be deeper too.
dram.verdict.bear.2: The market has already priced the peak: the shares fell more than 20% from their late-June highs on record results, and a forward P/E of 4–8 says outright that the market expects profits to fall.
dram.verdict.bull.0: The shortage is structural rather than an ordinary demand cycle: wafers keep being diverted to HBM (stacked memory), SK Hynix's chief says demand will exceed supply beyond 2030, and half the industry is already under long contracts (potentially reaching 70%).
dram.verdict.bull.1: The makers are keeping discipline and not overbuilding: investment rose only 14% against 30–50% in previous expansion phases, and new fabs deliver no volume until mid-2027 or 2028.
dram.verdict.bull.2: Ordinary memory has become more profitable than HBM per wafer: confirmed by TrendForce for Q1 2026, and Micron's long contracts specify a price floor guaranteeing a margin above the peak of any previous cycle.
dram.verdict.horizon: 12–18 months — the shortage holds through 2027, but then CXMT's ramp and new fabs turn the cycle down.
dram.verdict.keyQuestion: When does the DRAM cycle turn — and will China's CXMT flood the market with cheap memory before AI demand weakens?
dram.verdict.sizing: DRAM market revenue: ~$404B (2026, +144% in a year). Server DRAM is the fastest-growing segment: DDR5 +95% QoQ in Q1'26.
dram.verdict.summary: This is a combination that needs reading carefully: the growth is the highest of any link in the chain, the share price looks cheap (a forward P/E of 4–8), but the resilience to the cycle is the worst in the whole chain. The product is standard and substitutable, the customer has no reason to stay with a supplier, and the history is unambiguous: every previous shortage ended in the shares falling 50–60%. A low P/E here is not a sign of cheapness but the classic cycle trap: the market has already concluded profits will fall. Hence a 6, on a nine for growth.
dram.whatIsIt: Working memory — what the compute chip is operating on right now, holding the current task's data close at hand. It is fast, but it forgets everything when the power goes off, so it has to be constantly refreshed with current. An AI server needs a great deal of it: the larger the model, the more data has to be held ready beside the chip.

eda.competition.entryBarrier: The highest there are: you need certification at every fab (TSMC, Samsung, Intel), a database of proven designs going back decades, and a team of thousands of engineers with deep semiconductor physics knowledge — all at once. No startup has crossed that barrier in 30 years.

eda.competition.switchingCost: Leaving is all but impossible: the whole chip creation process is built as a chain — every step depends on the one before. Change the tool at one stage and every subsequent stage has to be redone. Engineers spend years learning specific programs, companies sign bundled 5–7 year contracts, and joint work with a fab (TSMC, Samsung) on a new process begins two years before production starts — conducted in Synopsys's or Cadence's tools. Even Apple and Nvidia use all three vendors at once for different stages of the same chip.
eda.competition.takeaway: The duopoly has been stable for more than a decade despite constant product turnover beneath it. The only real threat is not a competitor but a change of model: AI automation could compress the number of licences (fewer engineers means fewer seats), but the duopoly is already retooling around a token model, where AI tools consume 3–5x more computation per project.

The disagreement is about horizon: the market is looking at a quarter of China risk, we are looking at two contract renewal cycles.
eda.intro:
EDA (Electronic Design Automation) is the software in which a chip is designed before it physically exists. A modern chip is tens of billions of transistors on a die the size of a fingernail; designing that by hand is impossible, so the whole process rests on programs that automate every step.

How it works. An engineer describes not the transistors themselves but the behaviour of the future chip — what it must compute — in a specialised language (Verilog/VHDL). The software then does the rest: it turns that description into a circuit of millions of logic gates (synthesis); physically lays the transistors out on the die and connects them with conductors across 15–20 metal layers (placement and routing); and checks that the circuit will meet the required speed, will not overheat, and will match tens of thousands of a specific fab's design rules. There is no right to a mistake: once it has gone to manufacturing, transistors cannot be «moved».

Why verification is the most important and most expensive part. Proving there is not a single error in the chip consumes up to 60–70% of all development time and budget — more than the design itself. The reason is the cost of an error. If a bug is found after production has begun, the chip must be redesigned and a new mask set made: at a leading-edge node that is ~$20–40M and 3–4 months for a single cycle (an estimate). One missed bug means hundreds of millions lost and half a year behind the competition. So the future chip is first run in its entirety on dedicated emulation hardware — in effect a virtual copy is assembled and real software is run on it before a single dollar has been spent on silicon.

How much goes into this — and why buyers do not haggle. Designing one complex AI chip on a 3 nm node costs ~$500–700M, and the lion's share of that money goes to verification (an IBS estimate). So the hyperscalers, who now design their own chips for their own workloads, commit enormous development budgets and will pay almost any price for the tools: reliability and time-to-chip matter more to them than licence costs. It was precisely that shift — cloud giants beginning to commission their own chips — that created a new wave of demand for design software over the past 5 years.

Separately there is a market for ready-made circuit blocks (IP), licensed so that standard parts need not be designed from scratch (processor cores, for example). The design software market itself is ~$18B (2025), growing ~13% a year — twice as fast as the industry's total chip development spending. It is extremely concentrated — essentially held by two players, with entry all but impossible for a newcomer; why, we examine below.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.

eda.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: TSMC, Samsung and Intel decide themselves which tools are admitted to a node. Joint process debugging begins ~24 months before launch — conducted in Synopsys's and Cadence's tools. Insurmountable for a newcomer.
eda.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: design is a chain of dependent stages: change the tool at one and every subsequent stage has to be redone. Engineers learn for years, and contracts are bundled over 5–7 years. Even Apple and Nvidia use all three vendors at once.
eda.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: a base of proven designs, waveforms and coverage (Cadence JedAI) — a compounding advantage that AI only reinforces: more data → better models → a wider lead still.
eda.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: Synopsys $2.14B/yr (34% of revenue), Cadence $1.24B/yr (30%). The development spending gap is the technology gap; nobody has caught up in 30 years.
eda.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: the duopoly's tools are the industry's de facto language: they are taught at universities and every fabless company's flow is built on them. A network effect around skills and compatibility.
eda.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the one weakening vector: at mature nodes (45 nm) open-source software (OpenROAD) and startups already design chips without licences. At the frontier the barrier holds, but the pressure is rising.
eda.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection rests not on one factor but on a combination: fab certification + the switching chain + the data. Five of the six components are strong or strengthening. The one crack is AI workarounds at mature nodes; at the leading edge certification remains insurmountable. The duopoly is buying up the best AI startups (Cadence bought ChipStack), turning the threat into an asset.

The AI startups are venture, and the duopoly is more likely to buy the best of them than to lose to them.
eda.problems.items.0.gap: AI startups (ChipAgents, Astrus) and open-source software already design chips without licences — but only at mature 45 nm nodes. At the leading edge of 3/2 nm, without fab certification and a base of proven designs, their output simply will not be accepted for production. The gap is several technology generations and years, not quarters.
eda.problems.items.0.problem: Chip design comes down to people. At 2–3 nm nodes a single chip carries tens of thousands of rules and billions of transistors, while the number of design engineers in the world grows only ~3–5% a year. Demand for new chips — especially hyperscalers' custom chips (the big cloud owners') — grows several times faster. Without a breakthrough in design productivity the industry hits a talent ceiling: chips get more expensive and arrive more slowly.
eda.problems.items.0.solution: AI automation of design: agents place blocks, check timing and run verification themselves (proving there are no errors in the chip, which today consumes up to 70% of development time). Plus hardware emulation — the future chip is run on dedicated hardware before it is manufactured. Pricing shifts to consumption of compute tokens: the harder the chip, the more computation, and the more the customer pays. That turns the talent problem into a source of revenue growth rather than a ceiling.
eda.problems.items.0.winners: Synopsys (AgentEngineer) and Cadence (ChipStack plus a «virtual engineer» with Nvidia, and the Palladium and ZeBu emulators). They win precisely because AI has to be trained on something, and only the duopoly holds decades of proven design data and certification at TSMC/Samsung/Intel. Every emulator (~$50M a system) is a barrier in its own right, generating $2–3M of licences and $3–5M of maintenance a year.
eda.problems.takeaway: The industry's main barrier — a shortage of engineers — is being solved by means that themselves strengthen the duopoly: both AI and emulation run on data and certification a newcomer does not have. So a problem that could have capped the market instead raises both the prices and the barrier to entry.

eda.thesis.bigIdea: The market decided that artificial intelligence would kill chip design software. In fact the opposite is true: AI makes Synopsys and Cadence still more indispensable and increases their revenue. And the panic around it created a rare chance to buy the highest-quality business in semiconductors at a discount.
eda.thesis.stream.0.t: A business that cannot be routed around
eda.thesis.stream.1.t: Every chip in the world — from the processor in a phone to a $40,000 Nvidia accelerator — is born not in a fab but in a program. Before spending $500–700M on development and committing expensive silicon, engineers spend years designing and verifying the future chip in Synopsys and Cadence software. Without these programs a modern chip is physically impossible: this is the first and mandatory step from idea to silicon.
eda.thesis.stream.10.t: Every new dollar of revenue turns into profit at almost no cost. The result is a rare combination: the predictability of a utility with the margins of a software business.
eda.thesis.stream.12.t: This growth is paid for not by abstract «customers» but by the hyperscalers — the cloud giants. They now design their own chips for their own workloads, and every new chip means new licences. Hyperscalers' custom chips created $15–20B of new design demand in just five years — a segment that simply did not exist before. Systems companies (Apple, Google, Amazon, Meta) are already 45% of Cadence's demand.
eda.thesis.stream.13.items.0.n: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft — the very top of the chip demand funnel
eda.thesis.stream.13.items.1.l: of new design demand in 5 years
eda.thesis.stream.13.items.2.l: of Cadence's demand is systems companies
eda.thesis.stream.13.items.2.n: Apple, Google, Amazon and Meta design their own
eda.thesis.stream.14.t: Demand grows along three axes at once: more chips, harder nodes (the 3 nm → 2 nm move makes the tools 3–5x more expensive) and an AI-tool premium on top. All three pull revenue up simultaneously.
eda.thesis.stream.16.t: Designing a chip is a chain of dependent steps: describing the logic → synthesis into a circuit → placing billions of transistors → verification. Changing the tool at one step means redoing every step after it. Engineers spend years learning specific programs, and contracts are signed as bundles running 5–7 years.
eda.thesis.stream.17.t: But the real lock is verification. Up to 60–70% of the entire development budget goes not to the design itself but to verification: proving there is not a single error in the chip. The cost of an error is enormous: if a bug is found after production has begun, a new mask set has to be made — at a leading-edge node that is $20–40M and 3–4 months for a single cycle.
eda.thesis.stream.18.t: A fab — TSMC, Samsung, Intel — will not accept a chip for production unless it has been through tools the fab itself has certified. That is the real barrier: not the program but the right of entry to manufacturing.

eda.thesis.stream.19.items.1.label: PrimeTime — timing verification
eda.thesis.stream.19.items.2.label: Siemens Calibre — final physical verification
eda.thesis.stream.19.items.3.label: Design Compiler — logic synthesis
eda.thesis.stream.19.t: Share at each critical design step
eda.thesis.stream.2.t: This software market is tiny against the industry as a whole — yet the whole industry passes through it. Design software accounts for just 1–2% of a chip's cost. But without those 1–2%, the other 98% does not exist.
eda.thesis.stream.20.t: Why has nobody caught up in thirty years? Because the duopoly spends more on development each year than an average competitor's entire turnover. The R&D gap is the technology gap: catching up means not buying a company but making up decades of accumulated data and certifications.
eda.thesis.stream.21.items.0.n: 34% of revenue — a third of everything it earns goes into development
eda.thesis.stream.21.items.2.n: less — defending your own position (Calibre) is easier than attacking someone else's
eda.thesis.stream.22.t: 17 July 2026: the day the market took fright
eda.thesis.stream.23.t: And then news landed on this seemingly impregnable business. On 17 July 2026 the Chinese model Kimi K3 designed a complete chip in 48 hours using open-source tools — without a single Synopsys or Cadence licence. The reaction was instant: Synopsys lost $6.3B in one session and −14% over the week.
eda.thesis.stream.24.label: THE MARKET'S THESIS
eda.thesis.stream.24.t: «If AI can design chips for free, the duopoly is doomed. AI will reproduce what people paid Synopsys for and drive the value of licences to zero — exactly as is happening with ordinary SaaS.»
eda.thesis.stream.25.t: At first glance that is logical. It is precisely how AI undermines ordinary software: export the data, load it into a model, and a function costing tens of dollars a month becomes free. But applied to design software the reasoning breaks on two details the market, in its panic, did not notice.
eda.thesis.stream.27.t: Detail one: the node. The chip Kimi K3 designed was on 45 nm technology — a twenty-year-old level. At the leading edge of 3–2 nm there are tens of thousands of design rules, and without certified tools no fab will accept the order. AI does not abolish certification — it trips over it.
eda.thesis.stream.28.t: Detail two: AI has to be trained on something. Decades of proven design data, tie-ins to specific fabs' processes, ready-made libraries — only the duopoly has all of it. A startup can write a clever algorithm, but it cannot reproduce thirty years of industry data and a TSMC certification. So AI does not route around Synopsys — it strengthens whoever holds the data.
eda.thesis.stream.29.t: AI will not reproduce a building in a chat window — and just as surely it will not reproduce a fab-certified chip. The physical world does not accept probabilistic answers.
eda.thesis.stream.3.items.0.n: growing ~13%/yr — twice as fast as chip development spending
eda.thesis.stream.3.items.2.n: at Cadence — higher than any other link in the chain
eda.thesis.stream.30.t: The best indicator is where the smart money goes. Nvidia, the emblem of the whole AI wave, invested $2B directly into Synopsys — not into a startup that would route around it. Venture capital is meanwhile funding AI design startups (ChipAgents $50M, Astrus $8M), but not one of them works at a leading-edge node. Capital is voting for those who hold the data and the certification, not against them.
eda.thesis.stream.31.t: And the main thing the market missed: AI does not reduce design software revenue, it increases it. AI tools consume 3–5x more computation per project. The duopoly is already moving pricing to consumption — per token: the more actively a customer uses AI, the more they pay. The scenario the market fears (AI replacing engineers) means for Synopsys and Cadence not a fall but a rise in revenue per customer: fewer jobs, but several times more computation per project.
eda.thesis.stream.32.t: What is already in the price
eda.thesis.stream.33.t: While the market prices in fear, the numbers say the opposite. After the sell-off Synopsys trades at around 24x earnings — for the first time this market's leader is not priced as a leader (the historical norm is 30–35). Cadence is around 41x, a premium for its higher margin. Meanwhile the activist Elliott has taken a stake in Synopsys for the first time in its history and is pressing for value to be realised.
eda.thesis.stream.34.items.0.n: the historical norm is ~30–35x — quality at a discount
eda.thesis.stream.34.items.1.n: on fear, not on the business deteriorating
eda.thesis.stream.34.items.2.n: plus the activist Elliott — the smart money is already here
eda.thesis.stream.35.t: This is the classic error: the market prices in a scenario that in fact strengthens the business. When that becomes obvious — and the catalyst will be either the investor day on 30 September 2026 or the first token-priced contracts — the re-rating will close the opportunity.
eda.thesis.stream.37.t: The thesis is not unconditional. Three signals would prove the opposite — and it is those, rather than the AI headlines, that are worth watching:

eda.thesis.stream.38.rows.0.1: The lock is broken — the certification barrier no longer holds
eda.thesis.stream.38.rows.1.1: State champions such as Empyrean climb the nodes
eda.thesis.stream.38.rows.2.0: Order books shrink two quarters running
eda.thesis.stream.38.rows.2.1: The number of new design projects itself is falling — the market is contracting
eda.thesis.stream.39.t: None of these signals is lit yet.
eda.thesis.stream.4.t: The design software market by year, $B
eda.thesis.stream.40.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
eda.thesis.stream.41.t: Design software is not a victim of AI but one of the few software businesses AI makes stronger. Over the next 3–5 years the duopoly will monetise AI through tokens, expanding revenue, while fab certification remains a barrier startups will not pass at a leading-edge node. At mature nodes they will take some share — but that is not the part of the market where value is created.
eda.thesis.stream.42.t: Compressed into one thought: the market sold quality at the price of risk. Synopsys is the best entry point right now (cheaper, the activist Elliott, market expansion through the Ansys acquisition); Cadence is the surcharge for margin quality. AI here is not a destroyer but an accelerator.
eda.thesis.stream.6.t: Unlike fabs, which need tens of billions of capex for every new plant, design software is pure software with almost no physical costs. Customers buy not an annual licence but multi-year subscription access. Of the revenue, 70–83% is recurring, with 3–7% annual price increases and churn close to zero.
eda.thesis.stream.7.t: Revenue like that is visible years ahead. Synopsys's order book is $11B, roughly a year and a half of revenue. Cadence's is a record $8B, covering two thirds of next year's revenue before a single new contract is signed. Together that is $19B of demand already contracted.

eda.tldr.0: A Synopsys + Cadence duopoly: 75–85% of the market, with 70–83% of revenue on subscription. Order books: $11B + $8B = $19B of visibility. They grow ~13% a year — twice as fast as chip development spending (~7%).
eda.tldr.1: Why customers do not leave: the design process is a chain of dependent stages. Change the tool at one stage and every stage after it has to be redone. At leading-edge nodes (3/2 nm) there are 25,000+ design rules, and without certified tools a fab will not accept the chip.
eda.tldr.2: Two risks: AI automation on open-source software (so far it works only on legacy 45 nm nodes) and China (12–16% of revenue exposed to export controls). More in the news block below.
eda.unitEconomics.costCurve: R&D is the main line: Synopsys ~34% of revenue, Cadence ~30%, Siemens ~25–28%. The R&D spending gap is the technology gap — which is why nobody has caught the duopoly in 30 years.
eda.unitEconomics.grossMargin: Cadence: ~86% gross. Synopsys: ~80%. Emulation hardware is lower (capital-intensive). Arm: ~95% on royalties.
eda.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: Opaque: ELA contracts run $5–50M+ a year; the token model adds 3–5x the consumption per project. Every Palladium emulation system (~$50M) generates $2–3M of licences plus $3–5M of maintenance annually.
eda.unitEconomics.takeaway: The best unit economics in the semiconductor chain. An 80–86% gross margin, 40–45% operating, 70–83% recurring, 95–99% retention. AI monetisation (tokens plus the «virtual engineer») is a scenario where ARPU rises without any growth in customer count.
eda.unitEconomics.yields.1.note: every $1 of incremental revenue → ~$0.50 of operating profit (Cadence: 7+ years)

eda.update.summary: The EDA sector lived through its first real AI shock: on 17 July 2026 the Chinese model Kimi K3 (2.8T parameters) designed a complete chip in 48 hours on open-source tools without a single Synopsys or Cadence licence. The shares collapsed: SNPS −8–12%, CDNS −10%. But the chip was at 45 nm — twenty-year-old technology. At the leading edge of 3/2 nm there are 25,000+ design rules, and without certified tools a fab will not accept the order. BNP and Benchmark called the sell-off excessive. Elliott Management (an activist) has built a multi-billion position in Synopsys — the first disciplining investor in the company's history.
eda.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: AI automation could shift the value from per-seat licences to a token or consumption model. Cadence is already building three-tier monetisation: subscription + usage tokens + a «virtual engineer» priced like an extra headcount.
eda.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: The Synopsys/Cadence duopoly: synthesis (Synopsys Design Compiler at 84–85% share), timing verification (PrimeTime at 90%+), analogue design (Cadence Virtuoso, 450+ customers, no alternative), and physical verification (Siemens Calibre at 85%+). Without these tools no fab will accept a chip.
eda.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Minimal: this is software, not hardware. The main cost line is R&D engineers: Synopsys $2.14B/yr (34% of revenue), Cadence $1.24B/yr (30% of revenue). The exception is emulation hardware (Cadence Palladium, Synopsys ZeBu): systems at ~$50M each, generating $2–3M of licences plus $3–5M of maintenance a year.
eda.valueCapture.margins.1.source: operating ~39.5% non-GAAP; lower because of the Ansys integration
eda.valueCapture.margins.3.source: royalties on every chip produced; growth +21% y/y
eda.valueCapture.takeaway: The highest margin in the entire AI chip supply chain. A subscription model with 70–83% recurring revenue, annual escalators and near-zero churn. Every dollar of incremental revenue brings ~50 cents of operating profit (Cadence: 7+ years running).
eda.verdict.bear.0: China: 12–16% of revenue is exposed. Synopsys lost ~22% of its Chinese revenue in FY2025. A ban was imposed and lifted within 6 weeks in 2025 — the politics are unpredictable. State champions (Empyrean and others) are climbing the nodes.
eda.verdict.bear.1: Valuations leave no room for error: 70–90x+ earnings (Synopsys/Cadence), Arm above 300x. The July 2026 sell-off erased $6.3B in a session — showing how fast the multiples compress.
eda.verdict.bear.2: AI disruption is no longer theory but a market factor: Kimi K3 designed a complete chip in 48 hours without licensed software. Only at 45 nm so far, but startups (ChipAgents, Astrus) and open-source software could route around the paid tools at ever more advanced nodes.
eda.verdict.bull.0: AI automation expands the market and the pricing: a ~20% uplift on upgrading to AI tools, and a shift to token-based consumption pricing (paying for compute volume rather than for a licence). The duopoly owns the data, the fab certifications and the ready-made circuit blocks (IP) that get licensed — competitors cannot replicate that.
eda.verdict.bull.1: New customers: systems companies (Apple, Amazon, Google) are already 45% of Cadence's demand, and hyperscalers' custom chips (the big cloud owners') are a segment that did not exist 5 years ago. Every new ASIC programme (a bespoke chip for a specific task) means a new licence.
eda.verdict.bull.2: Ansys expands Synopsys's market to ~$31B and adds simulation to the design flow — cross-selling is beginning.
eda.verdict.horizon: 3–5+ years — growth in the number and complexity of chip design projects; the subscription model makes revenue predictable years ahead.
eda.verdict.keyQuestion: Does AI automation of chip design expand Synopsys's and Cadence's market — or let designers route around their tools using open-source software?
eda.verdict.sizing: The EDA+IP market: ~$18B (2025) → ~$28–30B (2030), ~13% a year. After the Ansys acquisition, Synopsys's expanded market is ~$31B.
eda.verdict.summary: The most predictable subscription revenue in the semiconductor chain, but that is usually reflected in the price (70–90x earnings). After the July 2026 sell-off Synopsys trades at ~24x forward earnings — a rare moment when quality is being sold at a discount.
eda.whatIsIt: The programs in which engineers draw a future chip — laying out billions of transistors and checking that it will work — before it goes into production. Without such software a modern chip cannot be created at all: it is the first and mandatory step from idea to finished silicon.
fabric.competition.entryBarrier: For the branded vendors: EOS is decades of development + 150 million installed ports. For white boxes: lower (standard chips + SONiC), but scale and hyperscaler relationships matter. Nvidia: GPU + network integration — nobody else can reproduce it.
fabric.competition.shareTrajectory.0.det: up from <4% in 2 years; Spectrum-X $2.1B/qtr (+193%); ~$31B of FY26 networking
fabric.competition.shareTrajectory.2.det: $19B FY26; HPS +81%; 10 active 1.6T programmes; −29% in a month = an entry point
fabric.competition.switchingCost: It depends on the type of equipment. Arista: high — companies trust its software (EOS), which behaves as a single system; moving to another vendor means retraining the team and rewriting the automation. White box (SONiC, open software): low — the hardware supplier can be changed without changing the software. Nvidia: very high — its NVLink binds the chips into a single cluster, and leaving it is only possible by changing the whole architecture.
fabric.competition.takeaway: A five-way fight: Nvidia (the bundle), Arista (the branded moat), Celestica (white-box AI), Cisco (the re-rater), Accton (the ODM). Ethernet has beaten InfiniBand. SONiC + white box commoditises branded margins. Nvidia's bundling is a structural threat.
fabric.demand.customerConcentration: Extreme: Celestica's top 10 = 79%, with three CCS customers at 32%/14%/12%. Arista: heavily weighted to the cloud titans. Hyperscaler capex ~$602B (2026), ~75% of it AI (~$450B).
fabric.demand.takeaway: Demand is insatiable; supply is the constraint (Arista: «1–2 years»). Backlogs are at records. Hyperscaler capex of ~$602B is the driver. But concentration is extreme — Celestica's top 10 = 79%, and Arista is heavily weighted to the cloud titans.
fabric.dependencies.correlation: A high-beta derivative of GPU shipments and hyperscaler capex (~$602B in 2026, ~75% AI). Tightly correlated with networking chips and photonics. Fabric utilisation gates GPU utilisation.
fabric.dependencies.downstream: Hyperscalers (Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, xAI), neoclouds, enterprises, sovereign AI, AI cluster operators. The fabric is the cluster's connectivity layer.
fabric.dependencies.takeaway: The fabric depends upstream on silicon (Broadcom/Nvidia) and optics (photonics), and downstream on GPU volume and hyperscaler capex. Assembly is not the bottleneck — components are. The fabric is not optional: 33% idle on a saturated cluster = >$1M/yr of wasted compute.

But the threats are real: Nvidia has become number one in Ethernet (21.5%, up from <4% in 2 years), and SONiC presses on the branded margin. Arista at ~44× forward is fairer than Celestica at ~50× on an 8.4% margin. HPE (networking +148%, >50% of operating profit) is underrated on scepticism about the Juniper integration.
fabric.intro:
The network fabric is the switches together with the control software (the network operating system) that connect thousands of GPU servers into a single compute cluster. It is a layer above the individual networking chip: the chip is a die inside the device, while the fabric is the devices themselves plus the software that builds routes and manages traffic. Without it every server computes on its own; with it thousands of GPUs work as one computer.

How it works. When training an AI model, all the GPUs have to exchange intermediate results at every step (an all-reduce style operation) before they can move on. That means the speed of the whole cluster is set not by the fastest link but by the slowest and most congested part of the network — the fabric directly determines whether expensive GPUs sit idle or work. A cluster has two levels of connectivity, built differently. Scale-up is the link between GPUs inside a single rack, where hundreds of GB/s and minimal latency are needed; today that is held by Nvidia's proprietary NVLink protocol (up to 3.6 TB/s), which works only with Nvidia chips. Scale-out is the link between racks over Ethernet or InfiniBand, where data travels in packets through switches. Separately, the fabric splits by hardware: branded systems with their own software against «white boxes» — standard chassis running an open network OS, roughly 20% cheaper.

The most important property, the one you cannot economise on, is GPU utilisation. A 33% idle rate on a saturated 512-GPU cluster is more than $1M a year of wasted compute (estimate), and a real cluster has tens of thousands of such GPUs. So the fabric is deliberately built with spare bandwidth: it costs 10–20% of the cluster budget but determines the return on the other 80–90% invested in the GPUs themselves. That is exactly why almost any price is paid for low latency and full (non-blocking) bandwidth — economising on the fabric means leaving far more expensive hardware idle.

Who is investing, and how much. Hyperscaler capex for 2026 is around $602B, of which ~75% is AI; networking within that sum is tens of billions. The price depends heavily on type: an Nvidia Spectrum-X switch port is ~$1,500, a standard port on an open OS ~$600, an InfiniBand switch $80–120k. The main shift of 2026: Nvidia has become number one in data-centre Ethernet switching (21.5% share against <4% two years earlier), tying the Spectrum-X switch to its own GPUs ($2.1B/qtr, +193%).

Ethernet has already beaten InfiniBand in scale-out (more than two thirds of the AI back end), and industry consortia (Ultra Ethernet, UALink) are trying to open the scale-up level to merchant chips as well. The AI switch market will exceed $100B by 2030 (Dell'Oro); data-centre Ethernet switches already run at ~$10B/qtr (+61% y/y).

A term that will come up later: the «node» (process technology), for example 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip-manufacturing technology. The figure in nanometres nominally denotes transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors, and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and more expensive that node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel are capable of the leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); the «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are a high-volume, cheap technology available to many.

fabric.problems.items.0.gap: The gap is in software and in time. NVLink is built into the CUDA/NCCL stack (Nvidia's software layers) on which every AI cluster already runs; leaving it is only possible together with changing the whole architecture. The first UALink products arrive only in 2026–2027 and still have to catch NVLink on speed (3.6 TB/s) and on software maturity — that is years, not quarters. On top of that, NVLink Fusion draws the possible competitors into Nvidia's orbit in advance.
fabric.problems.items.0.problem: The link between GPUs inside a single rack (scale-up) is held by Nvidia's proprietary NVLink protocol (an ultra-fast bus between GPUs), and there is no way around it. It is the fastest and most profitable part of the network (NVLink 6 = 3.6 TB/s), but it works only with Nvidia chips and Nvidia's software (NCCL, CUDA — Nvidia's software layers for GPU computation). As a result the whole intra-rack level is closed to independent switch manufacturers: between racks (scale-out) Ethernet has already won and taken more than two thirds of the AI back end, while inside the rack the value goes entirely to Nvidia. While scale-up stays closed, Broadcom, Marvell, Astera and the fabric manufacturers cannot enter the most expensive segment.
fabric.problems.items.0.solution: Industry consortia are building open standards to repeat what Ethernet did in the link between racks (scale-out). UALink (an open standard for GPU-to-GPU links) opens scale-up to merchant chips, and Ultra Ethernet (UEC — an enhancement of ordinary Ethernet) brings it down to InfiniBand latencies. The first products come in 2026–2027 (AMD MI400/Helios, UALink switches from Astera Labs and Broadcom). Dell'Oro forecasts that Ethernet will win inside the rack over the long run as it has already won between racks — at which point the closed NVLink level opens up and merchant chips gain a large new market (AI back-end switch spending will exceed $100B by 2030).
fabric.problems.items.0.winners: Today Nvidia wins: NVLink is closed, and Spectrum-X (its own switch, $2.1B/qtr, +193%) has already made it number one in Ethernet switching (21.5% against <4% two years earlier). If the intra-rack link (scale-up) opens, the winners are Broadcom (ready for any protocol: Ethernet, UALink, custom), Astera Labs (the Scorpio fabric for scale-up, targeting >$1,000 per accelerator at a 76% margin), Marvell, and in fabrics Arista (the EOS software) with Celestica (white boxes). Nvidia defends the level through NVLink Fusion (a programme for connecting other companies' chips to its bus) — bringing in MediaTek, Marvell and Alchip to its interconnect in order to head off potential competitors.
fabric.problems.takeaway: Here it works the other way round: relieving the constraint hurts the incumbent leader. While the intra-rack link (scale-up) stays closed, Nvidia wins; if open Ethernet/UALink bring it up to NVLink's level, the door opens to new players (Broadcom, Astera, Marvell, Arista). This is the one node where solving the problem plays against today's champion.

fabric.whatIsIt: The network fabric is the networking devices themselves (the switches) together with the control software that connects thousands of servers into one large compute cluster. It is a layer above the individual chip: the chip sits inside the device, while the fabric is the devices themselves plus the software that lays out routes and distributes data flows. Without it every server computes on its own; with it thousands of servers work as one computer.
fiber.competition.concentration: The top five cable makers (Corning, Prysmian, YOFC, Hengtong, Sumitomo) = ~46.5% globally (GM Insights). Corning leads with >21.5%. Preforms: the top three (YOFC, Corning, Prysmian) hold >40%. China is ~56% of global output, but is shut out of the West by duties.

The divergence is that the scarcity premium is already in the price at Corning, while the market ignores Shin-Etsu (the chokepoint) and CommScope (deep value).
fiber.intro:
Optical fibre is an extremely fine strand of ultra-pure quartz glass: ~125 microns on the outside, with a light-guiding core in the centre only ~9 microns across. Along that core light travels almost without loss over distances copper cannot reach, carrying data between data centres and inside them. Cables are assembled from these strands, holding up to several thousand fibres today and, in record examples, more than 13,000.

How fibre is made. First a preform is grown — a glass blank. By vapour deposition onto a seed, ultra-pure quartz is laid down layer by layer, defining the future core and cladding; the result is a transparent cylinder about a metre long and as thick as an arm, in which the entire structure of the future fibre is already «written». The purity required is extreme: any impurity or bubble becomes a loss of light along the whole length of the drawn strand. This is the most difficult and most capital-intensive stage.

The preform is then suspended in a draw tower several storeys high and its lower end is heated to ~2000 °C. The softened glass is drawn downwards into a thin strand; on the fly its thickness is controlled, it is cooled and coated with a protective polymer, and then wound onto spools. A single preform yields hundreds, and sometimes thousands, of kilometres of fibre. Finally the fibres are assembled into a cable — in loose tubes or in dense ribbon stacks — with protection against moisture and breakage.

The critical constraint is preforms. Draw-tower and cabling capacity can be added relatively quickly (~6–12 months), but the preform is the binding constraint of the whole chain. The lines that produce them run at close to 100% utilisation, the expansion cycle is 18–24 months, and Morgan Stanley puts the 2026 shortfall at ~12.5%. The technology for synthetic quartz of extreme purity belongs to a handful of manufacturers, and it cannot be reproduced quickly. So the value concentrates in whoever controls that particular stage, and in the vertically integrated players who run the chain from glass to cable.

Who is investing, and how much. AI has raised demand sharply: a single rack of 72 GPUs requires 16–36 times more fibre than an ordinary server rack, data-centre demand grew ~76% during 2025, and the CRU price index rose from a record low of 78.6 (March 2024) to 263.0 (March 2026) — the steepest rise on record; speciality fibre for AI is effectively sold out. The customers themselves are paying for the capacity expansion: Nvidia has put $3.2B into Corning to grow US optical capacity more than tenfold, Meta has contracted up to $6B, and another prepaid cable contract runs to €5.5B. They pay in advance because without fibre there is nothing to connect the expensive GPUs with, and capacity is reserved well ahead.

The market. World shipments were 662 million fibre-km in 2025, forecast at ~807 million by 2027; the cable market itself is ~$16–17B (2026), growing ~10% a year. Manufacturing is concentrated: the five largest hold ~46% of the market, and at the upstream preform stage there are fewer suppliers still.

fiber.mentalModel.framework: Optical fibre is for the most part commodity glass with one irreproducible key constraint: the preform. The fibre itself is mass-produced by Chinese manufacturers (~56% of the world), but the preform blank is made by only a handful, and its capacity cannot be added quickly — an 18–24 month expansion cycle at close to 100% utilisation. So most of the profit goes to those who control the preform (Heraeus, Shin-Etsu) and who are integrated from glass to cable (Corning, Prysmian): they earn a premium on speciality and AI-grade fibre (~40% gross margin against 15–25% for commodity) while ordinary fibre commoditises.
fiber.mentalModel.revenueFormula: Revenue = fibre volume (core-km) × ASP (the CRU index) × the share of speciality and AI-grade mix (bend-insensitive, high-density, hollow-core) over commodity G.652.D
fiber.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: a glass blank about 1 m long yields hundreds of km of fibre; expanding capacity takes 18–24 months, utilisation is ~100%, and the shortfall is ~12.5% (Morgan Stanley). Heraeus and Shin-Etsu hold the binding constraint of the whole chain.
fiber.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: Corning is the only near-pure integrated leader: preform → fibre → cable, plus the IP. Integration delivers both margin (~21% net in optical in Q1 2026) and priority in a shortage — which cable assemblers do not have.
fiber.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: Nvidia $3.2B (10× US capacity + >50% of US fibre), Meta up to $6B, Prysmian/Molex €5.5B with €550M upfront. The customer pays for the expansion and locks in demand — a structural reduction in cyclicality.
fiber.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: duties (China→US 33–78%, plus the EU and India) cut Chinese manufacturers off from the West and protect ASPs. But this is a political barrier rather than a structural one — it can change with trade policy.
fiber.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: Corning produces both conventional and hollow-core fibre (the NC plant with Heraeus), and multicore gives 4× the capacity in a standard 125 µm. Whoever owns both sides of the transition is protected from disrupting themselves.
fiber.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the weakest vector: standard fibre is commoditised, ~56% of output is Chinese, and ASPs have swung from −28% (2023) to +418% (2026). Without a speciality mix this is a race to the bottom against Chinese scale.
fiber.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The defence is twofold: the preform constraint (18–24 months, ~100% utilisation) plus vertical integration with customer-paid contracts. The weak link is commodity glass, where Chinese scale commoditises anything that is not speciality. The real advantage is not fibre volume but control of preforms and speciality grades; which is exactly why Shin-Etsu (the only listed preform controller) is strategically underrated.

fiber.problems.items.0.gap: New preform capacity (glass blanks) takes 18–24 months to build and qualify (CRU); without preform technology of one's own there is no way in, and anti-dumping duties (China → US 33–78%, plus EU and Indian duties) cut ~56% of Chinese output off from the Western market. The leaders' incremental capacity has already been prepaid and reserved by customers in advance.
fiber.problems.items.0.problem: All fibre production is bottlenecked on glass preforms — blanks of ultra-pure quartz glass from which the strand is drawn. This is the most difficult and capital-intensive stage: the lines run at close to 100% utilisation, the capacity expansion cycle is 18–24 months, and Morgan Stanley puts the 2026 shortfall at ~12.5%. AI has raised demand sharply — a single rack of 72 accelerators requires 16–36 times more fibre than an ordinary server — and the CRU price index has risen from 78.6 (March 2024) to 263.0 (March 2026), the steepest rise on record. Speciality fibre for AI is effectively sold out.
fiber.problems.items.0.solution: Capacity is being expanded with the customers' own money: NVIDIA has put $3.2B into Corning for a tenfold increase in US optical capacity and more than half the country's fibre capacity plus 3 plants; Meta has contracted up to $6B; Prysmian is doubling US fibre capacity; Shin-Etsu is expanding its Kashima plant. Draw towers scale faster (~6–12 months), but the binding constraint remains the preform (the glass blank). New preform capacity begins to arrive at the end of 2027 (CRU).
fiber.problems.items.0.winners: The owners of the preform stage — Heraeus and Shin-Etsu (synthetic quartz blanks; Shin-Etsu is the only publicly investable pure preform chokepoint) — together with the vertically integrated Corning (glass → cable, capacity financed by customers, an optical net margin of ~21%). They win because preform technology, decades of integration and customer prepayments locking up capacity cannot be reproduced in a couple of quarters.
fiber.problems.takeaway: Relieving the constraint runs back into the same leaders: the scarce preform stage (glass blanks) belongs to Corning, Shin-Etsu and Heraeus, and it is their expansion that the customers have prepaid. The only risk to them is overcapacity, if AI demand cools by the time the new lines arrive in 2027.

fiber.tldr.0: The optical fibre cable market is ~$13–18B (2025, the range depending on definitions), with a CAGR of ~9.5–10%. Data-centre demand grew 75.9% in 2025 and will rise from ~5% to ~30% of the global total by 2027 (CRU — the industry analyst). Prices (the CRU index): a record low of 78.6 (March 2024) → 263.0 (March 2026, +418% y/y for the G.652.D standard in China). The preform shortfall (blanks of ultra-pure glass) is ~12.5% in 2026 (Morgan Stanley).
fiber.tldr.1: The value sits in three positions: (1) glass preforms (the blanks the fibre is drawn from; the scarcest link: an 18–24 month expansion cycle at ~100% utilisation), (2) vertically integrated «glass to cable» leaders with customer-funded capacity (Corning: Meta up to $6B + NVIDIA $3.2B; Prysmian: Molex up to €5.5B), (3) speciality fibre (bend-insensitive, hollow-core, high-density at 1,728–13,824 fibres per cable).
fiber.tldr.2: The central tension: the recovery is real and structural, but the sector carries a fresh memory of the 2022–23 collapse (list prices −28%), valuations have re-rated sharply upwards (Corning ~52–57× forward earnings (P/E), Fujikura +344% over 12 months), and hollow-core fibre (the light travels through air inside the strand) plus multi-band coherent optics threaten conventional glass on a 5–10 year horizon. The key question: will AI demand absorb the new preform capacity arriving at the end of 2027, or will the sector repeat its overbuild?
fiber.unitEconomics.costCurve: High operating leverage: utilisation drove both the 2023 collapse and the 2025–26 surge. Corning's core operating margin +220 bps y/y (Q1 2026). Customer-funded capacity (NVIDIA/Meta) reduces the capex risk.
fiber.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: G.652.D bare fibre: RMB 83.40/fibre-km in China (+418% y/y, March 2026); EUR 7.94 in Europe (+159% y/y). AI data-centre fibre ~$7.14/fibre-km (QY Research). Speciality (bend-insensitive G.657): 50+ yuan/fibre-km.
fiber.unitEconomics.takeaway: Pricing power has returned after a record glut: CRU 78.6 → 263.0. The preform chokepoint plus a speciality mix means durable margins for the leaders. Customer-funded capacity is a structural de-risking of capex.

fiber.update.bottomLine: Optical fibre has moved from a glut into a structural shortage on the AI density surge. The preform chokepoint (18–24 months, ~100% utilisation) is the binding constraint until the end of 2027. The leaders (Corning, Prysmian) are de-risked through customer-funded capacity, but the valuations are extreme (52–57× forward P/E) and 2027–28 is an overcapacity risk window.

fiber.verdict.summary: The density jump from AI (16–36 times more fibre per rack) and the preform shortage (blanks of ultra-pure glass from which fibre is drawn; ~12.5%, Morgan Stanley) have created a structural shortage that has lifted prices (the CRU index) from a record low of 78.6 to 263.0 in two years. The competitive advantages are strong for the owners of the preform stage (Heraeus/Shin-Etsu) and for the vertically integrated leaders (Corning, Prysmian) with customer-financed contracts. But the multiples are extreme: Corning at ~52–57× forward earnings, the Japanese names +150–344% over 12 months — the sector already prices the recovery in. The cyclicality is real: the 2022–23 collapse is fresh in memory, and new preform capacity arrives at the end of 2027 — the risk window. The best choice: Corning (integration plus a hedge through hollow-core fibre, where the light travels through air inside the strand). Underrated: Shin-Etsu (the only listed owner of the preform stage) and CommScope (a deeply underrated turnaround).
fiber.whatIsIt: This is an extremely fine strand of ultra-pure glass, thinner than a human hair, along whose core light travels enormous distances with almost no loss. It is along such strands that data passes between data centres and inside them — glass carries it far further and faster than a copper wire can. Many such strands are assembled into cables, which today can hold several thousand fibres each. AI needs a great many of them: a single rack of accelerators requires dozens of times more fibre than an ordinary server.
