litho.update.summary: The paradox of July 2026: all five WFE leaders reported records (ASML's €39B order book, AMAT $7.91B, Lam $5.84B, TEL ¥2,443B, KLA's 62.6% margin), but the SOX index fell 20% from its high into a technical bear market. The causes: rotation out of semiconductors, the Kimi K3 shock to the adjacent EDA sector, and geopolitical worries. Fundamentally nothing changed — demand is confirmed 2+ years out.
litho.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Defect inspection (KLA): with every new generation (GAA, HBM, BSPDN) 10–100x more points on a wafer have to be checked. KLA is already seven times its nearest competitor and keeps pulling away.
litho.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: ASML is an absolute monopoly in EUV: a 100% share, 30 years of development, >$10B invested, exclusive Zeiss optics and its own Cymer light sources. No competitor can reproduce it. High-NA EUV (~$400M each) is the next level of the monopoly.
litho.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: High for the equipment makers: ASML spends ~€1.2B/qtr on R&D (~13–15% of revenue). But higher still for the buyers: one fab means $10–30B of capex.
litho.valueCapture.margins.1.source: the best of the big five; software + data
litho.valueCapture.margins.3.source: above 50% for the first time in 25 years
litho.valueCapture.takeaway: Margins are rising across the whole big five — a sign of a healthy cycle and strengthening pricing power. Service and the installed base (>100,000 chambers at Lam, €2.76B/qtr at ASML) turn into recurring income. KLA and Besi are the margin champions (62–65%).
litho.verdict.bear.0: Cyclicality: in 2022 SOXX (the semiconductor share index) fell 46%, AMAT ~57%, Lam ~59%, ASML ~55–60%. In July 2026 SOX entered a technical bear market (−20% from its high).
litho.verdict.bear.1: China is a double blow: the largest customer ($41B, 40% of the market in 2024) is leaving (toward ~20% in 2026) AND building its own industry at the same time (NAURA, AMEC, SiCarrier). AMAT has already paid a $253M fine for export violations.
litho.verdict.bear.2: Valuations: ASML ~42x forward earnings, Onto ~150x, ACMR above its DCF fair value. If fab capex slows, the multiples compress first.
litho.verdict.bull.0: Record order books: ASML at ~€39B, Lam at a record $5.84B in a quarter, AMAT at a record $7.91B. Visibility 8 quarters out, with 100+ active fab projects.
litho.verdict.bull.1: AI structurally raises equipment intensity: GAA transistors (a new three-dimensional transistor structure) add +15–25% process steps, HBM (ultra-fast memory) consumes 3x more wafers per bit, and advanced packaging grows >50% in 2026.
litho.verdict.bull.2: The monopolies are insurmountable: ASML spent 30 years and >$10B on EUV (printing with extreme ultraviolet), plus exclusive Zeiss optics and its own Cymer light sources. It cannot be reproduced.
litho.verdict.horizon: 3–5 years — tied to the AI capex cycle and the node transition (2 nm and beyond), where ASML's EUV machines are mandatory.
litho.verdict.keyQuestion: Will the fabs keep raising capex — or will capacity be overbuilt, as in every past cycle?
litho.verdict.sizing: The WFE market: $104B (2024) → $135B (2025) → $145–170B (2026) → up to $200–210B (2028). All equipment (including test and packaging): a record $156B in 2027.
litho.verdict.summary: The deepest monopolies in technology: ASML (100% of EUV — lithography in extreme ultraviolet), KLA (57% of defect inspection, a 62–63% margin), Applied Materials (the largest by revenue). Growth is double-digit and confirmed by order books and fab capex. But equipment is the most cyclical part of the chain: in 2022 the SOX index (of semiconductor shares) fell 46%, and individual names 55–60%. Valuations are high (ASML at ~42x forward earnings), and China is a double risk: both the largest customer and a rising competitor.
litho.whatIsIt: These are the machines that physically make every chip. A leading-edge chip is built in layers: some tools deposit ultra-thin films, others transfer the pattern of the future transistors onto them with light, others strip away the excess and hunt for defects a few atoms across — dozens of times over. The hardest and most expensive of these machines prints the pattern with a special short-wavelength light, and exactly one company in the world can build it.
nand.competition.concentration: six makers instead of three — the discipline is weaker than in working memory
nand.competition.entryBarrier.why: YMTC is not a hypothetical threat but an operating player with 13% of the market that doubled its share in a year and has filed to list to fund expansion. It is held back only by sanctions on equipment and by scale, but on storage density it is already the world leader. By 2027 China could take ~19% of all bits.
nand.competition.players.0.note: The largest by share, but NAND is diluted inside the conglomerate. In May 2026 it showed a 900-storey prototype made by bonding two blocks of 450.
nand.competition.players.0.tech: 236 storeys in production, 286 ramping; targeting a thousand by 2030
nand.competition.players.1.note: The best-positioned on the AI theme: its Solidigm division is the clear leader in the dense server drives bought for running models. Segment revenue grew 75% in a quarter.
nand.competition.players.1.tech: 321 storeys in production — the storey-count leader
nand.competition.players.2.note: A pure NAND bet with no working-memory cushion — hence both the maximum leverage and the maximum fall. Profit doubled in a year; in June 2026 it briefly overtook Toyota by market value.
nand.competition.players.3.note: The only American maker. Take-or-pay contracts cover about a third of its NAND volume through 2030 — which will soften the downturn more than for its competitors.
nand.competition.players.3.tech: 232 storeys; the first production drive on the new interface
nand.competition.players.4.note: Pure NAND, spun out of Western Digital in 2025. Up 33x in a year — the most extreme re-rating in the industry. It is developing ultra-fast flash together with SK Hynix.
nand.competition.players.4.tech: A joint manufacturing venture with Kioxia through 2034
nand.competition.players.5.name: YMTC (China)
nand.competition.players.5.note: The key structural shift: its share rose from ~8% to 13% in a year. The important difference from the Chinese players in working memory is that here the technology genuinely is world-class on density — only scale and equipment lag. It targets the cheap segment. It has filed to list in Shanghai.
nand.competition.players.5.tech: The world record for storage density, and without access to leading-edge equipment
nand.competition.switchingCost: For server drives, customer qualification takes several quarters, and after it suppliers are changed reluctantly — real protection, if not ironclad. In the consumer segment there is none at all, and that is exactly where China is going.
nand.competition.takeaway: Six players instead of three is the root reason NAND historically earns less than working memory. In this cycle the discipline has held, but it is exactly what breaks first once YMTC scales output. Watching China's share matters more than any other metric in this sector.
nand.demand.backlog: The makers' inventories are at an all-time low. One important nuance: module assemblers' inventories are elevated instead — consumer demand is weak. So the shortage is in the server segment rather than across the whole market.
nand.demand.contractStructure: Take-or-pay contracts have appeared: Micron's 16 strategic agreements cover about a third of its NAND volume through 2030, with roughly $22B of prepayments and a guaranteed price floor. Micron says outright that it can cover only 50–66% of its customers' demand. This is a fundamentally new thing for a commodity market — and it will soften the coming downturn.
nand.demand.customerConcentration: Demand has shifted to data centres: servers are already more than 40% of consumption, and Micron's server drive sales passed $5B in a quarter, doubling in three months. But phones and laptops are still around 40% — and it is they that swing the balance, with demand there weak because of the price increases.
nand.demand.pricing: Price growth has already stopped: Q3 2026 is just 0–5% after +72% in Q2. The cause is consumer buyers running into their budget ceiling. The price outlook stays positive through 2027, but balance is restored in H2 2027.
nand.demand.takeaway: AI demand is real and backed by take-or-pay contracts — the best revenue visibility in the segment's history. But the stall in Q3 shows where the limit is: the consumer can no longer take it, and everything from here rests on data centres alone.
nand.intro:
NAND is memory that holds data without power: switch a server off and its working memory forgets everything, while NAND retains it. A bit is written as an electrical charge locked inside an insulated cell; the insulation holds it for years without current, which is what makes the memory non-volatile. Per gigabyte NAND is several times cheaper than working memory but also markedly slower, so its job is storing volume: it is what solid-state drives (SSDs) are made of, and they are displacing hard disks.

How capacity is increased — two ways at once. First, storeys: cells stopped shrinking in the plane long ago and are instead grown vertically, layer upon layer. Production dies today carry around 300 layers (321 at the leader), with a thousand targeted by 2030; to connect all the storeys, deep vertical channels are etched through the whole «building» at once. The more layers, the more capacity on the same die area and the cheaper the gigabyte. The second way is how many bits one cell holds: by charge level a cell distinguishes several values, and three bits (TLC) or four (QLC) are written into one. QLC gives a still lower price per gigabyte, but the cell has to distinguish more charge levels, so it writes more slowly and wears out faster. For AI that is acceptable: when a model runs, the data is mostly read rather than rewritten — and reading barely wears the cell at all.

Where the limit is, and what is expensive here. The main technical difficulty is the height of the «building»: the more storeys, the more the silicon wafer bows under mechanical stress, the harder it is to align the layers with one another, and the harder it is to remove heat. Above roughly 300 storeys a single die gets ever harder to build, so the industry is moving to bonding — two finished wafer blocks joined into one (Samsung showed a 900-storey sample made from two blocks of 450). That raises the value of the suppliers of deep-channel etch equipment. But unlike HBM, there is no uncopiable technological lead here: the world record for storage density is held by China's YMTC, despite its equipment restrictions.

Who pays, and why they pay in advance. The main constraint here is not physics but the number of players: there are six makers rather than three as in working memory, and six find it harder to agree on output restraint — so supply regularly overshoots demand, and NAND has historically been the least profitable part of memory. In this cycle the discipline has held for the first time: a new fab costs more than $10B and nobody is rushing to build one, so investment is rising only 5% in a year (from $21B to $22B), while Samsung and SK Hynix deliberately hold NAND back in favour of more profitable AI memory. Against that parsimony, data-centre demand is real, and buyers have for the first time accepted take-or-pay contracts: Micron's 16 agreements cover about a third of its volume through 2030, with ~$22B of prepayments and a guaranteed price floor, even though it can only cover 50–66% of its customers' demand. They pay in advance because server drives are sold out, and part of the demand is also spilling over from hard disks, which are themselves sold out through the end of 2026.

The market: six makers with shares of roughly 29 / 18 / 14 / 13 / 13 / 13% (Samsung, SK Hynix with Solidigm, Kioxia, Micron, SanDisk and China's YMTC), with YMTC having doubled its share to 13% in a year. Segment revenue is ~$147B for 2026 (+112% in a year) and above $175B for 2027; prices rose roughly 4.2–4.5x over three quarters, but in Q3 2026 the rise has already stopped (+0–5%).
nand.marketSizing.bomShare.note: server drives as a share of the whole segment's revenue: 43% in Q1 2026, passing 60% by year end. NAND's centre of gravity moved from phones and laptops to data centres in a single year.
nand.marketSizing.cagr: segment revenue ~$147B in 2026 (+112% in a year)
nand.marketSizing.chartTitle: NAND CONTRACT PRICE GROWTH, % PER QUARTER
nand.marketSizing.takeaway: The growth is entirely price rather than volume, and it has already stopped in Q3 — the first and most important signal for the decision. The AI theme here is real (server drives heading to 60%+ of revenue), but entering on a price plateau is not at all the same as entering a year ago.
nand.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.mix: The whole segment is put at ~$147B for 2026 and above $175B for 2027. But something else matters more: 2026 is the first year in which server drives outweigh the entire consumer side combined on revenue.
nand.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.price: Explosive growth, and already a stop: +58% in Q1 2026, +72% in Q2 (overtaking working memory for the first time), and just +0–5% in Q3. A concrete example: a 30 TB drive went from ~$3K to ~$17.5K over three quarters.
nand.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.volume: Volumes are barely growing: Micron's bit shipments rose by low single digits while prices rose 80%+. Kioxia said outright that its record came from price on FALLING shipments. AI storage demand grows around 40% a year while output grows only 14–17%: hence the shortage.
nand.supply.capacityAdds.0.detail: Investment is rising only 5% in a year (from $21B to $22B) — extremely parsimonious. There will be no new fabs before late 2027 or 2028.
nand.supply.capacityAdds.1.detail: The most aggressive: investment +41%, to $4.5B — for ramping new memory generations.
nand.supply.capacityAdds.2.detail: Deliberately holding NAND back to direct the money into more profitable AI memory. This is the main reason for the sector's discipline.
nand.supply.capacityAdds.3.detail: The only one adding meaningful capacity: around 150,000 wafers a month now and, on Reuters' reporting, potentially more than 450,000 by 2028.
nand.supply.crowdingOut: A separate and underrated driver: hard disks are sold out through the end of 2026, with contracts signed to 2028–29 and prices up roughly 46% since September 2025. Customers who could not get disks are forced to buy solid-state drives — additional demand not directly tied to AI.
nand.supply.leadTime: Volume growth comes not from new fabs but from adding storeys on existing lines: bit output grows around 17% a year against a historical 20–30%. New fabs will not yield product before late 2027 or 2028.
nand.supply.takeaway: The shortage holds through 2026 and probably into the first half of 2027 — the industry cannot and will not expand quickly. The turning point is named outright: H2 2027. The exit signal is spot prices turning and YMTC's output rising sharply.
nand.supply.utilization: The fabs are loaded and the makers' inventories are at an all-time low. At the same time capacity is deliberately not being expanded — the money is going into AI memory.
nand.tldr.0: The sharpest upswing in NAND's history (non-volatile memory): prices rose roughly 4.2–4.5x over three quarters, server drives delivered a record $18.5B in a quarter (+86%), and the segment reached record profitability for the first time.
nand.tldr.1: The driver is inference (a finished model at work, answering queries): models mostly read data, so they take cheap QLC memory (four bits in one cell — the lowest price per gigabyte) in large volumes. Kioxia and SanDisk demand 100% prepayment for 2027+ volumes.
nand.tldr.2: But this is the most cyclical and least protected part of memory: six makers instead of three, China heading toward ~19% of the market by 2027, balance restored in H2 2027 — and the shares already entered a bear market in late July 2026.
nand.unitEconomics.costCurve: Cost per gigabyte is reduced two ways: adding storeys and bonding finished wafer blocks. The paradox: the world record on storage density is held by China's YMTC despite its equipment restrictions — the leaders' technological lead is smaller here than in HBM.
nand.unitEconomics.grossMargin: The segment has become genuinely profitable for the first time in years: Kioxia at a 59.7% operating margin, SanDisk at 34% net, Micron at 84.9% gross. But these are peak values — historically NAND was the least profitable part of memory, and its prices only overtook working memory from Q2 2026.
nand.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: The average price rose 80%+ in a quarter, with server drives up roughly 80%. Concretely: a 30 TB data-centre drive went from ~$3K to ~$17.5K over three quarters, nearly 6x.
nand.unitEconomics.takeaway: Record profitability across the whole segment should be a warning rather than a comfort: the least profitable part of memory only sets records at a peak. More durable profit sits with the controllers: theirs grows from drives getting more complex rather than from the memory price.
nand.unitEconomics.yields.0.label: Operating leverage
nand.unitEconomics.yields.0.value: At its limit: Kioxia's operating profit rose 314% in a quarter on 84.5% revenue growth. It works in reverse too — when prices fall, profit folds just as fast.
nand.unitEconomics.yields.1.label: The gap between segments
nand.unitEconomics.yields.1.value: Server drives carry a high margin (SanDisk's data-centre revenue tripled in a quarter), while consumer NAND remains a thin-margin commodity.
nand.unitEconomics.yields.2.label: The historical norm
nand.unitEconomics.yields.2.value: NAND is historically the least profitable memory node. Today's 60–85% is the top of the cycle, not a new norm.
nand.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Next the constraint becomes the physics of the storeys: the taller the «building», the more the silicon wafer bows, the harder it is to align the layers and to remove heat. So the industry is moving to bonding finished blocks — and that raises the value of the equipment makers.
nand.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Output is capped not by equipment but by the makers' deliberate decision: they cut output across 2023–2025, and 2026 investment is rising only 5%. Samsung and SK Hynix are deliberately holding NAND back to throw resources at more profitable AI memory.
nand.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: A new fab costs more than $10B, and nobody is rushing to build one now: the money is going into AI memory. That parsimony is exactly what created the shortage — but it also means there will be no surplus capacity when demand turns.
nand.valueCapture.takeaway: Margins are at records everywhere right now, but they are of different quality: at the memory makers they are at a peak and will fall with prices, while at the controller and equipment makers (Silicon Motion, Phison, Lam) they are lower but more durable, growing from drives getting more complex rather than from the memory price.
nand.verdict.bear.0: China (YMTC, the Chinese NAND maker) is scaling output: China's share heads toward ~19% of all bits by 2027, with around $24B of state support, targeting the cheap segment where a glut forms first.
nand.verdict.bear.1: Six players and a cycle turn: balance is restored in H2 2027, and memory is already in a bear market — down more than 20% from the highs.
nand.verdict.bear.2: Structurally low margins and a re-rating that has already happened: NAND is historically the least profitable part of memory, and price growth in Q3 2026 has already stalled at 0–5%.
nand.verdict.bull.0: AI demand is structural rather than one-off: server drives went from 43% to 60%+ of segment revenue in a year, and Micron's server drive sales passed $5B in a quarter, doubling in three months.
nand.verdict.bull.1: The discipline is holding and hard disks are sold out: NAND investment is rising only 5% in a year, with a 4–5% shortfall through 2026, and hard disks are sold out through the end of 2026 with contracts running to 2028–29.
nand.verdict.bull.2: There is optionality on top: ultra-fast flash (samples in H2 2026), next-generation controllers, a possible Kioxia–Western Digital merger, and Micron's price-floor contracts through 2030.
nand.verdict.horizon: 6–18 months — the cycle is nastier than DRAM's; the key point is H2 2027, when on TrendForce's forecast supply catches demand.
nand.verdict.keyQuestion: Will server SSDs stay short — or will five makers plus China's YMTC return NAND to ordinary commodity economics by 2028?
nand.verdict.sizing: NAND segment revenue: ~$147B (2026, +112% in a year). Server SSDs go from 43% to 60%+ of revenue. Server SSD prices are +70%+ in a quarter.
nand.verdict.summary: The growth is at a maximum, but everything else runs against it. There are six makers rather than three and the product is standard — agreements on discipline have historically broken here first. The cyclicality is the worst in the whole memory complex, and the re-rating has already happened: individual names rose several-fold and in some cases tenfold in a year, after which a bear market began in late July. And the first sign of a turn is already visible — in Q3 2026 price growth stalled at 0–5%. Hence a 5: the theme is real, but the time to enter it was a year ago.
nand.whatIsIt: Memory that holds data without power: switch a server off and its working memory forgets everything, while this retains it. Per gigabyte it is several times cheaper than working memory but also slower, so its job is storing large volumes: it is what solid-state drives are made of, and they are displacing hard disks. In an AI data centre it is where the models themselves live, along with the data they read.
nuc.picks.0.group: Operating capacity and equipment — money today
nuc.picks.0.note: They monetise AI demand right now — through contracts on operating reactors or through scarce equipment and fuel, without betting on any particular new design.
nuc.picks.0.rows.0.exposure: the largest US nuclear fleet; contracts with Microsoft (the Crane/TMI restart) and Meta (Clinton, 1,121 MW, 20 years)
nuc.picks.0.rows.0.priced: P/E 26.7×; the AI premium is already substantial; regulatory risk and execution on large capital projects.
nuc.picks.0.rows.0.why: Operating round-the-clock generation plus the optionality of uprates, life extension and restarts. It moves output out of the spot market into long-term contracts with a premium for clean firm capacity.
nuc.picks.0.rows.1.exposure: Susquehanna + the Amazon contract of up to 1,920 MW to 2042
nuc.picks.0.rows.1.priced: Concentration in a few assets and one customer; regulatory disputes over co-location; sensitivity to plant outages.
nuc.picks.0.rows.1.why: Smaller than Constellation, so a single large contract moves EBITDA, debt capacity and the valuation much more. Amazon as an anchor customer removes market risk.
nuc.picks.0.rows.2.exposure: nuclear + gas + retail + storage in the data-centre growth regions
nuc.picks.0.rows.2.priced: P/E 24.5×; a less pure nuclear bet — the outcome depends on gas, weather and retail margins.
nuc.picks.0.rows.2.why: An AI system does not run on nuclear alone: it needs baseload, peaking, reserve and storage. Vistra earns on the general rise in prices and consumption, not on a single contract.
nuc.picks.0.rows.3.exposure: nuclear components, fuel, naval reactors, service
nuc.picks.0.rows.3.priced: P/E 46×; a premium for scarce nuclear manufacturing; the commercial upside may come slowly.
nuc.picks.0.rows.3.why: Picks and shovels: it participates across several reactor types and defence programmes — no need to guess which small reactor wins. Q2 2026: revenue $901.6M, backlog ~$8.4B.
nuc.picks.0.rows.4.exposure: uranium mining + the fuel cycle + a stake in Westinghouse
nuc.picks.0.rows.4.priced: Uranium cyclicality; long-term contracts slow the pass-through of spot prices; the valuation already reflects the nuclear revival.
nuc.picks.0.rows.4.why: Diversified Western exposure: it earns not only on the uranium price but on the industry's expansion (equipment and service through Westinghouse).
nuc.picks.1.group: The fuel bottleneck and small reactors — upside and risk
nuc.picks.1.note: A strategic shortage or technological optionality — but the valuations are high, and cash flow from small reactors mostly arrives after 2030.
nuc.picks.1.rows.0.exposure: American uranium enrichment and HALEU; a $900M DoE contract; a backlog of ~$2.3B
nuc.picks.1.rows.0.risk: Heavy dependence on the state; HALEU demand is tied to reactors actually being built; a P/E of ~68× — the strategic value is already in the price.
nuc.picks.1.rows.0.why: A rare regulated enrichment technology; the US wants to end its dependence on Russia; HALEU is needed by many new reactors.
nuc.picks.1.rows.1.exposure: small reactors + a model of owning the asset and selling the electricity to the customer
nuc.picks.1.rows.1.risk: It takes on construction, fuel, regulatory and financial risk; there is no large commercial fleet yet — the valuation already assumes serious future success.
nuc.picks.1.rows.1.why: It retains most of the reactor's economics across its whole life — potentially more attractive than simply selling reactors.
nuc.picks.1.rows.2.exposure: a listed pure-play small reactor developer
nuc.picks.1.rows.2.risk: The previous large project was cancelled on cost growth; loss-making; a large gap between technical progress and cash flow; shareholder dilution.
nuc.picks.1.rows.2.why: A long track record with the NRC and a well-known modular design; the ability to site several modules together.
nuc.picks.1.rows.3.exposure: the Xe-100 small reactor + TRISO fuel; backed by Amazon, up to 960 MW
nuc.picks.1.rows.3.risk: Licensing, the timeline of the first project, the cost of TRISO fuel, scaling up manufacturing. Private — no direct access.
nuc.picks.1.rows.3.why: A strong anchor customer (Amazon) and a fuel business of its own; a modular architecture.
nuc.picks.1.rows.4.exposure: advanced reactors; a contract with Google for a series of units
nuc.picks.1.rows.4.risk: The technology is unproven at commercial scale; timelines after 2030; a new fuel chain. Private — no direct access.
nuc.picks.1.rows.4.why: The first corporate contract for a fleet rather than a single demo project — learning carries across units.
nuc.thesis.bigIdea: The market reads «AI + nuclear» as a reactor renaissance and buys everything in sight — small reactor startups, uranium, enrichment. But the scarcest thing here is not fission technology or a new reactor: it is a gigawatt of round-the-clock capacity that is already built, licensed and connected to the grid. A new unit would deliver the same electricity, but in 7–15 years and for $6–10B; an operating one can be recontracted today — which is exactly what Microsoft, Meta and Amazon are doing, signing 15–20 year contracts. So up to 2030 the money goes to the owners of working plants (Constellation, Talen), to the fuel bottleneck (Centrus) and to equipment manufacturers (BWXT), not to futuristic reactors — and much of it is already in the price.
nuc.thesis.stream.0.t: A single AI campus is now an energy facility
nuc.thesis.stream.1.t: A modern AI campus needs anything from a few hundred megawatts to several gigawatts. A 1 GW campus consumes about as much in a year as one large nuclear reactor produces. So building a data centre is now not only GPUs and networking but negotiation with generating companies, [[power|grid operators|not generation, but connection]], regulators and [[transformers|transformer|the steel inside it]] suppliers. And the key metric is no longer the price of electricity per MWh but time to power: how many years it will take actually to connect the site.
nuc.thesis.stream.10.t: A plant's revenue is simple: MWh produced × price. A 1 GW reactor at a 92% capacity factor delivers ~8.06 million MWh a year. At $60/MWh that is ~$484M of revenue, at $100/MWh ~$806M. The difference between $60 and $100 is more than $320M of additional annual revenue from a single gigawatt of continuous capacity. That is exactly why a long-term AI contract can radically revalue an already-built nuclear asset: the owner gets high utilisation, predictable revenue, less commodity risk and a higher residual value for the plant.
nuc.thesis.stream.11.items.0.l: output of 1 GW at a 92% capacity factor per year
nuc.thesis.stream.11.items.0.n: the basis of a long-term contract
nuc.thesis.stream.11.items.1.l: revenue of 1 GW at $60 → $100 per MWh
nuc.thesis.stream.11.items.1.n: a spread of >$320M/yr from a single gigawatt
nuc.thesis.stream.11.items.2.l: the term of the hyperscalers' contracts
nuc.thesis.stream.11.items.2.n: a volatile spot price traded for a fixed cash flow
nuc.thesis.stream.12.t: Fast megawatts: licence extension, uprate, restart
nuc.thesis.stream.13.t: New reactors take a long time to build, so the relatively fast source of additional megawatts is the existing fleet, through three mechanisms. Licence extension: many units can run for 60–80 years after modernisation. An uprate is an upgrade that adds capacity (more efficient turbines, pumps, fuel): even +5% on a 1 GW reactor gives 50 MW — enough for a large AI site. Restarting closed units: the site, the interconnection and part of the staff already exist — cheaper than a new reactor, but with risk around equipment condition and licensing.
nuc.thesis.stream.14.items.0.l: a reactor's service life after modernisation
nuc.thesis.stream.14.items.0.n: faster and cheaper than a new unit
nuc.thesis.stream.14.items.1.l: the gain from an uprate on a 1 GW reactor
nuc.thesis.stream.14.items.1.n: enough for a large AI site
nuc.thesis.stream.14.items.2.n: a closed asset returns to service
nuc.thesis.stream.15.t: Why new large reactors will not save the day before 2030
nuc.thesis.stream.16.t: Conventional nuclear's main problem is not reactor physics but project execution: complex engineering, a shortage of skilled staff, expensive financing, weak serial production, lengthy licensing. The US Department of Energy puts a first-of-a-kind advanced reactor at $6,000–10,000 per kW — that is $6–10B for a 1 GW unit, and that is the overnight cost, before interest over the years of construction, delays and interconnection. Serial construction theoretically cuts that by ~40%, but a successful series has to be built first. Time to start-up is 7–15 years. So before 2030 a new large reactor physically does not solve the problem.
nuc.thesis.stream.17.items.0.n: $6,000–10,000 per kW — before interest and delays
nuc.thesis.stream.17.items.1.l: time to start-up for a new unit
nuc.thesis.stream.17.items.1.n: which is why it does not solve the problem before 2030
nuc.thesis.stream.17.items.2.l: potential cost reduction from a series
nuc.thesis.stream.17.items.2.n: but a successful series has to be built first
nuc.thesis.stream.18.t: Fuel is a scarcer link than uranium itself
nuc.thesis.stream.19.t: Investors often look only at the uranium price, but the strategic shortage is not in the ore — it is in conversion and enrichment. Many new reactors require HALEU, more highly enriched uranium; the Western commercial HALEU chain is limited, and historically the expertise sat with Russia. That creates a circular problem: without reactors there is no demand for HALEU, and without guaranteed fuel the reactors cannot be financed. State contracts are the attempt to break it.
nuc.thesis.stream.2.items.0.n: +465 TWh — the equivalent of ~53 GW of continuous generation
nuc.thesis.stream.2.items.1.n: the same as one large reactor produces
nuc.thesis.stream.2.items.2.l: data centres' share of world electricity by 2030
nuc.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: and the AI part of it will triple over that time
nuc.thesis.stream.20.t: The scale of the gap shows in the numbers. Even on a conservative estimate — counting only the reactors already planned — the US will need around 50 tonnes of HALEU a year by 2035, while only ~1 tonne is produced commercially today: a shortfall of almost 98%, meaning roughly 50 times more capacity is required. The most direct listed way to bet on this is Centrus Energy: effectively the only commercial HALEU producer in the US (it has already delivered ~900 kg to the Department of Energy), with a contract backlog of ~$2.3B and a $900M DoE contract; but even the expanded Piketon plant will only reach ~12 tonnes a year — so the gap is structural, not temporary. The second, early player is General Matter: a new entrant with DoE backing, but the company is private, so there is no direct access on the exchange.
nuc.thesis.stream.21.items.0.l: HALEU in the US: today → demand by 2035
nuc.thesis.stream.21.items.0.n: a ~98% shortfall; roughly 50× more capacity is needed
nuc.thesis.stream.21.items.1.l: Centrus's ceiling with an expanded Piketon
nuc.thesis.stream.21.items.1.n: still below demand — the gap is structural
nuc.thesis.stream.21.items.2.n: the market does not finance enough capacity on its own
nuc.thesis.stream.22.t: Equipment and service: a bet that requires no guess about the reactor
nuc.thesis.stream.23.t: The best-protected position is not to guess which reactor design wins but to supply what any of them needs: reactor vessels, valves, pumps, steam generators, fuel, inspection and service. That kind of nuclear-grade manufacturing requires certification and years of experience — not just any factory can enter. The key listed player is BWX Technologies: Q2 2026 revenue of $901.6M, net income of $89.1M, a backlog of ~$8.4B (plus the defence naval business as a foundation). The diversified analogue in fuel is Cameco (uranium + the fuel cycle + a stake in Westinghouse).
nuc.thesis.stream.25.t: The hidden risk: co-location and the allocation of grid costs
nuc.thesis.stream.26.t: Many of the deals are co-location: the data centre is placed right next to the plant to bypass the interconnection queue. The upsides are fewer new lines, a short path and high reliability. But that is also the source of the main regulatory argument: should such a customer pay for the shared grid; what about the electricity that previously went to other consumers; will household tariffs rise; will a giant block others' access to the plant. The allocation of system costs is one of the key constraints on the «nuclear → data centre» model. So future deals will probably be hybrids: a PPA + grid supply + transmission charges + reserve + customer investment in infrastructure.
nuc.thesis.stream.27.t: Where it is heading — and where the money is going
nuc.thesis.stream.28.t: Capital is already going into acquiring and revaluing operating generators, long-term PPAs, life extension, uprates, restarts, uranium enrichment, nuclear manufacturing, [[transformers|transformers and substations|the steel inside it]] and transmission. Global nuclear spending is still far below spending on renewables and fossil fuels: to meet the stated targets, annual nuclear investment would have to rise from roughly $75B to $250B.
nuc.thesis.stream.29.t: Over a 5–10 year horizon come the first commercial small reactors, HALEU plants, TRISO fuel production, standardised nuclear components, the conversion of coal sites to nuclear, and private microgrids for AI campuses. Small reactors (Oklo, NuScale, X-energy, Kairos) are probably the next big cycle, but after 2030; today they are technological and financial optionality, not cash flow.
nuc.thesis.stream.3.t: The scarcity is not energy in general, but round-the-clock power in the right place
nuc.thesis.stream.30.note: State programmes + direct corporate investment. The LPO's >$300B is a lending limit, not money disbursed.
nuc.thesis.stream.31.t: What is already in the price
nuc.thesis.stream.32.t: The AI-energy thesis is no longer a secret — much of it is already in the quotes. So simply buying «all of nuclear» can deliver poor risk-adjusted returns even if the sector forecast is right. The right question is not «is the forecast correct» but «will earnings grow faster than the market already expects».

nuc.thesis.stream.36.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
nuc.thesis.stream.37.t: AI is not creating the nuclear industry from scratch — it is raising the value of round-the-clock capacity that already exists and giving the industry a new customer who can pay. Before 2030 the main benefit goes to the owners of operating plants and to suppliers of fuel, equipment and grid infrastructure. Small reactors are probably the next big cycle, but after 2030; today they are optionality, not guaranteed cash flow.
nuc.thesis.stream.38.t: The conclusion: the scarcest thing here is neither uranium nor fission technology, but a licensed, grid-connected and physically available gigawatt of round-the-clock capacity. Constellation and Talen are the most direct bets on that today; BWXT and Cameco are the picks and shovels that require no guess about the reactor; Centrus is the strategic fuel bottleneck (but expensive); small reactors (Oklo, NuScale) are a small optional position, not the core. And almost everywhere the thesis is already partly in the price.
nuc.thesis.stream.39.head.1: What to cover the theme with
nuc.thesis.stream.39.note: Not a recommendation — a match of instrument to style; the decision is the investor's.
nuc.thesis.stream.39.rows.0.1: Constellation, Talen — owners of operating reactors with hyperscaler contracts
nuc.thesis.stream.39.rows.1.0: Neutral — not guessing the reactor design
nuc.thesis.stream.39.rows.1.1: BWXT, Cameco — equipment, fuel and service are needed whoever wins
nuc.thesis.stream.39.rows.2.0: A bet on the fuel bottleneck
nuc.thesis.stream.39.rows.2.1: Centrus — American enrichment and HALEU (but the valuation is high)
nuc.thesis.stream.39.rows.3.1: Vistra — nuclear + gas + storage in the growth regions
nuc.thesis.stream.39.rows.4.1: small reactors: Oklo, NuScale, and private X-energy/Kairos — in small positions, on a 2030+ horizon
nuc.thesis.stream.4.t: AI's problem is not producing more kilowatt-hours. The value lies in the ability to deliver a lot of energy, round the clock, at a specific point and within an acceptable timeframe. Nuclear fits that: the US nuclear fleet's capacity factor is above 90% (it runs almost without stopping), a single site delivers 1–2 GW on a small footprint, and fuel is a small share of the cost — which makes an already-built, partly depreciated reactor extremely valuable. Sun and wind are cheaper, but they do not provide guaranteed round-the-clock firm power without a multiple of surplus generation, batteries, gas backup and new lines.

nuc.thesis.stream.5.items.1.n: a small footprint, high power density
nuc.thesis.stream.5.items.2.n: the main cost is construction; a finished unit is especially valuable
nuc.thesis.stream.6.t: The main asset is the operating reactors, not the new ones
nuc.thesis.stream.7.t: Until recently many American reactors were struggling with low wholesale prices, cheap gas and subsidised renewable energy — some were at risk of early closure. AI has changed their owners' negotiating position: the hyperscalers are willing to sign 15–20 year contracts for guaranteed access to capacity. Below are the actual deals, not intentions.

The market prices pure-play lasers as if the 30% shortfall will never balance out — even though LightCounting expects it to balance as soon as end-2026.

photonics.expectations.takeaway: The fundamentals are at records across the chain, but the pure-play lasers trade with zero margin of safety — their price already embeds a permanent EML shortage. The anomaly is not that quality is expensive (it deserves to be) but that the market ignores the shortage balancing by end-2026. Playing the theme through Fabrinet and MACOM is cheaper and calmer.
photonics.expectations.verdict: Pure-play lasers (Coherent, Lumentum) — expensive; Fabrinet and MACOM — fair
photonics.expectations.weThink: Value does concentrate in EML/DSP rather than assembly, and the laser companies do win whatever the CPO outcome — that much is right. But 100x+ leaves no room for error: on 2 July 2026 AOI fell −17% and Coherent/Lumentum −10% in a day, out of nowhere. The disagreement is about horizon: the market pays for a permanent shortage, while we see it balancing by end-2026 and margins peaking. Fabrinet (an agnostic assembler) and MACOM (components, a 58.5% margin) give the same theme more cheaply.
photonics.intro:
Optics is needed in an AI cluster because copper has physically stopped coping. At 200 Gbit/s per lane an electrical signal on a copper wire decays within tens of centimetres, while servers have to be connected across metres and hundreds of metres. So data inside the cluster is converted into light: it travels through glass fibre with almost no loss and no distance limit. The device that performs that conversion is an optical transceiver; a scale-out network uses about six of them per GPU.

How it works. The signal passes through a chain of physical conversions. First a laser emits a continuous beam of light — made not on silicon but on indium phosphide (InP), because silicon barely emits light at all. A modulator then switches that beam on and off in time with the data bits, up to 200 billion times a second; in an EML design the modulator is built into the laser itself. A silicon-photonic die then combines several light channels of different wavelengths into one fibre. At the far end a photodetector turns the light back into a weak electrical signal, and a separate chip (an optical DSP) cleans it up and reconstructs it. The newest architecture is co-packaged optics: the optics sits right against the switch chip, removing the long electrical path to a pluggable module and saving up to 70% of the transmission energy.

The narrowest and most expensive point is the laser and its yield. Silicon does not emit light by its own physics, so the light source has to be made on indium phosphide wafers — a temperamental material with low yield, and only a handful of fabs worldwide can produce it in volume. Demand for such lasers exceeds supply by roughly 30% (LightCounting), and a production 200 Gbit/s-per-lane laser is essentially available from one supplier today. It is the laser that sets how many transceivers can physically be built: without it the finished silicon photonics, optical DSP and assembly all sit idle. This cannot be relieved quickly — moving from 3-inch InP wafers to 6-inch (4x+ more devices at half the cost per device) takes years of process development, not quarters.

Who pays, and how much. The shortage is so critical that in March 2026 Nvidia invested $2B directly into each of two key laser suppliers ($4B in total) — into light production specifically, not assembly. For the buyers this makes sense: optics is only ~3–5% of a compute node's cost, but without it the expensive GPUs cannot exchange data and sit idle, so lasers are paid for with almost no haggling. The modules themselves get cheaper as volume ramps (800G ~$360–450, 1.6T ~$1,300–1,500), but the value settles in the laser and the optical DSP rather than in assembly, where margins are thin.

The AI optics market: $16.5B (2025) → ~$26B (2026, +60%, LightCounting); the laser shortage is forecast to ease by late 2026 or early 2027.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.

photonics.mentalModel.framework: Optics connects the GPUs inside a cluster, and its volume grows with cluster size. The profit arises not in module assembly (which Chinese makers have mastered at thin margins) but in two scarce components inside it — EML/InP lasers and optical DSPs, which only a few companies in the world can produce. Control of those components (Coherent and Lumentum in lasers, Marvell and Broadcom in DSP) holds margins at 55–60%, while assembly gives most of the value away.
photonics.mentalModel.revenueFormula: Revenue = number of GPUs × ~6 transceivers per GPU × module price (rising each generation) × the share of value that stays in the laser/DSP
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.0.not: only a handful of companies in the world can get workable yield on 6-inch InP wafers. Coherent doubled its 6-inch InP in a year (Sherman, Texas), and Lumentum is the only 200G/lane EML supplier in volume. The ~30% physical shortfall is directly confirmed: Nvidia invested $4B in Coherent plus Lumentum.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.1.not: Marvell ~60–70% + Broadcom >30% = >90% of high-end PAM4. A 3 nm tape-out at $500M+ is an entry barrier. But LPO (modules without a DSP, 40–50% less power) takes a bite out of demand at the low end.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.2.not: qualifying a transceiver at a hyperscaler takes months; customers certify at least 3 sources per speed grade. Patent royalties run up to ~8% of ASP. But module assembly itself is competitive, so switching is possible.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.3.not: vertical integration of silicon photonics (InnoLight at ~70% of high-speed on SiPh) and foundry capacity (TSMC's COUPE, mass production in 2026) raise the bar. CPO packaging is a new layer of complexity where value migrates to the lasers and the SiPh foundry.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.4.not: InnoLight supplies ~80% of the 1.6T modules for Nvidia's GB200; incumbency is sticky. Nvidia's $2B into Coherent and $2B into Lumentum lock in laser supply for both pluggable and CPO.
photonics.moatBreakdown.components.5.not: the one obvious crack: assembly is commoditising. Chinese makers hold 7 of the top 10 places (63% of the market) at prices 20–25% below Western ones. China's share rose from 55.6% to 63.2% in a year. The «box» is getting cheaper — the value moves into the components.
photonics.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection rests not on the module but on what is inside it: EML/InP lasers and DSPs are physical and IP bottlenecks that China has not yet reproduced. Five of the six components are strong or strengthening; the weak link is assembly itself, and that is exactly what is being handed to China. The rule is simple: own the bottleneck (lasers, DSP), not the box.

photonics.problems.items.0.gap: Chinese module assemblers have grown explosively (InnoLight +192%, Eoptolink +187% of revenue), but the EML laser inside their modules is still Western or Japanese. Starting your own InP (indium phosphide) production at acceptable yield means years of process development and the capital for a fab; a qualified 200 Gbit/s laser cannot be replicated in a quarter or two. So the value settles in the laser rather than in assembly (assembly margins run ~8%, while Lumentum's laser margins are structurally higher and rising).
photonics.problems.items.0.problem: All of AI optics is constrained by one component — the EML laser on indium phosphide (InP, the material the light source inside every module is made from). Demand exceeds supply by roughly 30% (LightCounting), and at 200 Gbit/s per lane only Lumentum produces it in volume. Yield on InP wafers is low, and only a handful of fabs in the world can make them. Without the laser the rest of the module (silicon photonics, the DSP chip that reconstructs the signal, assembly) sits idle — it is the laser that sets how many modules can physically be built, and a scale-out network (linking servers) needs about 6 of them per GPU.
photonics.problems.items.0.solution: Moving from 3-inch InP (indium phosphide) wafers to 6-inch: a single wafer yields more than 4x the devices at half the cost per device. Coherent is building such a line in Sherman, Texas and in Zurich, and has tripled its InP output in a year with a plan to double again by end-2026. Lumentum is expanding EML laser capacity by more than 50% through its Japanese fab. LightCounting forecasts the shortage easing by late 2026 or early 2027. Beyond that, the co-packaged optics architecture (CPO — placing the light source right against the switch chip) removes part of the demand, but brings its own problem: yield and reliability in assembly (18 photonic dies in a single Quantum-X module).
photonics.problems.items.0.winners: Lumentum is the only supplier producing 200 Gbit/s per lane in volume, its Japanese fab is fully allocated, and its operating margin is rising toward 35–36%. Coherent is the only one with a full cycle (indium-phosphide lasers + silicon photonics + modules + CPO) and its own 6-inch InP lines. Both received $2B each from Nvidia in March 2026 — direct confirmation that the laser shortage is real and that the money is going straight to the scarcest link. They win because an indium-phosphide fab means decades of process development, not building a new hall.
photonics.problems.takeaway: Relieving the laser shortage strengthens the incumbent leaders: only Lumentum and Coherent have 6-inch indium-phosphide lines and a qualified 200 Gbit/s laser, and Nvidia's money goes straight to them. No newcomer appears here — the barrier is not assembly but the physics of producing indium phosphide.

photonics.roadmap.disruption.0.angle: Base case: pluggable survives to 2027–2028; CPO scales from 2028. The laser companies win in either scenario.
photonics.roadmap.disruption.0.detail: Nvidia's Spectrum-X CPO is in production (CoreWeave, Lambda, Oracle). Broadcom has Bailly/Davisson. CPO means 70% less optical power and 50%+ lower cost. But the module leaders (Coherent, Lumentum) supply the CPO lasers too.
photonics.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: Assembly is commoditising; value migrates to components (lasers, DSP, SiPh). InnoLight is the exception: SiPh vertical integration gives it pricing power.
photonics.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: Chinese makers hold 7 of the top 10. InnoLight >23%, Eoptolink no. 3. Prices 20–25% lower. Their share rose from 55.6% to 63.2% (2025). But the EML, DSP and TIA inside are almost all Western.
photonics.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: LPO is the cash cow of 2026–2027 for low-risk deployments. But at 200G/lane a DSP is still needed for coherent and DCI.
photonics.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: LPO: 40–50% less power, near-zero latency. >1/3 of 800G intra-data-centre by 2026–27. MACOM and Semtech win. Marvell/Broadcom: «re-timed and LPO coexist».

photonics.thesis.bigIdea: The next constraint on AI is not computation but moving data between chips. At high speeds copper burns ever more energy and loses signal, while clusters grow toward a million accelerators — and when the network cannot keep up, expensive GPUs sit idle. Optics carries data as light rather than electricity: more data per pass, over greater distance, at lower energy. The thesis is not that «copper disappears» but that optics moves step by step closer to the chip itself — from pluggable modules to bonding beside the chip and on to optical I/O at the GPU. And since the AI build-out's scarcest resource is electricity (and it is the frontier of the US–China race), whoever makes the interconnect more energy-efficient wins. The core names are Broadcom, Marvell and Coherent; the riskier bets are packaging (TSMC) and optical I/O (Ayar Labs).
photonics.thesis.stream.0.t: AI's next constraint is not computation but interconnect
photonics.thesis.stream.1.t: In the boom's first phase, performance grew through GPU count and data-centre size. The next limit is different: thousands and tens of thousands of accelerators must work as one machine and constantly exchange weights, gradients and activations. When the interconnect cannot keep up, an expensive accelerator sits idle waiting for data — and that is not an abstraction: training GPT-4 across 25K accelerators saw real utilisation fall to 32–36%, and a 100K-GPU cluster running at 60% utilisation instead of 90% loses on the order of $300M a year (an H100 costs ~$3–4 an hour). The question shifts from «who has the fastest chip» to «who assembles the most efficient system as a whole».
photonics.thesis.stream.10.t: Optics is already widely deployed in data centres — but as pluggable modules on the front panel of a switch. A switch is the device that binds servers into one network and routes data between them; a pluggable module is a small insert that turns an electrical signal into light and back. That is how servers, racks and whole buildings are connected at 400 → 800G → 1.6T (the throughput of a single channel). Everyone uses these [[transceivers|modules|optical transceiver]] — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, Oracle, xAI, CoreWeave. But a plug-in module on a panel is not yet optics bonded to the chip itself. And here is what matters: optics is starting to move inward — into the tight accelerator-to-accelerator links that used to run on copper.
photonics.thesis.stream.11.items.1.n: 2.6x in a year; components are the constraint
photonics.thesis.stream.11.items.2.n: it became the main solution on cost and energy
photonics.thesis.stream.12.t: Where it is going — optics moves closer to the chip
photonics.thesis.stream.13.t: The transition is not one leap but a series of steps, and they all point the same way: optics moves ever closer to the chip itself. First the light is created in a pluggable module on the switch panel; then the module is simplified; then the optics moves onto the board beside it; then right up against the chip's package; then it is bonded directly to the switch chip (this is what CPO — «optics in one package with the chip» — means); the next step is optics right at the GPU; and eventually optical interconnect at the level of a whole rack and data centre. Each step removes part of the long copper path and cuts energy use.
photonics.thesis.stream.14.rows.0.1: pluggable modules dominate; 800G ramps and 1.6T goes on sale; copper still holds the short links
photonics.thesis.stream.14.rows.1.1: the first CPO in top-end switches (Nvidia, Broadcom); 51.2–102.4 Tbit/s switches strain the panel
photonics.thesis.stream.14.rows.2.1: the inflection: chip-bonded optics in top-end switches, optical accelerator links between racks, optics right at custom accelerators
photonics.thesis.stream.14.rows.3.1: optics beside the GPU; memory disaggregated over optics; optical chiplets
photonics.thesis.stream.16.t: The main argument is energy. Bonding optics to the chip (CPO) shortens the path: switch chip → a short link → an adjacent photonic engine → fibre. Nvidia claims 3.5x the energy efficiency and 4x fewer lasers on its Spectrum-X Photonics platform, and a fifth of the energy per 1.6T port compared with pluggable modules, plus several times the reliability. At the scale of hundreds of thousands and a million GPUs, powering pluggable modules becomes untenable — and that is where CPO has a clear economic argument.
photonics.thesis.stream.18.t: Why this is a strategic frontier — energy and the race with China
photonics.thesis.stream.19.t: The AI build-out's scarcest resource is [[power|electricity|not generation, but connection]], and the interconnect takes a growing share of that budget. Whoever makes data transmission more energy-efficient fits more computation into the same megawatt — direct leverage in the US–China race, where energy is the constraint. The money confirms it: in just three months of 2026 Nvidia invested around $6.5B in photonics — $2B each into Coherent, Lumentum and Marvell (lasers and networking chips) and up to $3.2B into Corning (glass and fibre). The optical-I/O startup Ayar Labs drew competitors in together — Nvidia, AMD and MediaTek, in a $500M round. Strategics are entering optics before the winning standard is settled — a strong signal that everyone considers it strategically important.

photonics.thesis.stream.21.t: What it costs, what buyers will pay, and the order books
photonics.thesis.stream.22.t: The price of it. One 800G optical module costs roughly $900–1,300, and 1.6T about twice that; 2026 is being called «the year of 1.6T». Customers are willing to pay in advance: hyperscalers sign multi-year purchase agreements (Nvidia with Corning, up to $3.2B including purchases). Order books are already booked years out: Lumentum has more than $400M plus a separate several-hundred-million chip-bonded optics order for delivery in 2027; Coherent's orders run into 2028–2030 on a record book. So the demand is not a promise but contracted money.
photonics.thesis.stream.23.items.2.l: how far out Coherent's orders run
photonics.thesis.stream.24.t: Who is already using it, and what the leaders say
photonics.thesis.stream.25.t: CPO is no longer only a laboratory matter. Broadcom has assembled the Tomahawk 5-Bailly platform (a 51.2 Tbit/s switch with bonded optics) and calls it one of the first volume CPO deployments; its position is «the technology works, the question is the pace of adoption». Nvidia has built photonics into real platforms — Quantum-X (InfiniBand) and Spectrum-X (Ethernet) — meaning it treats CPO as part of the commercial roadmap rather than distant research. Marvell guides more cautiously — a meaningful inflection around 2028 — but has already shown 200 Gbit/s-per-lane optical engines and CPO for future switches. TSMC is building the COUPE packaging platform (photonic engine + SoIC + [[pkg|CoWoS|became the main event]]): its actions are a stronger signal than words.

photonics.thesis.stream.27.t: Who is betting on the future — optical I/O
photonics.thesis.stream.28.t: The most distant and most asymmetric link is optical I/O right at the compute chip. I/O is how a chip takes data in and sends it out; making it optical means converting data to light at the chip itself. Serious money has already arrived. Ayar Labs (the TeraPHY chiplet, mounted beside a GPU, CPU or [[asic|custom accelerator|earns on every chip]]) has raised $870M — $500M of it in 2026 at a $3.75B valuation — and is ramping volume production; its investors include Nvidia, AMD, Intel, GlobalFoundries, Applied Materials and MediaTek. Lightmatter (the Passage platform) has raised $850M at a $4.4B valuation, with Google and T. Rowe Price among its investors. And Celestial AI (optical links to memory) has already been bought by Marvell — for ~$3.25B, up to $5.5B on revenue milestones. Volume shipments are still small — these are bets on 2028–2030+ — but large capital and the buyers themselves are already in.
photonics.thesis.stream.3.t: Why copper is hitting its limit
photonics.thesis.stream.30.t: The most durable value is wherever it is needed under any standard. Lasers: every architecture needs light, so the laser makers (Coherent, Lumentum) are least dependent on who wins. Packaging is the main constraint: few can align optics and electronics to within fractions of a micron ([[pkg|TSMC, BESI, ASMPT|became the main event]]). Networking chips and SerDes (Broadcom, Marvell) benefit from co-designing the switch and the optics. [[test|Test|hardware and software]] gets more valuable, because one package now holds expensive electronics and optics together. And the modules themselves (Innolight, Eoptolink, Fabrinet) are the near-term beneficiaries — but they are precisely where CPO takes value away into integrated engines.
photonics.thesis.stream.31.t: With what confidence — a map of the bets

photonics.thesis.stream.34.t: Pluggable modules may get cheaper and better, delaying the move to CPO. Operators value serviceability: a failed module is swapped in a minute, while a failed photonic engine inside a package means an expensive repair of the whole switch. Then there is heat (optics is sensitive to warmth beside a hot chip), the yield of complex packages, vertical integration (Nvidia, Broadcom and the hyperscalers could take optics in house and squeeze the independents), module commoditisation against Chinese capacity, standards fragmentation, and high valuations — a correct thesis earns nothing if the price already embeds rapid adoption.

photonics.thesis.stream.38.t: The thesis is not that «copper disappears» but that interconnect becomes AI's constraint, and optics moves step by step closer to the computation — to the switch, to the accelerator, to memory. The optical content per system grows, and new pools of value appear: lasers, photonic engines, packaging, test, optical I/O. And since the frontier is energy, photonics is also strategic leverage in the US–China race; capital is already flowing there.
photonics.thesis.stream.39.t: There is no single «right» name here — there is an instrument to suit your style. Below is not an instruction to buy X through Y but a map: what to cover the theme with, depending on what you are willing to take on. One risk is common to all of them — that pluggable modules last longer and that Nvidia and the hyperscalers take optics in house.
photonics.thesis.stream.4.t: Copper does not stop working all at once — it just becomes harder and costlier to use. The industry is moving from 100 to 200 Gbit/s per electrical lane, and at those speeds attenuation, loss, crosstalk and heat all rise. Preserving the signal takes retimers, complex digital processing, thicker cables, shorter traces, more power and more cooling. In an ordinary switch the path is long: switch chip → a long board trace → a connector → a pluggable optical module → fibre. It is that electrical stretch that hits the limit.
photonics.thesis.stream.40.head.1: What to cover the theme with

photonics.thesis.stream.6.label: ALTERNATIVES TO OPTICS
photonics.thesis.stream.6.t: Over short distances copper still holds: direct copper cables (up to ~2 m) and active copper cables are cheaper than optics. And «linear» optical modules — simplified and cheaper than the usual kind — delay the move to expensive chip-bonded optics. Those are optics' real competitors.
photonics.thesis.stream.8.t: Silicon photonics uses semiconductor manufacturing to build the parts that create, guide, modulate and capture light. Electrical data is turned into an optical signal: laser → modulator (encoding data into light) → waveguide → multiplexer (combining several wavelengths into one fibre) → fibre → photodetector → back to an electrical signal. Silicon itself emits light poorly, so the lasers are made from a different material (indium phosphide). A separate and hardest part is packaging: the photonic die, the electronic control chip, the laser and the fibres must be aligned to within fractions of a micron.
photonics.tldr.0: The AI/Ethernet optics market (Ethernet being the mass networking standard): $16.5B (2025) → $26B (2026, +60%). Shipments of modules at 800G and above (the number is speed, gigabits per second): 24M (2025) → 63M (2026, 2.6x). Three generations (800G/1.6T/3.2T) are ramping at the same time rather than in sequence.
photonics.tldr.1: The hyperscalers (the largest cloud companies) are integrating vertically: investing in module makers to lock in supply. That signals how strategically important optics is to AI clusters.
photonics.tldr.2: InnoLight is the world's no. 1 in optical modules (>23% share): ~80% of the 1.6T modules for Nvidia's GB200. Q1 2026 revenue +192% y/y. Chinese makers hold 7 of the top 10 places, but the EML lasers, the DSP (the chip that reconstructs the signal) and the TIA (the amplifier for the weak signal from the photodetector) inside their modules are almost all Western or Japanese.
photonics.tldr.3: Co-packaged optics (CPO — optics built right against the switch chip, removing the long electrical path to a pluggable module) is the next shift: Nvidia's Spectrum-X went into production (May 2026), and Broadcom has Davisson 102.4T. CPO cuts optics power consumption by ~70%, but the module leaders (Coherent, Lumentum) supply the lasers for CPO too. The main question: does the value stay in the module, or move into the chip package?

photonics.unitEconomics.takeaway: Margins are best in DSP (Marvell ~59%, MACOM ~59%) and lasers (Lumentum expanding). Module assembly is thinner, but InnoLight and Eoptolink hold 40–48% on SiPh integration. 1.6T is structurally accretive. CPO lowers the cost of optics, but the value migrates to lasers, SiPh and switch silicon.
photonics.update.bottomLine: AI optics is one of the fastest-growing subsegments (Ethernet +60%, 800G+ 2.6x). The EML bottleneck is confirmed by Nvidia's $4B. CPO is shipping but additive — the laser companies win in either scenario. Enter on drawdowns (as on 2 July): the fundamentals are at records, but 100x+ P/E means zero margin of safety.

photonics.verdict.summary: One of the fastest-growing subsegments in semiconductors: AI optics +60% in 2026, Lumentum +90%, InnoLight +192%. Deep competitive advantages in EML/InP lasers (indium-phosphide lasers, which generate the light signal itself) and in the DSP duopoly (the chip that cleans up and reconstructs the signal on receive). But co-packaged optics (CPO — optics built into the switch chip's package) threatens pluggable modules after 2028, Chinese assembly dominates (63% of the market), and valuations are sky-high (Coherent/Lumentum at 100–158x forward earnings). The answer: own the scarcest link (lasers, DSP chip IP), not the box (module assembly).
photonics.whatIsIt: A small device that turns data into short flashes of light and sends them down a thin glass strand from one server to another. Copper wire cannot carry the signal at these speeds — it decays within tens of centimetres, while servers in an AI cluster have to be connected across metres and hundreds of metres, so data inside the cluster travels as light. Each compute chip needs about six of these light converters: without them the expensive chips cannot exchange data and sit idle.

Second suppliers take the overflow, not the market.

pkg.intro:
Advanced packaging is the final assembly of an AI accelerator from several separate dies into one package. Processors used to be made as a single piece of silicon that got cheaper with every generation. That no longer works: transistors have all but stopped getting cheaper, and a lithography tool prints a rectangle of limited area in one pass (~858 mm²) — a large AI processor no longer fits inside it. So it is cut into several smaller dies and assembled together with HBM memory stacks on a shared base. Without this assembly a modern accelerator physically does not exist.

How it works. Compute dies and memory stacks are produced separately at leading-edge fabs, and then have to be joined to each other over a very short distance and at very high connection density. To do that they are mounted not directly on a board but on an intermediate silicon interposer. It carries tens of thousands of ultra-fine wires — denser than an ordinary board allows — and it is those wires that connect processor to memory at the required speed. The sequence runs: (1) the dies are mounted on the interposer, aligned to within microns and bonded across thousands of contacts at once; (2) the assembled block is seated on an organic package substrate; (3) the whole thing is encapsulated in a protective compound, ground flat and tested. Once encapsulated, a package cannot be taken apart.

Why this comes down to yield and capacity. What matters here is not the ability to assemble but the share of packages assembled without defects. The larger the interposer, the more it warps when heated and the more often contacts break: a large monolithic silicon interposer yields around 60% against ~90% for the version using local silicon bridges — which is why the industry is moving to bridges. The cost of a single error is high: if a package is scrapped, neither the processor nor the memory can be recovered from it — ~$4,000–4,600 of components are lost, and in the worst case the full chip value ($5,700–7,300). So the winner is whoever assembles most cleanly at maximum volume. The second constraint is capacity itself: there is essentially one assembly line for the whole leading-edge AI class, the queue for it runs from one to three years (52–156 weeks), and building a new line takes about 18 months.

Who pays, and how much. Demand has nearly tripled in two years: from 370K wafers (2024) to ~1M (2026). The price of assembling one wafer has reached ~$10K — as much as the leading-edge processor silicon itself costs — and was raised several times by 10–20% across 2025–2026. Customers pay in advance to stake out volume: in summer 2026 one of them put $1.5B of prepayments with a contractor against future deliveries. The holder of the key technology directs 10–20% of all its capex to packaging and related work — on a total 2026 budget of $60–64B, that is roughly $6–13B a year. They pay with almost no haggling: without this assembly a finished chip cannot be produced, and its share of the chip's cost (~15%) is in any case smaller than the cost of missing the delivery entirely.

Market structure. The high-end AI packaging segment grows about 23% a year and reaches ~$28B by 2030 (Yole estimate). Concentration is extreme: essentially the whole AI class is assembled by one player (TSMC, the CoWoS technology), with the simpler final part of the work handed to a few neutral contractors.

pkg.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: TSMC is 12–24 months ahead across the whole chain of assembly + interposer + 3D bonding, and assembles most cleanly: yield on large packages runs 65–95%, and it is the spread in scrap that decides the profit. When a single error costs thousands of dollars, the cleanest producer wins.
pkg.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: the film for package substrates is made effectively by Ajinomoto alone (almost the whole world), and high-precision die dicing almost monopolistically by Disco. These are real monopolies at the input, and they underwrite the economics of the whole link regardless of the fight for orders.
pkg.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: 11 packaging plants in Taiwan; output nearly doubles across 2026 (from ~75K to 120–140K wafers a month). But it is TSMC's scale that drives supply up and shrinks the shortage itself.
pkg.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: handing assembly to a new contractor means re-qualifying the chip over several quarters, plus the queue itself. But the protection is weakening: Nvidia itself paid Amkor $1.5B of prepayments so that a second supplier would exist outside TSMC.
pkg.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: Besi and ASMPT between them hold about half the bonding-machine market; Besi works alongside Applied Materials at TSMC. The larger the package, the more precision matters — this layer strengthens with every generation.
pkg.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the main crack: an assembly plant takes ~18 months to build (it used to be 3–5), Intel and Samsung are entering as alternatives, and the shortfall has already halved. Plus the shift to panels and glass bases after 2028 could redeal the cards among substrate suppliers.
pkg.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is real at TSMC (leadership on scrap and on the whole chain) and at the equipment and materials makers (Besi, Disco, Ajinomoto), but weak at the independent assembly houses, where the work is closer to contract labour. Unlike memory, supply here is relieved fast and paid for by the customers themselves — a less impregnable monopoly.

pkg.picks.0.rows.1.priced: ~55x, +164% in a year — the quality is real, but the price already reflects it in full.
pkg.picks.0.rows.1.why: The best layer on margin, and it earns however the shares split among the assemblers. Leverage on the shift to hybrid bonding.
pkg.picks.0.rows.2.exposure: the second large maker of assembly equipment
pkg.picks.0.rows.2.priced: Cyclical; part of its revenue is outside AI. Cheaper than Besi, but the position is weaker too.
pkg.picks.0.rows.2.why: Direct leverage on next-generation hybrid bonding; it wins alongside rising package complexity.

pkg.picks.1.note: A genuine shortage, but priced as a permanent monopoly on a 14–26% contract margin. They fall hardest in a cycle.

pkg.picks.1.rows.0.why: Profit +90% in a year, takes 40–50% of the overflow on basic assembly, advanced packaging above $3.5B in 2026.
pkg.picks.1.rows.1.exposure: the no. 2 independent assembler; the Arizona plant, Nvidia's $1.5B prepayment
pkg.picks.1.rows.1.risk: Meaningful revenue only from 2029; a 14% gross margin; ~37x for a contractor's position.
pkg.picks.1.rows.1.why: A real second source for Nvidia; a $7B plant in the US.
pkg.picks.1.rows.2.exposure: its own assembly technology; first external orders in H2 2026
