pkg.picksTakeaway: The constraint is real, but it should be bought through the layer where the margin stays: TSMC (a monopoly plus a fab) and equipment (Besi, ASMPT). The re-rated assembly houses (ASE ~56x, Amkor ~37x) are a monopoly price for contract work and a crowded bet on a finite shortage; they fall hardest in a cycle.
pkg.problems.items.0.gap: Second suppliers are real but arrive slowly: Amkor's $7B Arizona plant yields output only from early 2028 and meaningful revenue from 2029; TSMC's US plant is also 2029. To hand assembly to a new contractor, the chip must be re-qualified — several quarters, plus the queue itself. TSMC's 12–24 month lead across the whole chain makes the core — large AI packages — nearly impossible to capture.
pkg.problems.items.0.problem: All AI-accelerator assembly comes down to one technology — TSMC's advanced CoWoS packaging (processor and memory assembled on a shared silicon substrate): without it an Nvidia accelerator physically cannot be built. TSMC holds nearly 100% of AI-class assembly, the queue runs from 52 to 156 weeks (up to three years), the price has reached ~$10K a wafer, and the shortfall in 2025 was ~20%. Demand has nearly tripled: 370K wafers (2024) → ~1M (2026). The most delicate point inside it is the large silicon interposer (an intermediate wafer carrying thousands of connections between chips): the bigger the package, the more it warps and the more scrap it produces — which is why Nvidia had to cancel the largest version of a future chip.
pkg.problems.items.0.solution: TSMC is expanding its 11 packaging plants in Taiwan: output rises from roughly 75K to 120–140K wafers a month across 2026. The key advantage over memory is that an assembly plant takes ~18 months to build rather than 2–3 years, so the shortage clears faster. The large-interposer problem is routed around with the CoWoS-L variant: instead of one monolithic silicon wafer, local silicon bridges are used (small silicon inserts only where dense connection is needed). Customers fund second suppliers with prepayments — Nvidia put $1.5B with Amkor against future volume. The assembly equipment itself is made by Besi and ASMPT (thermocompression and hybrid die bonding — joining chips under pressure and heat), the grinding and dicing by Disco, the encapsulation by Towa.
pkg.problems.items.0.winners: TSMC (NYSE: TSM) — holds nearly the whole AI class and is 12–24 months ahead of competitors across the chain of assembly + substrate + 3D bonding. But the main margin sits not in the assembly itself but in the equipment: Besi (AMS: BESI) at a 62% gross margin, and ASMPT (HKG: 522), where every bonding tool is a barrier of its own. The independent contractors Amkor and ASE take only the overflow that TSMC deliberately hands to «neutral» players, and earn just 14–26% gross on it — their work is closer to contract labour.
pkg.problems.takeaway: Relieving this shortage strengthens the incumbent leader — TSMC and the equipment makers (Besi, ASMPT) — not the independent assembly houses. But unlike memory, diversification has already begun and is paid for by the customer itself (Nvidia's prepayment), so this is a barrier that gradually weakens rather than one that holds forever.
pkg.risks.0.note: The main risk of the theme. Amkor +336% in a year, Ibiden ~+500%, AT&S ~+1140%, Besi on a forward P/E of ~55. The easy money is made; any disappointment brings a sharp fall.
pkg.risks.1.note: Nvidia is ~60% of demand, TSMC is nearly all of production. A double dependence: on one buyer and on one supplier.
pkg.risks.2.note: Nearly all AI-class assembly is physically in Taiwan. A stoppage would collapse accelerator output worldwide. Alternatives arrive slowly: Amkor in the US in 2028, TSMC in 2029.
pkg.risks.3.note: TSMC's expansion plus overflow to the contractors plus Intel and Samsung could level the market. The first sign is already there: output growth slows to ~26% a year.
pkg.risks.4.note: Calmer than memory, but the shares are high-beta: Amkor lost 34% in the 2025 tariff shock and 30% in a single month. The semiconductor index has fallen 30%+ in every cycle for 30 years.
pkg.risks.5.note: Failing to master the shift to panels, glass or still larger packages. The limit has already shown itself: Nvidia had to cancel the largest version of its chip.
pkg.risks.6.note: Practically ruled out: it takes enormous investment, years of learning through scrap, and scale. Customers prefer to pay in advance (Nvidia's $1.5B prepayment) rather than build their own.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.0.angle: This is not a threat to packaging as a whole but a change of suppliers: the losers are the makers of today's substrates — Ibiden (TYO: 4062), Unimicron (TPE: 3037), AT&S (VIE: ATS) — which are precisely the names that rose most. An important risk if you hold them.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.0.detail: At large package sizes the familiar organic substrate starts to warp and no longer holds its geometry. Glass is stiffer and flatter. Closest to volume is Absolics (an SKC division) with its Georgia plant, followed by Samsung (after 2027) and LG (2028); the glass itself comes from Corning, AGC and SCHOTT.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.0.tech: Glass bases instead of ordinary substrates
pkg.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: The main technology risk in this link. It undercuts the «bigger package = more revenue» growth plan, but at the same time raises the value of those who can solve the precision problem — Besi's and ASMPT's equipment, and glass bases.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: The larger the package, the more it warps under heat and the more scrap it produces. That is exactly why, according to one industry source, Nvidia cancelled the largest version of a future chip (4 dies) and replaced it with one half the size. This is the first case of packaging constraining chip architecture.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: Does not affect the decision. Cutting a chip into pieces is not the problem — it is precisely the industry's answer to the size limit.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: An alternative approach: rather than cutting the chip into pieces, make one enormous one. It works at individual companies but stays a niche — the volumes are not comparable to ordinary assembly and are unlikely to become so.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.3.angle: More of a plus: it makes assembly harder and raises its price, which increases this link's revenue. The same TSMC and its contractors win.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.3.detail: The light source is placed inside the package, next to the processor, so data leaves «straight from the chip» as light. TSMC begins volume production in 2026, and Amkor already has three such projects.
pkg.roadmap.disruption.3.verdict: a new market, not a threat
pkg.roadmap.generations.0.note: The Nvidia H100 and Google chip generation. Cheaper, but already at its size limit.
pkg.roadmap.generations.1.note: The current generation (Nvidia's Blackwell and Rubin, AMD's MI400). It costs 3–4x the basic version — the main revenue driver of this link.
pkg.roadmap.generations.2.note: A bigger package still, and more memory. The larger the package, the more the precision-bonding equipment matters — Besi and ASMPT win.
pkg.roadmap.generations.3.note: This is where package warping physics starts: the technology risk is real (see the cancellation of the largest Rubin version).
pkg.roadmap.generations.4.gen: Panel assembly instead of a round wafer
pkg.roadmap.generations.4.note: On a round wafer the edges go to waste; a rectangular panel uses the area more fully. It reshuffles the balance of power in equipment.
pkg.roadmap.takeaway: The technology sells itself: each package generation costs 3–4x the last, so revenue grows even without more chips. But two warnings: the physical package-size limit has already shown itself, and the shift to glass bases could wipe out the advantage of today's substrate makers.

pkg.scenarios.cases.1.note: the shortage holds through 2027 and melts gradually, package content grows (5.5 → 9.5 fields), TSMC holds its share. Revenue growth is eaten by the de-rating of high multiples
pkg.scenarios.cases.2.name: Bull
pkg.scenarios.cases.2.note: the shortage holds longer, packages grow to 14 fields, in-package optics and panels raise the assembly price; equipment (Besi, ASMPT) accelerates on orders
pkg.scenarios.expectedReturn: ~+5…+8%/yr (probability-weighted) — but with a wide spread and worse asymmetry than in less-played links
pkg.scenarios.takeaway: The upside is capped by the fact that the shares are already up 5–12x, while the downside from the re-rating is large — the asymmetry is skewed downward. The only way to soften it is name selection: TSMC and equipment (Besi, Disco, Towa) plus the laggards (Onto, Powertech) instead of the re-rated assembly houses.
pkg.supply.capacityAdds.0.detail: 11 packaging plants in Taiwan; output rises from roughly 75K to 120–140K wafers a month across 2026. A US plant only by 2029.
pkg.supply.capacityAdds.1.detail: A $7B Arizona campus: construction to mid-2027, output from early 2028, meaningful revenue from 2029. Funded in part by Nvidia's prepayment.
pkg.supply.capacityAdds.2.detail: Expanding in Taiwan and Malaysia, ~$6B invested over a year.
pkg.supply.capacityAdds.3.detail: Building their own assembly as an alternative to TSMC: Intel expects first orders in H2 2026, and Samsung's plant is already fully loaded.
pkg.supply.crowdingOut: The first sign of a slowdown is already there: TSMC's assembly output growth slows to ~26% year on year in 2026, where volumes used to double.
pkg.supply.leadTime: The key difference from memory: an assembly plant takes ~18 months to build — it used to be 3–5 years. An ordinary chip fab takes 2–3 years. So an assembly shortage is far easier and faster to relieve than a memory shortage.
pkg.supply.takeaway: The shortage holds through 2027, but it is melting: the gap has already halved. This is not a «shortage forever» story the way memory is. The exit signal is the queue falling below 40 weeks or the shortfall dropping below 5%.
pkg.supply.utilization: The plants are running flat out: ~90% at the independent contractors, and TSMC's AI-class assembly is effectively at 100%, all of it booked.
pkg.thesis.bigIdea: Advanced packaging (CoWoS) is the real physical constraint on the whole AI build-out: without it no accelerator can be assembled, TSMC holds nearly 100%, and the queue is booked three years out. But the market overdid it: independent assembly houses are up 5–12x and trade at 50–70x earnings — as if the shortage were permanent. It is not; it clears faster than memory, and packaging's share of chip cost is actually falling (from 19% to 15%). The constraint is real — but it should be bought through whoever keeps the margin (TSMC and Besi's equipment), not through re-rated assembly contractors.
pkg.thesis.stream.1.t: You can design a chip (in [[eda|chip software|impossible to route around]]), print it on [[litho|ASML's machines|impossible to replicate]] and build [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] memory stacks beside it — and still not ship an accelerator. Because the last step — joining the compute die and the memory stacks on one substrate so data can fly between them — is exactly what became the constraint on the whole AI build-out. Demand for that assembly has nearly tripled in two years, and TSMC's queue for it is booked three years ahead.
pkg.thesis.stream.10.t: Who holds the market — and who gets TSMC's overflow
pkg.thesis.stream.11.t: TSMC does ~100% of AI-class assembly. Of Nvidia's ~595K wafers for 2026, TSMC assembles ~510K itself and deliberately passes the overflow to «neutral» contractors (Amkor, SPIL) — specifically so the orders do not go to its rival Samsung. Amkor is building a $7B plant in Arizona (output from 2028; Nvidia put down $1.5B of prepayments in July 2026). ASE/SPIL take 40–50% of the overflow on basic assembly.

pkg.thesis.stream.15.t: And here is what is interesting: the constraint is real, but the margin does not sit where the market is looking. Independent assembly houses (ASE, Amkor) run on gross margins of just 14–26% — their work is closer to contract labour. The real margin sits with the equipment maker Besi (62% gross) and with TSMC itself (66–68%).

pkg.thesis.stream.18.t: What the market thinks: «the shortage is forever»
pkg.thesis.stream.19.t: The market saw a shortage and bought it as permanent pricing power. Assembly houses and materials makers are up 5–12x in a year (Amkor +336%, Ibiden ~+500%, AT&S ~+1140%) and now trade at 50–70x earnings (Besi ~55x, ASE ~56x, Ibiden ~70x). The bet is simple: constraint = forever.

pkg.thesis.stream.22.t: Three things the euphoria misses. First: the shortage is finite and clears faster than memory. TSMC is doubling assembly capacity, Amkor and Intel add a second source from 2028, and new methods (silicon bridges, panel-level assembly) take part of the load off. Historically assembly houses fell 30–50% in a cycle.
pkg.thesis.stream.23.t: Second, and this is the main point: packaging's share of an AI chip's cost is not rising but falling — from 19% two years ago to 15% today, because [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] memory rose in price several times faster. The constraint is here, but the money accumulates in memory. You pay a scarcity premium on a shrinking share.
pkg.thesis.stream.24.t: Third, the margin structure: what rose most was precisely the assembly houses, and that is a low-margin contract layer (14–26%), not a monopoly. Buying ASE at 56x earnings is paying a monopoly price for contract work.
pkg.thesis.stream.25.t: The constraint is real — but the easy money is made. Our difference with the market is not about demand, but about the fact that the price already treats the shortage as permanent when it is finite.
pkg.thesis.stream.26.t: What is priced in — and how to buy this properly
pkg.thesis.stream.27.t: The verdict breaks down by layer. The assembly houses (ASE ~56x, Amkor ~37x) are priced for a permanent shortage that is finite — expensive. TSMC (66–68% margin, a genuine monopoly) and equipment (Besi, 62% margin, earning however the shares split) are the fair way to own the same constraint.

pkg.thesis.stream.29.t: Put simply: own the constraint through the layer where the margin stays (TSMC and equipment), not through re-rated assembly houses priced as a permanent monopoly.
pkg.thesis.stream.3.t: What «packaging» is and why it became the main event
pkg.thesis.stream.30.t: Where the technology is going — and where the money is going
pkg.thesis.stream.31.t: Technically, packaging moves up a clear ladder, and every step reshuffles the winners. Today it is 2.5D assembly (chip and memory on a shared interposer). When a large monolithic interposer hits physics, the industry moves to silicon bridges, then to panel-level assembly (rectangular panels instead of round wafers — more area and cheaper per package) and glass substrates (flatter and larger, for giant packages). The end goal is 3D assembly (logic mounted directly on logic through direct bonding, with no solder). The larger and denser the package, the more it matters who mastered the next step first.
pkg.thesis.stream.32.t: Where the money is going: TSMC is doubling assembly capacity (~70K → ~140K wafers a month) and building several new packaging plants. Amkor is putting $7B into an Arizona plant, and Nvidia has placed $1.5B of prepayments there to stake out future volume. Intel is investing in its own packaging as a way back into the game — it talks of deals worth «billions a year». The equipment makers (Besi, ASMPT) are investing in direct bonding (hybrid bonding), the next big transition. And the hyperscalers pay up front to guarantee themselves a place in the queue.

pkg.thesis.stream.33.items.2.n: content grows — revenue on the same number of chips
pkg.thesis.stream.34.t: What the key players are betting on: TSMC — on being first to master every next step (silicon bridges, 3D assembly) and staying a monopoly. Nvidia — on staking out capacity with prepayments while spreading orders across a second and third source (Amkor, Intel, Samsung) so as not to depend on one supplier. Intel and Samsung — on packaging as the route back to the top tier: you can compete here even while behind on transistors. The equipment makers — on direct bonding, which 3D assembly requires. The next battlefield is not the substrate itself but direct bonding and glass bases.
pkg.thesis.stream.35.t: The market's attention and its capital are converging here: packaging has gone from a boring finale to the place that decides how many AI chips exist at all. But the winner is not whoever's share price rose loudest — it is whoever masters the next step first and holds the margin, and that list can change at every transition.

pkg.thesis.stream.39.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
pkg.thesis.stream.4.t: Packaging used to be the boring last step — «put the chip in a case». It is now the hardest stage. A modern accelerator is not one chip but a compute die plus 6–8 [[hbm|HBM|decoupled from the cycle]] memory stacks, which must sit millimetres apart on a shared silicon interposer (a tiny «board» cut from silicon) so data moves between them instantly. That assembly is what CoWoS means. Without it the fastest GPU and its memory simply cannot be joined, and with each generation the package gets larger and more complex.
pkg.thesis.stream.40.t: Advanced packaging is a real physical toll gate on the AI chip: without it no accelerator can be assembled, TSMC holds nearly all of it, and the queue is booked three years out. But the market has already priced that shortage as permanent — and it is finite, clears faster than memory, and packaging's share of chip cost is actually falling (19% → 15%). And what rose loudest was precisely the low-margin contract layer, not the monopoly itself.
pkg.thesis.stream.41.t: The conclusion: own the constraint through the layer where the margin stays — TSMC (a monopoly plus a fab) and the equipment makers (Besi, ASMPT), who earn however the shares split. The re-rated assembly houses (ASE, Amkor at ~50x for a 14–26% contract margin) are a crowded bet on a finite shortage, and they fall hardest in a cycle.

pkg.thesis.stream.6.t: Why it all comes down to scrap
pkg.thesis.stream.7.t: The whole economics of this link is about yield. A large monolithic interposer is hard to make without defects: ~60% yield against ~90% for the version using silicon bridges (small silicon links embedded in the substrate instead of one large monolithic wafer) — which is why the industry moved to silicon bridges at larger sizes. And the cost of one error is enormous: if a package is scrapped, neither the processor nor the memory can be recovered — $4,000–4,600 of components are lost, and in the worst case the whole chip ($5,700–7,300).

pkg.thesis.stream.9.t: Whoever assembles most cleanly takes the profit — and that is TSMC: 12–24 months ahead, 11 packaging plants and the whole chain tuned. The next constraint will be physics itself: at very large package sizes the package starts to warp and scrap rises — according to an industry source, that is precisely why Nvidia cancelled the largest version of a future chip.
pkg.tldr.0: Advanced packaging (the final assembly of chip and memory into one package) is the real binding constraint on AI-chip output, and TSMC controls it (nearly 100% of AI-class assembly, a 52–156 week queue, ~$10K per wafer).
pkg.tldr.1: But here is the paradox: packaging's share of an AI chip's cost is shrinking (19% → 15%) while memory takes the money for itself (52% → 63%). The constraint is here and the profit goes there.
pkg.tldr.2: The theme is already heavily played: Amkor +336% in a year, Ibiden ~+500%, AT&S ~+1140%, Besi on a forward P/E of ~55. The best return-for-risk is equipment and materials (Besi, ASMPT, Disco, Towa) plus TSMC itself, not the re-rated assembly houses.
pkg.unitEconomics.costCurve: TSMC is the cheapest producer at volume: lower depreciation, better defect-free yield, and the whole chain tuned. For the independent contractors only the simpler part of the work pays — final mounting and test.
pkg.unitEconomics.grossMargin: Inside TSMC, packaging still earns less than the company average (66%), but it has a path upward: assembly does not need ultra-expensive lithography tools, so equipment depreciation is lower. At the independent contractors gross margin is only 14–26%.
pkg.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: Assembling one wafer costs ~$10K. It yields 25–28 finished interposers. Per chip that works out at ~$750 for the basic version of the assembly and ~$1,000–1,100 for the advanced one (nearly 50% more). In total, packaging is 10–15% of an AI chip's cost.
pkg.unitEconomics.takeaway: The economics of this link is about scrap: when an error costs thousands of dollars, the winner is whoever assembles most cleanly, and that is TSMC. The contractors have meaningful operating leverage too: ASE's profit grew 90% in a year on just 30% revenue growth — at full utilisation they earn disproportionately.

pkg.update.bottomLine: The bottom line: the constraint is genuine and prices are still rising, but this is not «shortage forever» — an assembly plant takes ~18 months to build, the shortfall has already halved, and Nvidia is paying for a second supplier itself. Meanwhile the link's shares are up 4–12x in a year. So the sensible bet here is not «buy the shortage» but buy the equipment and materials layer (Besi, ASMPT, Disco, Towa) plus TSMC — they earn regardless of who wins the fight for orders.
pkg.update.headline: The constraint is real — but it is clearing, and the shares have already played it
pkg.update.stories.0.detail: On 23 July 2026 Amkor announced a multi-year advanced-packaging agreement with Nvidia carrying $1.5B of prepayments against capacity expansion; Amkor's shares jumped about 17%. The meaning is twofold: Nvidia is directly paying for a second supplier to exist outside TSMC — so TSMC's monopoly is not permanent. Earlier, in June 2026, Amkor and TSMC signed a 10-year agreement to transfer TSMC's technology to the Arizona plant — TSMC deliberately routes its overflow to «neutral» contractors so the volume does not go to Samsung. But real volume out of Arizona only comes from 2028–2029.
pkg.update.stories.0.title: Nvidia put down $1.5B of prepayments with Amkor
pkg.update.stories.1.detail: The key disclosure on this theme: how much packaging brings the company, and what it says about assembly volumes. TSMC is nearly doubling output (to 120–140K wafers a month), with another 50–60K added by contractors. While volumes and margin keep rising, the shortage thesis holds.
pkg.update.stories.1.title: TSMC in Q2: 67.7% gross margin, packaging above 10% of revenue on the 2026 plan
pkg.update.stories.1.verdict: the most reliable leading signal on AI-chip demand stays strong
pkg.update.stories.2.detail: According to one industry source (SemiAnalysis, needs confirmation), Nvidia dropped the chip version with four dies and 16 memory modules: at that size the package warps and scrap becomes unacceptable. It was replaced by a design half the size. This is the first case of packaging constraining the architecture of the chip itself — a direct blow to the «packages will keep growing forever» thesis.
pkg.update.stories.2.title: The largest Rubin version was cancelled
pkg.update.stories.2.verdict: the physical limit has shown itself
pkg.update.stories.3.detail: On 1 July 2026 ASE raised advanced-packaging prices by more than 20%, and Powertech raised memory prices by up to 30%. The price of assembling a wafer holds around $10K. While the makers keep raising prices and customers keep paying, the thesis works.
pkg.update.stories.3.title: Prices are still being raised
pkg.update.stories.3.verdict: the pricing power is still theirs
pkg.update.stories.4.detail: On Epoch AI's data, memory's share of an AI chip's cost rose from 52% to 63% over two years, while packaging's fell from 19% to 15%. So the binding constraint is physically here while the profit accumulates in memory. Meanwhile the four largest designers took more than 90% of all assembly and memory by value but only ~12% of leading-edge silicon — which explains why the binding constraints in 2025 were packaging and memory rather than the processors themselves.
pkg.update.stories.4.title: The money goes to memory, not packaging
pkg.update.stories.4.verdict: the key nuance of the theme
pkg.update.stories.5.detail: TrendForce (15 June 2026), citing institutional investors: the supply–demand gap in assembly will narrow from roughly 20% to 10% by the end of 2026, with conditions improving further in 2027. The cause is TSMC nearly doubling output, plus orders flowing to the contractors. In memory the shortage holds through 2027; here it melts sooner.
pkg.update.stories.5.title: The shortage began to narrow: from ~20% to ~10%
pkg.update.summary: July 2026 brought several important pieces of packaging news at once: Nvidia paid a second supplier up front, the largest version of a future chip was cancelled on physics, and the shortage officially began to narrow. Here is what of that changes the picture for an investor.
pkg.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Next the constraint becomes memory (which has to be bought before assembly can start) and physics: at very large package sizes the package starts to warp and scrap rises. According to one industry source, that is exactly why Nvidia cancelled the largest version of a future chip.
pkg.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Right now the constraint is the assembly of large packages at TSMC itself: both the basic and the advanced versions are fully booked. The cause is the large silicon interposer, which is hard to make without defects.
pkg.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: TSMC directs 10–20% of all its investment to packaging and related work (on a total of $60–64B in 2026, that is ~$6–13B). One important advantage: packaging does not need $150M+ lithography tools, so it requires far less investment per unit of output than an ordinary chip fab.
pkg.valueCapture.takeaway: The margin sits in equipment (Besi at 62% gross) and at TSMC — not at the independent assembly houses, where it is 14–26%: their work is closer to contract labour. That says directly who to take the exposure through: Besi (AMS: BESI), ASMPT (HKG: 522), TSMC (NYSE: TSM).
pkg.verdict.bear.0: Oversupply by 2027–2028: the shortfall drops below 5%, the queue shortens, and plant utilisation falls below 85%.
pkg.verdict.bear.1: The money goes to memory, not packaging: packaging's share of chip cost falls further — below 15%.
pkg.verdict.bear.2: A pause in AI spending hits high-beta names: the giants cut spending guidance and Nvidia trims orders (historically assembly houses fell 30–50%).
pkg.verdict.bull.0: The shortage holds to 2027 and pricing power with it: the queue stays longer than 52 weeks, price increases from TSMC and ASE stick, and the shortfall does not fall below 10%.
pkg.verdict.bull.1: Each chip needs more packaging — revenue grows even without more chips: the package grows from 5.5 to 9.5 «reticle fields» (the area of a single lithography pass, ~858 mm²), and the number of memory chips per package reaches 12 and beyond.
pkg.verdict.bull.2: Equipment and materials earn however the shares split: orders accelerate at Besi and ASMPT, and solderless bonding (dies joined directly, with no solder ball) goes into volume.
pkg.verdict.horizon: 2–3 years — the window of advanced-assembly (CoWoS) shortage through 2027–2028; after that, the risk of the winners changing on the shift to panels and glass substrates.
pkg.verdict.keyQuestion: Will the advanced-packaging shortage hold through 2027 — or will TSMC's expansion and the arrival of Intel/Samsung level the market and strip away the pricing power?
pkg.verdict.sizing: Advanced packaging (CoWoS): 370K wafers/month (2024) → 670K (2025) → ~1M (2026). The high-end segment grows ~23%/yr to 2030.
pkg.verdict.summary: The constraint is real: without this assembly no accelerator can be produced, and effectively only TSMC (the world's largest contract chipmaker) does it. But two drawbacks pull the score down. First, the entry price: the sector has already been re-rated (individual names are up 5–12x in a year), so the easy money is made. Second, the shortage clears faster here than in memory: the supply–demand gap is already narrowing from ~20% to ~10%, and a new assembly plant takes only ~18 months to build. The protection from competitors is high at TSMC and at the assembly-equipment makers (Besi), but low at ordinary assembly houses, where the work is closer to contract labour. Hence a 6, not an 8.
pkg.whatIsIt: This is the final assembly of an AI accelerator: a large processor no longer fits on one piece of silicon, so it is cut into several smaller dies and assembled into a single package together with the memory stacks. All the dies sit on a shared silicon interposer carrying tens of thousands of ultra-fine wires that connect processor to memory, and the whole thing is encapsulated in a protective compound and ground flat. Without this assembly a modern accelerator physically does not exist.

power.thesis.bigIdea: The common bet is «AI needs energy — everyone who produces it wins». But AI is not buying abstract kilowatt-hours; it is buying a very specific product: hundreds of megawatts or gigawatts at a single point on the grid, available in 2–4 years rather than ten, round the clock and with a high-voltage connection. And the scarcity sits in several places at once: available generation, connecting a large load, transmission and substations, high-voltage transformers and switchgear, gas turbines, ready sites. So the excess returns go not to regulated utilities selling more kilowatt-hours (the regulator hands their rent to the consumer) but to the owners of dispatchable generation already running, to suppliers of scarce equipment, and to whoever shortens the time to connection. The rule: own the constraint, not «just a power company».
power.thesis.stream.0.t: Electricity turned out to be scarcer than chips
power.thesis.stream.1.t: Electricity has become one of the hardest constraints on AI infrastructure — but the conclusion is not that «every producer of power wins». AI creates demand not simply for kilowatt-hours but for a specific product: a large block of capacity at a single point, available within 2–4 years, reliable 24/7, able to scale up, and with a high-voltage connection. That is exactly why the shortage exists simultaneously in generation, connection, transmission, [[transformers|transformers|the steel inside it]], turbines and sites. All of it has to be assembled at once — and any single missing link stops the campus.
power.thesis.stream.10.t: The power chain is long: fuel → plant → step-up transformer → high-voltage transmission → substation → step-down transformer → distribution → data centre → UPS and switchgear (distribution boards) → GPU. Building the plant is not enough — every link has to be ready. At the end of 2025 the US interconnection queues held ~1,312 GW of generation and ~749 GW of storage (about 8,200 projects) — some ~2,061 GW in total, more than the country's entire installed capacity. But a queue is a wish to connect, not an ability to build: the span from application to start-up has grown from under two years in 2008 to ~5 years in 2024, and most projects are cancelled once the cost of the grid upgrades becomes known.

power.thesis.stream.13.t: Large [[transformers|transformers|the steel inside it]] are one of the most underrated constraints. A large transformer is designed individually, weighs hundreds of tonnes, requires special electrical steel, is rarely replaceable by a standard equivalent, and has few manufacturers. Lead times have stretched to 80–120 weeks, and for some models beyond three years. Switchgear, breakers and cables are under the same pressure. The result is paradoxical: even completed generation and a finished data centre can sit idle for want of one missing component.

power.thesis.stream.23.t: Merchant against regulated — and the capacity payment
power.thesis.stream.24.t: A regulated utility invests in generation and the grid, the regulator adds it to the rate base and allows a return of ~9–11%: growth is predictable, but the upside is capped and much of the rent goes to the consumer. A merchant generator lives on the market price, capacity payments and corporate contracts — it feels the shortage more keenly and leaves more upside to the shareholder, but it is also more volatile. The most direct channel from «shortage» to «money» is the capacity market: in PJM the capacity payment has risen sharply, and that flows straight to the owners of generation. But it is not a permanent rent: high prices themselves call forth new construction.

power.thesis.stream.26.t: The economics of power — timing matters more than price
power.thesis.stream.27.t: A 1 GW campus at 85% utilisation and a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.2 consumes ~7.45 TWh a year: the electricity bill is ~$298M at $40/MWh, ~$447M at $60 and ~$745M at $100. For a campus costing tens of billions that is significant but not dominant. Whereas if a lack of capacity delays bringing GPUs online by a year, the lost compute revenue far exceeds the premium on an expensive contract. So the hyperscaler optimises not the price per MWh but the total cost of reliable and timely capacity — and time to connection often matters more than LCOE.

power.thesis.stream.30.t: AI is setting off several parallel investment cycles at once — and they have already moved from talk to orders. At the end of 2025 NextEra showed an investment plan for 2025–2032 of roughly $295–325B; GE Vernova's order backlog grew from ~$119B to ~$150B during 2025 and to ~$176B by the middle of 2026, with data-centre-related orders passing $5B. The capital spreads across the layers — and the best-protected of them is not generation itself but equipment and grid construction.

power.thesis.stream.37.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
power.thesis.stream.38.t: Electricity will not become «the new oil» in any literal sense: an electron cannot be shipped and stored cheaply around the world — so the shortage is local and fragmented. Value is created at a specific grid node, in a specific hour and at a specific reliability. Which means the main asset in AI power is not a megawatt-hour but a reliable megawatt in the right place, with a connection in place and room to expand. Up to 2030 the structure is existing nuclear + new gas + a great deal of solar and wind + grid batteries + transmission upgrades + on-site generation + long contracts.
power.thesis.stream.39.t: The conclusion: not «AI needs energy, so buy anything with power, nuclear or data centre in its name». Own the constraint — where supply cannot answer price quickly: licences and operating reactors (Constellation, Vistra), turbine and grid-equipment manufacturing (GE Vernova, Eaton, Hitachi's transformers), transmission and substation construction (Quanta), sites with real capacity. Regulated utilities offer steady rate-base growth, but the rent goes to the consumer; merchant assets in scarce regions carry more upside and more cyclicality. The main danger is an expensive share in which the whole future shortage is already capitalised.
power.thesis.stream.4.t: In the US the shift is sharper still: data-centre consumption rose from ~58 TWh in 2014 to ~176 TWh in 2023, and the 2028 forecast is 325–580 TWh — from 4.4% to 6.7–12% of the country's entire demand. But more important than the headline figure is the concentration. Data centres are not spread evenly across the country: several gigawatts can arrive at a single grid node that was never designed for that kind of growth. So globally there may be enough energy, while locally getting 500 MW in the right place at the right time is close to impossible.

rack.intro:
This node covers two things at once: the AI-scale rack itself (the physical machine) and the business that buys such racks on debt and rents out their compute time (a neocloud). A modern model cannot be trained on a single accelerator — it simply does not fit in its memory — so dozens of GPUs have to be joined so that they work as one machine. That is what an AI-scale rack is, and without it training frontier models is physically impossible.

How it works — the hardware. The current generation's flagship is the GB200 NVL72: 72 Blackwell accelerators and 36 Grace processors, joined by the ultra-fast NVLink bus into a single 13.8 TB memory domain. The model is spread across all 72 accelerators at once, and each reads its neighbour's memory at nearly the speed of its own — so the rack behaves like one giant accelerator rather than 72 separate servers. The price of that density is heat: a single rack draws more than 120 kW (an ordinary server draws single-digit kW), and air can no longer carry it away, so coolant runs directly over plates on the chips. An assembled rack costs $3–8M.

How it works — the rental economics. The operator borrows against its future GPUs, buys thousands of chips (access to them is the main growth limiter), installs them in data centres and sells capacity on 3–5 year take-or-pay contracts: the customer pays for reserved capacity even if it goes unused. That shifts idle risk onto the customer and gives the operator a predictable stream to service the debt.

The most critical property. A rack is valuable exactly as long as all 72 accelerators work as one: a single failed node or bus fault stops training across thousands of GPUs at once, so the reliability of the interconnect and the cooling matters more than any individual specification. In the rental economics, utilisation is critical: break-even sits at around 70% utilisation, with almost no margin of safety. Plus an unresolved question about useful life: in the accounts GPUs are depreciated over 4–6 years, while their real economic life may turn out to be 2–3 (an estimate) — in which case the paper profit disappears.

Who pays, and how much. Capital intensity is extreme: the market leader's capex is $31–35B for 2026, around five years of revenue, with roughly $28B raised in debt and equity over 12 months. More than 40% of every capex dollar goes to Nvidia as the GPU supplier; lenders charge anywhere from SOFR+2.25% (investment grade) to ~15% on early loans. The customers — AI labs and hyperscalers — pay almost any price, because access to scarce GPUs matters more to them than the cost, and building their own infrastructure takes longer than renting ready capacity.

Size and concentration. Neocloud revenue passed $25B (2025), growing more than 200% in a year; forecasts for 2030–2031 differ sixfold — from $65B to $400B. The leader (CoreWeave) has around 600K GPUs and a $99.4B order book, but also around $35B of debt and negative cash flow of $4.7B in a quarter. Hence the central question: are neoclouds durable infrastructure platforms, or temporary operators earning only on a GPU shortage?

rack.mentalModel.drivers.1.var: Cost of capital / access to debt
rack.mentalModel.drivers.2.note: break-even is ~70% utilisation: at 85% a 1,024-GPU cluster earns +$340K/month, at 55% it loses $330K. While reserved pricing rises (+40%) and spot falls (−64–75%), the shortage still feeds it; when the spread compresses, the thesis breaks.
rack.mentalModel.framework: A neocloud buys GPUs on debt and rents out the compute time on 3–5 year contracts. The profit is the spread between the GPU-hour rental rate and the cost of servicing the debt. The risk is that the asset itself depreciates faster than the loan against it amortises: the H100 spot rate has fallen 64–75% while the debt remains. The position holds while a GPU shortage keeps reserved rates (+40%) above the cost of capital; once the shortage ends or the chip obsolesces, the spread compresses and the debt obligations stay.
rack.mentalModel.revenueFormula: Revenue = number of GPUs × utilisation (>70% is needed to break even) × GPU-hour rental rate (spot falling, reserved rising +40%)
rack.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: CoreWeave has ~600K GPUs, >1 GW of active capacity and a $99.4B order book (10 customers at ≥$1B). Scale unlocks investment-grade financing and hyperscaler-class contracts that smaller players cannot get. But the hyperscalers themselves are an order of magnitude larger.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: the main differentiator, but a weakening one: 300+ new players entered in 2025, Nvidia's Lepton marketplace is commoditising rental, and Nvidia is spreading its allocation ever wider. The advantage is real, but the pressure is rising.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: the new binding constraint and a growing protection: whoever has contracted gigawatts (CoreWeave 3.5 GW, Nebius 3.5 GW) holds a genuinely scarce resource. CoreWeave's failed bid for Core Scientific ($9B for 1.3 GW) showed how hard it is fought over.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: the first investment-grade GPU-backed financing ($8.5B, A3/A(low)) is a structural barrier to smaller players. But the leverage is fragile: the model requires permanent market access against collateral that obsolesces faster than the debt.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: the weak link: take-or-pay contracts lock in the payment but not the loyalty — the workloads themselves are portable, and a customer can move to another provider in days. The only real lock-in runs through GPU allocation, not through the product.
rack.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the weakest vector: AWS/Azure/GCP are 63% of cloud infrastructure and can take the niche back. Meta Compute (July 2026) is a customer turned competitor. A structural threat, not a hypothesis.
rack.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is thin (a composite score of 4/10) and shifting: the old support — scarce GPU access — is eroding, and the new one is contracted gigawatts of power plus investment-grade financing. The real advantage now belongs to whoever holds capacity and cheap capital, not to whoever holds the GPUs. Switching costs are close to zero, and the hyperscalers can take the market back.

rack.problems.items.0.gap: A new player without secured power must join a 5–7 year grid connection queue (ERCOT, MISO, PJM) — a wait that money cannot shorten. That is precisely why only about 25% of contracted capacity across the industry has actually been brought online. The binding constraint is years of waiting for power, not capital: chips can be bought in weeks, a gigawatt connection cannot.
rack.problems.items.0.problem: Neocloud growth is no longer constrained by chips but by electricity. A single GB200 rack (the flagship 72-accelerator cabinet) draws more than 100 kW, and a large AI site needs hundreds of megawatts and whole gigawatts of capacity. In the US the queue to connect new generation to the grid is stretching to 5–7 years (ERCOT, MISO, PJM — the regional grid operators). Of the capacity already contracted, only about 25% has actually been brought online — the rest is stalled precisely for lack of power. Tellingly, CoreWeave lost a $9B auction for Core Scientific — an attempt to acquire 1.3 GW of ready capacity.
rack.problems.items.0.solution: Capacity is being sourced around the grid: on-site generation — gas turbines and small nuclear reactors — plus long-term power purchase contracts and buying plots that are already connected. A separate source is converting former crypto-mining sites: they already have a large grid connection and power contracts built for mining, and they are being switched to AI workloads. Liquid cooling (coolant running directly over the chips instead of air) packs more computation into each megawatt, reducing how much energy a unit of work requires.
rack.problems.items.0.winners: The winners are those who already hold capacity and connected sites: CoreWeave (3.5 GW contracted), Nebius (3.5 GW → more than 4 GW), IREN (a 4.5 GW pipeline). Former miners are especially well placed because their grid connection is already built: TeraWulf (a 12.8 GW pipeline, with Google holding 8% of the equity), Hut 8 (8.5 GW), Cipher (1.3 GW, with an AWS contract). The owners of connected land — Equinix (3 GW of ready land) and Digital Realty (5 GW) — lease it out with no GPU (accelerator chip) obsolescence risk.
rack.problems.takeaway: This barrier rewards those who already have the power — former miners with connected sites, neoclouds with gigawatt contracts and owners of ready land — and may let new players (the miners) in at the expense of pure GPU operators without secured capacity.

rack.supply.capacityAdds.1.name: Nebius: 3.5 GW contracted → >4 GW. Capex $20–25B (2026). >$6B raised in Q1 2026
rack.supply.capacityAdds.2.impact: A ~$50B near-term funding gap. Only ~25% of leased capacity delivered. Delivery is the key de-risking event
rack.supply.capacityAdds.3.impact: 63% of cloud infrastructure. Meta Compute. Alphabet's $205B capex. The long-term competitive threat
rack.supply.crowdingOut: 300+ new GPU cloud providers entered in 2025 (Value Add VC), fragmenting the on-demand/spot tier and driving the H100 price decline. The reserved tier remains differentiated.
rack.supply.leadTime: NVIDIA GPU allocation is the primary lead time. Blackwell is sold out through 2026. Power/data centres are the emerging constraint (CoreWeave's failed $9B Core Scientific bid for 1.3 GW). HBM memory runs 36–52 week lead times.
rack.supply.takeaway: Supply is bifurcated: reserved is tight (the primary moat), spot is oversupplied (300+ entrants). Both the shortage and the glut narratives are true. Capacity expansion is explosive ($31–35B at CoreWeave alone). GPU scarcity is the moat, but it is eroding. Power is increasingly the binding constraint.
rack.supply.utilization: Break-even is ~70% on debt-financed clusters. 55% utilisation = −$330K/month on a 1,024-GPU cluster; 85% = +$340K. «Almost no margin of safety.» CoreWeave reports a 95% re-booking rate on H100 batches.
rack.thesis.bigIdea: Neoclouds borrow to buy GPUs and rent them out. The equity market prices them as the power plants of the AI era; the credit market prices them as bankruptcy candidates: CoreWeave's 5-year CDS (default insurance, whose price is the market's view of the risk) embeds a ~50% chance of default. Both valuations describe the same company. The real margin is taken by Nvidia (which sells the GPUs, takes a stake in the buyer and gets its own money back) and by the lenders, leaving the shareholder only a thin residual — what is left after them — on a fast-depreciating asset. The bet belongs on the company without heavy debt (Nebius), not on the leveraged bet that can go to zero in a bad scenario (CoreWeave).
rack.thesis.stream.0.t: The business that borrows to buy GPUs and rents them out
rack.thesis.stream.1.t: A neocloud is a company that buys tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs (mostly with borrowed money), assembles them into clusters and rents out the computation by the hour. Everything converges here: chips from the [[asic|custom accelerators|earns on every chip]] and [[hbm|memory|decoupled from the cycle]] sections, plus the [[power|electricity|not generation, but connection]] without which the cluster cannot be switched on. The market exploded and called these operators «the power plants of the AI era».

rack.thesis.stream.11.t: So the «AI cloud growth story» mostly enriches Nvidia and the lenders. The shareholder owns a thin, leveraged slice — strong while GPUs hold their price, and dangerous when they stop.
rack.thesis.stream.12.t: The real constraint is not demand — it is capital and GPUs
rack.thesis.stream.13.t: There are three constraints. First, Nvidia's GPU allocation: this is both the main barrier and the main dependency, and you live or die by how many chips you are sold. Second, access to [[power|electricity|not generation, but connection]] and sites: CoreWeave bid $9B for Core Scientific purely for 1.3 GW of capacity. Third, permanent access to capital markets: the model works only while the debt can be refinanced.

rack.thesis.stream.15.t: The disputed detail: how fast a GPU loses value
rack.thesis.stream.16.t: And here is the number the whole model rests on — how fast a GPU actually loses value. The operators write GPUs off over 4–6 years (CoreWeave 6, Nebius 4). But Nvidia ships a new generation almost every year (Hopper → Blackwell → Rubin), and sceptics argue the real useful life is closer to 2–3 years. If so, the depreciation in the accounts is understated by tens of billions, and much of the reported profit is on paper. Spot rental prices already hint at this: H100 rates have fallen 64–75% from a peak above $8/hour as 300+ new entrants flooded the market.

rack.thesis.stream.17.items.0.n: CoreWeave 6, Nebius 4; the «profit» depends directly on this
rack.thesis.stream.17.items.1.n: Hopper → Blackwell → Rubin — the old kit devalues faster than it is written off

rack.thesis.stream.18.t: A business that rents out a fast-depreciating asset bought on debt is durable while the asset holds its price — and fragile the second it stops.
rack.thesis.stream.19.t: The equity market and the credit market disagree about one company
rack.thesis.stream.2.items.1.n: a $99.4B order book; anchors are OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta
rack.thesis.stream.2.items.2.n: one of the fastest-growing segments of AI infrastructure
rack.thesis.stream.20.t: Here is the key signal. The equity market and the credit market look at CoreWeave and see opposite things. Analysts rate it a buy with a target of ~$142. Its 5-year CDS — the cost of insuring its debt against default — embeds roughly a 50% chance of default. Equity is pricing a growth star; credit is pricing a bankruptcy candidate. About the same company.

rack.thesis.stream.21.items.2.n: if GPU residual values collapse, nobody yet knows
rack.thesis.stream.22.t: When the equity market and the credit market disagree this sharply about one company, the credit market is usually the one to respect.
rack.thesis.stream.24.t: CoreWeave at ~6–9x revenue looks inexpensive — until you remember the ~$35B of debt and −$4.7B of quarterly cash flow that the multiple ignores. The market prices the $99.4B order book as if it were guaranteed to convert into revenue on a 6-year GPU life. Nebius at ~8–9x forward revenue treats a $7–9B ARR target almost as fact — but it has a clean balance sheet and conservative 4-year depreciation to back it.
rack.thesis.stream.25.t: Our read: Nebius (clean balance sheet, conservative depreciation) is the fair bet; CoreWeave is a leveraged bet that cannot be taken in size. Cheap on the multiple, expensive on the risk.
rack.thesis.stream.26.t: Where the sector is going — and where the money is going
rack.thesis.stream.27.t: Where the model is going: from renting bare GPUs to full managed AI platforms — the winners become sticky infrastructure rather than swappable rental. Spot rental is commoditising (H100 −64–75%, 300+ players), but reserved pricing is rising (+40% in six months) as large players sign multi-year contracts. The next differentiator is not the GPUs themselves but access to power and reliability.
rack.thesis.stream.28.t: The main shift ahead is from training to inference. Training a model is a one-off burst, while inference (answering queries) runs continuously and will become the bulk of computation. That changes the economics: in inference what matters is not peak capacity but utilisation and cost per token — the winner is whoever has cheaper energy and higher utilisation. In parallel «sovereign AI» is rising: countries are building their own national clusters so as not to depend on foreign clouds — funds in the UAE (MGX), Saudi Arabia (HUMAIN) and the EU are investing tens of billions.
rack.thesis.stream.29.t: Where the money is going: Nvidia seeds capital into its own customers (7% of CoreWeave, $2B in Nebius) to guarantee demand; investment-grade debt is scaling (the first rated GPU-backed financing, at $8.5B); the hyperscalers and labs sign anchor contracts (OpenAI, Microsoft and Meta at CoreWeave; Microsoft's $9.7B at IREN). And the picks and shovels are the site landlords (Equinix, Digital Realty, Applied Digital), who lease powered land and carry no GPU obsolescence risk at all.

rack.thesis.stream.31.t: The scale of capital is no longer venture but infrastructure. Direct-lending and infrastructure funds are moving into GPU data centres (Blackstone, Apollo, the $30B+ BlackRock–Microsoft–MGX–Nvidia partnership) — financing construction against long-term contracts, like roads or pipelines. Securitisation of GPU debt is appearing too: bonds backed by future rental. For leaders with anchor contracts this is cheap capital; for everyone else it is the absence of capital.
rack.thesis.stream.32.items.0.n: increasingly borrowed infrastructure capital rather than equity
rack.thesis.stream.32.items.1.n: only a few will survive — consolidation is inevitable
rack.thesis.stream.32.items.2.n: the UAE (MGX), Saudi Arabia (HUMAIN), the EU — tens of billions
rack.thesis.stream.33.t: Hence the coming consolidation. 300+ operators flooded the market, but only a few will survive: three things decide it — access to [[power|energy|not generation, but connection]], balance-sheet strength and Nvidia's allocation. Weak players on expensive debt and spot pricing break first when the cycle turns, and their capacity and contracts pass to the strong. So this theme is a bet not on «neocloud growth» in general but on specific survivors.
rack.thesis.stream.34.t: The specifics: the whole model rests on anchor contracts and staked-out power. Here is who has signed with whom, and who has the best capacity position.
rack.thesis.stream.35.note: Sources: deal press releases and filings, 2025–2026.
rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.0.3: weak: the $9B bid for Core Scientific (1.3 GW) failed
rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.1.3: its own data centres + a clean balance sheet — it builds to contract
rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.2.3: the best: a 4.5 GW pipeline, its own fleet and power

rack.thesis.stream.35.rows.4.3: the price leader, but with no large power position
rack.thesis.stream.36.t: The next race is for power. Best positioned are those who have already staked out gigawatts: IREN (a 4.5 GW pipeline), Nebius (its own sites) and landlords like Applied Digital. CoreWeave, the no. 1 on contracts, is the weakest on owned power — its $9B bid for Core Scientific for 1.3 GW of [[power|capacity|not generation, but connection]] failed. Whoever locks up gigawatts under contract first takes the next wave of deals.
rack.thesis.stream.37.t: Who actually buys this computation? Three groups. First, the hyperscalers themselves, renting others' capacity to cover their own shortfall: Microsoft is the single largest buyer, renting from CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN and Lambda at once. Second, AI labs without their own data centres: OpenAI (the CoreWeave deal), plus Anthropic, Mistral and xAI. Third, and growing, corporations and states building «sovereign AI» (the same UAE and Saudi funds). Tellingly, even hyperscalers that could build their own choose to rent — because speed and access to power matter more than building from scratch.
rack.thesis.stream.38.t: What the players are betting on: Nvidia bets on many neoclouds at once (diluting demand, reducing dependence on the hyperscalers); the neoclouds bet on staking out power and anchor contracts before the GPU cycle turns; and an investor who wants the theme with less risk bets on the landlords (bond-like contracts, no GPU risk) and on a clean balance sheet (Nebius) rather than on a leveraged operator.

rack.thesis.stream.41.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
rack.thesis.stream.42.t: Neoclouds are real infrastructure, and the demand is real. But the model is renting a fast-depreciating asset on debt, and the value goes first to Nvidia and the lenders. The shareholder gets the residual: strong while GPUs hold their price, and brutal when they stop.
rack.thesis.stream.43.t: Compressed into one thought: play the theme through a clean balance sheet (Nebius) and the landlords (bond-like contracts, no GPU risk), not through the leveraged bet (CoreWeave). And the main beneficiary of all this renting is not the operator but Nvidia, which sells the hardware, takes a stake in the customer and gets its money back.
rack.thesis.stream.5.t: A single H100 GPU costs $25–40K, and fully deployed — with power, cooling and networking — around $45–50K. It rents for $1.80–3.50 an hour (the budget segment) and up to $8–11 at the hyperscalers. At first glance the economics look brilliant: CoreWeave has a 69% gross margin and 56% adjusted EBITDA. But that is BEFORE depreciation and interest on the debt.
rack.thesis.stream.6.t: After those, the picture changes. In one quarter CoreWeave posted a GAAP loss of −$740M: interest on the debt alone ate ~46% of EBITDA, and cash flow was minus $4.7B. The gross margin is real — but it is a mirage above two expenses that consume it: the asset depreciates fast, and the debt used to buy it demands interest.

rack.thesis.stream.8.t: Where the margin actually leaks to
rack.thesis.stream.9.t: Follow the money. Nvidia takes more than 40% of all capex, selling GPUs at a ~75% margin — and then takes a stake in its own customers (7% of CoreWeave, $2B in Nebius) and gets its own money back. The lenders earn a secured return (SOFR+2.25% for the best of them). And the neocloud's shareholder gets only the residual — what is left after Nvidia and the lenders.
rack.tldr.0: Neocloud revenue (companies renting out compute capacity with accelerator chips) passed $25B (2025, Synergy Research), growing >200% in a year. CoreWeave leads (~600K GPUs, 43 data centres, >1 GW of capacity). But analysts cannot agree on the market's size: forecasts run from $65B to $400B by 2030–2031 — a sixfold spread. The main source of that uncertainty: whether the hyperscalers take this niche back once their own GPU supply is sorted.
rack.tldr.1: CoreWeave is the most aggressive player: $5.1B of revenue (+170%), a $99.4B order book, adjusted EBITDA (profit before interest, tax and depreciation) of ~56%. But ~$35B of debt, negative cash flow of $4.7B in a quarter, interest expense at ~46% of EBITDA, and Microsoft at 67% of 2025 revenue. Nebius is the preferred pure play: $399M of revenue in a quarter (+684%), $9.3B of cash, GPUs depreciated over 4 years (more conservative). The former crypto miners (APLD, IREN, WULF) essentially lease space to hyperscalers on 15-year terms.
rack.tldr.2: A sensible strategy: cap neoclouds at 2–4% of the portfolio and prefer the infrastructure landlords — the data-centre owners who lease space (Digital Realty, Equinix) — plus Nvidia, which captures most of the value, over debt-funded GPU renters. Nebius is the best pure choice among the neoclouds. CoreWeave is a high-leverage option (heavily dependent on borrowed money), and the position size must survive a refinancing shock.
rack.unitEconomics.costCurve: A 100-H100 cluster (Mercatus): $4.5M capex; year-3 residual ~25% ($1.1M); operating cost $0.41/GPU-hr. At 75% utilisation the 3-year IRR is 7–33% (driven entirely by the alternative cloud cost). Against hyperscaler on-demand at $3.50/hr it is decisively positive; against reserved at $1.80/hr it is marginal.
rack.unitEconomics.grossMargin: CoreWeave: 69.4% GM (TTM), adj. EBITDA ~56%, GAAP net −$740M in Q1 (after depreciation + interest). Nebius AI cloud at 45% adj. EBITDA. Lambda ~50% GM (~61% ex-hardware). Operating cost ~$0.41/GPU-hr (power + colo + ops). Break-even ~70% utilisation.
rack.unitEconomics.takeaway: High headline returns (55–69% GM before depreciation), but radical asset-life uncertainty (4–6 years in the accounts against Burry's 2–3 year estimate). Break-even at ~70% utilisation leaves almost no margin of safety. IRR depends critically on residual values and on the alternative cloud cost. Not comparable to traditional colo (15–20 year assets, 7–9% cap rates).
rack.unitEconomics.yields.0.note: Down 64–75% from the 2023 peak above $8/hr. 300+ new entrants are driving spot down. Reserved is rising +40%
rack.unitEconomics.yields.3.note: Burry: a 2–3 year economic life against 6-year books = ~$176B of understated depreciation across 2026–2028. Intrator: 95% re-booking at original pricing
rack.update.bottomLine: Genuine hypergrowth ($25B+ of revenue, 58–165% a year) alongside an extreme set of risks: debt, fast GPU obsolescence, customer concentration and circular financing. The facts so far lean toward the leaders becoming durable platforms — but their valuations already embed that outcome as near-guaranteed. This is a high-volatility satellite position: Nebius is the cleanest option (no debt burden), Equinix/DLR the best protected (no chip obsolescence risk), and CoreWeave the bet with maximum leverage and maximum risk. One question decides it: will the contracted take-or-pay payments cover debt amortisation if GPU residual values collapse?
rack.update.headline: Neoclouds: $25B+ of hypergrowth — the durability bet is unresolved, and the CDS-versus-equity divergence is extreme
rack.update.stories.0.detail: NVIDIA holds stakes in the operators (7% of CoreWeave, $2B in Nebius) and is now discussing a large backstop for an AI lab. When one player finances both the capacity producers and their customers, interdependence rises: trouble at any link hits the entire chain.

rack.update.stories.4.verdict: The GPUaaS market grows ~165% a year; CoreWeave is the largest player by a wide margin

rack.update.stories.5.title: CoreWeave: a $99.4B backlog, with CDS pricing ~50% five-year default odds
rack.update.stories.5.verdict: The category leader with unmatched scale, but the most financially stressed name. Credit and equity markets diverge: CDS looks distressed while the analyst target is ~$142 Buy against a $60–77 spot price
rack.update.summary: Neocloud revenue passed $25B (2025, +223% y/y in Q4). CoreWeave: a $99.4B order book, ~600K GPUs — but ~$35B of debt, with CDS pricing a ~50% chance of default. Nebius is the cleaner alternative ($9.3B of cash, 4-year depreciation). Reserved GPU prices are rising (+40%); spot has fallen 64–75%. Meta launched its own Meta Compute cloud (July 2026) — a customer turned competitor. The circular financing of Nvidia→neocloud→lab raises the question: is this real demand, or capital being recycled?
rack.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: Hyperscaler capacity recapture (Meta Compute, Alphabet's $205B capex). GPU generation transitions (Rubin R100, H2 2026). The sustainability of circular financing. A depreciation reality check (6 years versus a 2–3 year economic life).
rack.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: NVIDIA GPU allocation is both the primary moat and the primary dependency. Power/data-centre capacity is the emerging binding constraint (CoreWeave's failed $9B Core Scientific bid was a grab for 1.3 GW). Debt and equity capital markets — the model requires continuous access. HBM memory (36–52 week lead times).
rack.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Extreme: CoreWeave's capex is $31–35B (2026, ~5x its annual revenue). Nebius $20–25B. ~$28B raised in debt and equity over 12 months (CoreWeave alone). The model requires continuous access to capital markets.
rack.valueCapture.margins.0.source: Data-centre revenue $194B (FY2026). Captures most of the margin plus equity upside (7% of CoreWeave, $2B in Nebius) plus Lepton fees
rack.valueCapture.margins.1.source: Compressed from ~15% floating (2023). The first investment-grade GPU-backed financing ($8.5B, A3/A(low))
rack.valueCapture.margins.2.source: Adj. EBITDA ~56%. But a GAAP loss of $740M. Interest expense $536M = ~46% of EBITDA. Cash flow minus $4.7B
rack.valueCapture.margins.3.source: Revenue $399M in the quarter (+684%). Cash >$9.3B. A clean balance sheet. GPUs depreciated over 4 years
rack.valueCapture.margins.4.source: Private, valued at ~$5.9B. The price leader: H100 at ~$2.49/hr against CoreWeave's $4.25. An IPO is planned for H2 2026
rack.valueCapture.takeaway: NVIDIA captures the majority of capex. Debt providers earn secured returns. Neocloud equity holders earn the residual spread — which looks strong at adj. EBITDA (~56%) and collapses at GAAP net after depreciation and interest. Whether that is a durable margin or temporary arbitrage of GPU scarcity is unresolved.
rack.verdict.bear.0: Earning on a price spread with borrowed money, for as long as the shortage lasts: H100 spot prices (one-off rental at the current moment) have fallen 64–75%, 300+ new entrants fragment demand, and the main advantage (a shortage of GPUs — scarce accelerator chips) is eroding precisely in the segment where pricing is set.
rack.verdict.bear.1: A fragile capital structure: CoreWeave has ~$35B of debt, cash flow of minus $4.7B in a quarter, interest expense at ~46% of EBITDA (profit before interest, tax and depreciation), and CDS (default insurance) pricing in a ~50% chance of default over 5 years. The model depends on permanent access to capital markets, against collateral (GPUs) that obsolesces faster than the debt amortises.
rack.verdict.bear.2: Circular financing + customer concentration: Nvidia invests in neoclouds → the neoclouds buy GPUs → AI labs (funded by Nvidia) rent capacity from the neoclouds. Meta Compute (July 2026) is a customer that became a competitor. If one link breaks, the chain fails systemically.
rack.verdict.bull.0: Demand really is insatiable and confirmed by data: Google's token processing (units of text a model handles) grew 7x in a year to 3.2 quadrillion a month. Corporate AI spending grew 22x in two years ($1.7B→$37B). Reserved GPU prices (scarce accelerator chips) are up +40% — neoclouds (companies renting out compute capacity) serve the fastest-growing segment.
rack.verdict.bull.1: The financing model is maturing: GPU-backed debt has reached investment grade (A3/A(low), SOFR+2.25%), spreads over the base rate have compressed 175 basis points (1.75 percentage points) in a year, and take-or-pay contracts (the customer pays for reserved capacity even if unused) shift idle risk onto customers.
rack.verdict.bull.2: Order books give multi-year visibility: CoreWeave $99.4B (75% within 4 years), Nebius >$46B, TeraWulf >$12.8B, Applied Digital ~$16B — with customer diversification.
rack.verdict.horizon: 3–5 years — enough for a full GPU generation turnover (Hopper → Blackwell → Rubin) and the first serious debt stress test; that is when it becomes clear whether the model is durable.
rack.verdict.keyQuestion: Are neoclouds long-term platforms, or temporary arbitrageurs of a GPU shortage who get squeezed by the hyperscalers once supply normalises?
rack.verdict.sizing: Neocloud revenue >$25B (2025). Forecasts $65–400B (2030–2031). A single-digit % of total cloud infrastructure ($25B against ~$107B/quarter for all cloud), but over-indexed to the fastest-growing GPU/AI slice
rack.verdict.summary: Genuine hypergrowth ($25B+, >200% a year) — but with an extreme spread of forecasts ($65–400B by 2030–2031). The competitive advantages are thin: GPU allocation (scarce accelerator chips) from Nvidia + a proprietary software platform + long-term contracts — against hyperscalers building their own capacity and 300+ new entrants turning one-off rental into a commodity with no mark-up. Leverage + accelerated write-down of chip value + customer concentration + circular financing (money going round in a loop between the chip supplier and its own customers) = very high risk. Reserved GPU prices are rising (+40%), but spot prices (one-off rental at the current moment) have fallen 64–75%. The reserved-versus-spot price dynamic is the key real-time indicator: if the gap between them narrows, the shortage is ending. The verdict: a high-beta satellite position, not a portfolio core.
rack.whatIsIt: A large cabinet packed with compute chips, wired together so that all of them work as one enormous machine. A modern AI model cannot be trained on a single chip — it does not fit — so dozens of chips have to be bound into a single whole. The node's second meaning is the companies that buy these cabinets on debt and rent out their compute time to those training models. In an AI data centre this is the basic working unit: without it, training a frontier model is physically impossible.
renewables.picks.0.group: Owners of the scarcity — scale, grid and differentiation
renewables.picks.0.note: The value is moving from the panel to the scarcity: interconnection, transmission, storage, firm capacity and differentiated equipment. These names are the ones that own it.
renewables.picks.0.rows.0.exposure: regulated FPL + the largest developer of renewables and storage + transmission
renewables.picks.0.rows.0.priced: Sensitive to rates and tax policy; large capex; not a pure renewable (gas and data centres are growing).
renewables.picks.0.rows.0.why: Scale, cost of capital and a pipeline aimed at large load: a ~33 GW backlog after Q1 2026, +4 GW in the quarter, a ~110 GW battery pipeline, and ~21 GW of large-load requests at FPL. One of the strongest AI-power compounders.
renewables.picks.0.rows.1.exposure: hydro + solar + wind + storage; a global capital-recycling platform
renewables.picks.0.rows.1.priced: A complex financial structure and debt; sensitivity to the cost of financing; not to be confused with Brookfield Corporation.
renewables.picks.0.rows.1.why: It is not obliged to hold an asset forever: it develops, contracts, finances, sells a stake and reinvests. Hydro provides the firmness that pure solar portfolios lack. The 10.5 GW Microsoft framework validates the position.
renewables.picks.0.rows.2.exposure: grid equipment + gas turbines + wind + electrification
renewables.picks.0.rows.2.priced: The wind division has historically carried warranty and pricing risk; the AI-power premium is already in the price.
renewables.picks.0.rows.2.why: It takes the capital regardless of whether AI's electricity comes from renewables, from gas or from grid modernisation. Grid and gas offer better near-term economics than manufacturing wind turbines.
renewables.picks.0.rows.3.exposure: CdTe thin-film modules, manufactured in the US
renewables.picks.0.rows.3.priced: Profitability depends heavily on tax credits and tariffs; backlog concentration; risk of cancellations and policy change.
renewables.picks.0.rows.3.why: Differentiated technology independent of China's crystalline silicon, with US protection. A 45.1 GW backlog ($13.6B), Q2'26 revenue $1.06B, net income $423M — a rare margin for modules.
renewables.picks.0.rows.4.exposure: solar trackers (turning the panels to follow the sun) + control software
renewables.picks.0.rows.4.priced: Price competition, steel costs, customer concentration; cheap modules can push buyers towards simple fixed-tilt mounts.
renewables.picks.0.rows.4.why: A less commoditised layer of the chain than the panel: hardware plus software raises output, and switching supplier is harder than buying a module; outside cell and wafer economics.
renewables.picks.1.note: More directly tied to storage, or carrying more execution risk and leverage; not to be confused with a pure bet on the scarcity.
renewables.picks.1.rows.0.risk: Not a pure renewable bet — the valuation is set by all of Tesla; cell prices, Chinese competition, fire and warranty risk.
renewables.picks.1.rows.0.why: A more direct beneficiary than panel manufacturing: demand for grid storage is growing and manufacturing scale matters; a recognised integrated product and a creditworthy counterparty.
renewables.picks.1.rows.1.risk: A 13.7% hardware margin, project delays, working capital, competition from vertically integrated Chinese suppliers — high-beta execution, not a compounder.
renewables.picks.1.rows.1.why: Direct access to the grid battery market; a $5.3B backlog, ~85% of 2026 revenue covered, guidance of $3.2–3.6B.
renewables.picks.1.rows.2.risk: High leverage and project complexity; sensitivity to rates and regulation.
renewables.picks.1.rows.2.why: Development and asset ownership with hyperscaler contracts; exposure to the growth of contracted generation.
renewables.picks.1.rows.3.exposure: wind turbines + a large service base
renewables.picks.1.rows.3.risk: Aggressive competition for market share, and warranty, inflation and execution risk in turbine manufacturing.
renewables.picks.1.rows.3.why: Service means long contracts, recurring revenue and a better-protected margin than selling new turbines.
renewables.picks.1.rows.4.risk: Regulatory and regional complexity; the outcome depends on tariff decisions.
renewables.picks.1.rows.4.why: Grids plus generation — exposure to the transmission shortage, not only to panels.
renewables.thesis.bigIdea: The market argues in extremes: some say «AI needs power 24/7, and sun and wind are intermittent — a bad bet», others say «AI needs energy, buy any renewable». Both are wrong. Sun and wind have already won on the cheapest and fastest new megawatt-hour, and the hyperscalers have turned them into bankable 10–20 year contracts. But cheap does not mean round the clock, and generation is becoming abundant: the world added 692 GW during 2025. So the value is moving away from the panel itself (already a commodity) towards the scarcity: grid connection, transmission, storage, firm capacity and shovel-ready permitted projects. The winner is not whoever makes more panels, but whoever owns that constraint.
renewables.thesis.stream.0.t: What it is, and what AI needs it for
renewables.thesis.stream.1.t: Sun and wind are the cheapest and fastest new source of electricity: onshore wind ~$33 and solar ~$44 per MWh, with no fuel risk, and they can often be built faster than nuclear or large gas. Hyperscalers contract them 10–20 years ahead. But there is a limit to this: a [[rack|data centre|borrows to buy GPUs]] needs power every second, while the sun delivers current by day and the wind delivers by weather. So renewables can cheaply cover a large share of annual consumption, but on their own they do not provide 24/7 reliability without batteries, transmission, surplus capacity and firm generation.
renewables.thesis.stream.10.items.0.l: investment rating of commodity solar modules
renewables.thesis.stream.10.items.1.l: rating of developers with a secured connection
renewables.thesis.stream.10.items.1.n: the scarcity is the right to connect, not the panel
renewables.thesis.stream.11.t: The grid is the real constraint
renewables.thesis.stream.12.t: The shortage is not of projects but of the ability to connect them and move the current. At the end of 2024 ~10,300 projects were sitting in US interconnection queues — some ~1,400 GW of generation and ~890 GW of storage; of these, ~408 GW already had an interconnection agreement but had not yet been built. The most valuable asset is not the technology but the right to inject electricity into the grid at a commercially usable point (which needs [[transformers|transformers and substations|the steel inside it]] and [[power|the connection itself|not generation, but connection]]). And as solar grows, so does curtailment: in H1 2026 California curtailed ~4.5M MWh of renewables — more than in the whole of 2025.
renewables.thesis.stream.13.items.0.l: of generation in the interconnection queue (US)
renewables.thesis.stream.13.items.0.n: plus 890 GW of storage — a queue, not a shortage of projects
renewables.thesis.stream.13.items.1.l: with an agreement, but not yet built
renewables.thesis.stream.13.items.1.n: the constraint is connecting and transmitting, not building
renewables.thesis.stream.13.items.2.l: renewables curtailed by California in H1 2026
renewables.thesis.stream.13.items.2.n: more than in all of 2025 — the value of storage is rising
renewables.thesis.stream.14.t: Batteries are a more direct beneficiary than panels
renewables.thesis.stream.15.t: Storage is a more direct beneficiary of AI than most panel manufacturing. A battery shifts daytime solar into the evening, regulates frequency, provides fast reserve and participates in the capacity market — the revenue comes from several sources at once (arbitrage, ancillary services, capacity payments, tolling). Lithium is strong over a 1–4 hour horizon, but a four-hour system does not cover several days of poor weather. Long-duration technologies (iron-air, flow, pumped hydro) offer more upside, but carry far more commercial risk.
renewables.thesis.stream.16.items.0.l: cost of a grid battery (depends on duration)
renewables.thesis.stream.16.items.0.n: −93% since 2010, but 4 hours does not cover several days
renewables.thesis.stream.16.items.1.l: of new solar projects in the queue come with storage
renewables.thesis.stream.16.items.1.n: more solar means more batteries are needed
renewables.thesis.stream.16.items.2.l: of California's solar already paired with batteries
renewables.thesis.stream.16.items.2.n: storage moves midday into the evening
renewables.thesis.stream.17.t: Who is buying — the hyperscalers are changing the financing
renewables.thesis.stream.18.t: The main effect of AI is not a rise in the spot price of solar but the appearance of a creditworthy long-term buyer next to a large load. A 10–20 year power purchase agreement (PPA) turns an unfinanceable project into a bankable asset: it puts a floor under revenue, removes price risk, allows debt to be raised and the asset later sold to an infrastructure fund. Below are the disclosed deals; note also the shift from «annual coverage with certificates» towards firm, local, hourly clean energy.
renewables.thesis.stream.19.note: A PPA is a long-term power purchase agreement; it is what makes a project bankable.
renewables.thesis.stream.19.rows.0.2: almost 8× the previous record corporate PPA
renewables.thesis.stream.19.rows.1.2: the largest corporate buyer 5 years running; 100% coverage in 2024
renewables.thesis.stream.19.rows.2.2: 20 years on Clinton (1,121 MW nuclear) + geothermal
renewables.thesis.stream.19.rows.3.2: future contracts will reward output shape and storage
