transformers.valueCapture.margins.2.sour: $671M of EBITDA (Q2 2026) against $314M. Hundreds of basis points of margin expansion. The clearest financial signal
transformers.valueCapture.margins.3.sour: ~38–42% of the OLTC market. Close to a monopoly = structural rent extraction. The best pure component position
transformers.valueCapture.margins.4.sour: A ~$48.5B order book (Q1 2026). A beneficiary of the grid build-out. A rising share of fixed-price contracts
transformers.valueCapture.takeaway: A supply-constrained regime: pricing power has shifted to the OEMs holding scarce production slots and to the GOES chokepoint. The utilities are price-takers. The margin expansion is real (Siemens at 15.8%, GEV's EBITDA doubled).
transformers.verdict.bear.0: The 2027–28 wave of new capacity could normalise lead times and compress the price premium: Siemens's Charlotte plant, Hitachi USA, GE Vernova and expanded GOES output all reach the market in 2027–28 and ramp gradually.
transformers.verdict.bear.1: AI electricity demand may be overstated: at the PJM grid operator, 65–80% of the announced capacity left the queue before connecting; «phantom» demand inflates the real transformer orders.
transformers.verdict.bear.2: The multiples already embed flawless execution: GE Vernova at a P/E above 100. An order slowdown or a margin retreat means asymmetric downside.
transformers.verdict.bull.0: Lead times and order books prove the demand is real and durable: pricing power holds through 2027–28 and margins are rising (Siemens Grid Technologies — the grid division — from 15.8% to 16–18%; GE Vernova's electrification EBITDA has doubled). Supply is structurally behind demand.
transformers.verdict.bull.1: GOES (the specialised electrical steel for the core) and the talent shortage keep supply below demand through 2030: even as new plants start, the shortage of electrical steel and the time needed to train staff protect the incumbent makers' economics.
transformers.verdict.bull.2: Data centres + reshoring + renewables + an ageing fleet = a decade-long supercycle: >$1.1T of US utility capex across 2025–2029; ~70% of US large transformers are more than 25 years old.
transformers.verdict.horizon: 3–7 years — a structural grid renewal supercycle; with volatility around the quarterly order data.
transformers.verdict.keyQuestion: Will new capacity (Siemens, Hitachi) normalise lead times and prices by 2028 — or will supply stay short through 2030?
transformers.verdict.sizing: Power transformers ~$30B (2025) → ~$42B (2030). The broader transformer market ~$65B. US data-centre electrical equipment $20B → $65B (2030)
transformers.verdict.summary: The scarcest link in the physical electrification of AI: lead times of 128–160+ weeks, prices up 77% since 2019, and record order books (backlogs — accumulated orders not yet delivered: GE Vernova $42.4B, Siemens €154B). The competitive advantages are durable: a consolidated top tier, high barriers (capital, customer qualification cycles, specialised talent), reinforced by regulation (Chinese transformers are excluded from US critical infrastructure). Demand is structural and multi-factor: data centres + an ageing fleet (average age ~40 years) + renewables + reshoring. But the multiples already embed years of flawless execution (GE Vernova at a P/E above 100). The recommendation: a moderate overweight built in stages — a barbell strategy of grid companies plus optional GOES (the specialised electrical steel for the core) and EPC contractors (grid engineering and construction).
transformers.whatIsIt: A large steel tank of copper windings around a steel core, filled with oil, that changes the voltage of electric current. A power station, transmission lines and data-centre equipment all run at different voltages, and at every junction the current has to be converted — otherwise the site simply cannot be connected to the grid. Without this device a new data centre physically cannot be powered, which makes it a mandatory link along the whole path of the current from station to servers.

wbg.intro:
Power semiconductors manage the electricity inside a data centre: they step the voltage down from the grid to around 1 V, which is what a GPU runs on, and at the final step deliver hundreds of amps to the die. In essence they are fast switches: a transistor opens and closes thousands of times a second, chopping the current into portions, and a filter smooths them into the required steady voltage. Every such switching event loses some energy as heat — and the higher the voltage and frequency, the more those losses matter.

How it works, and where silicon hits its limit. While rack power stayed moderate, silicon switches were enough for the whole chain. But racks are growing from ~120 kW toward ~1 MW, and on the old 48 V bus the current becomes so large that copper losses and copper weight get out of hand. The answer is to raise the voltage: from 2027 racks move to 800 V DC (the Kyber architecture, Rubin Ultra), because at a higher voltage the same power travels at a lower current — less copper, fewer losses. But silicon can no longer switch 800 V efficiently: at that voltage it either overheats badly or requires a thick, slow die. This is where wide-bandgap materials are needed.

Why SiC and GaN are more efficient. Silicon carbide (SiC) withstands high voltage across a very thin layer, so it switches faster and loses less energy — it goes on the 800 V input and into solid-state transformers. Gallium nitride (GaN) switches at a higher frequency still, and the higher the frequency the smaller the inductors and capacitors need to be — the whole converter becomes more compact and lighter. Together, the move to 800 V with these materials delivers up to 5% energy savings across the whole chain and cuts copper wiring cost several-fold (on one estimate, from $14 to $5 a foot).

The critical property, and its cost. The binding constraint is not the chip but the substrate (wafer) beneath it, especially for SiC: it is hard to grow without defects, capital-intensive, and 200 mm capacity is limited. How hard it is shows in the fact that the technology leader in SiC substrates went through bankruptcy (Chapter 11, 2025) while building exactly that capacity. The main lever for relieving the shortage is moving substrates from 150 to 200 mm: a 200 mm wafer yields roughly 1.7x the dies.

Who invests, and how much. Power chip content per rack is growing faster than anything else in the AI chain — from ~$11,200 (the B200 generation) to ~$191,000 (Feynman), nearly 17x across four GPU generations (a Morgan Stanley estimate). The large makers with their own fabs are putting billions into SiC lines: one of them runs capex of ~€2.7B a year plus a separate €5B fab. They pay willingly, because without working power the most expensive accelerator is dead weight, and power chips' share of a rack (~0.5–5%) is far smaller than the cost of downtime. The GaN market grows from $355M (2024) to ~$3B by 2030 (~42% a year), the SiC market to roughly $10B by 2030; the large players alone put the addressable AI-power market at €8–12B by the end of the decade.

wbg.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: MPS's main advantage in voltage regulators is real but weakening: its GPU share fell from ~80%+ (Hopper) to ~70% (Rubin), Infineon takes 60–70% of Blackwell, and the hyperscalers buy directly. Deutsche Bank: up to 15% of MPS's revenue is at risk.

wbg.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: the key constraint is substrates: 200 mm SiC is limited (Wolfspeed leads but went through bankruptcy), and GaN is moving to 8-inch and 300 mm. Reliability qualification (Navitas's GaNSafe) is a real barrier that strengthens with scale, but it is still fragmented.
wbg.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: Vicor holds patents on factorised power and won an ITC exclusion order (~$300M of licences). But this is a high-density niche rather than a broad market, and production revenue only arrives from 2027.
wbg.moatBreakdown.components.5.factor: Protection from power being integrated into the GPU
wbg.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: the main crack: Nvidia and TSMC are working on delivering power from the underside of the die (power-on-package / backside power delivery), which could eliminate discrete regulators entirely. The horizon is multi-year, but the threat is structural — this is the worst case for MPS and Vicor.
wbg.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is fragmented — nobody holds a firm monopoly as in substrates or EDA. The best combination belongs to Infineon (scale + breadth + IDM). There are two cracks at once: Nvidia is multi-sourcing regulators already and could integrate power into the GPU package in future. Value is migrating from silicon regulators to the new SiC/GaN layer.

wbg.picksTakeaway: «Content grows 17x» ≠ «everyone wins». Own the theme through broad, supply-constrained manufacturers (Infineon, onsemi) that win however the spot beside the GPU is redealt. MPS, Vicor and Navitas are priced as though content growth guaranteed them the win — while inside the layer the shares are being redistributed and there is a risk of power being built into the GPU itself.
wbg.problems.items.0.gap: The barrier here is capital and yield rather than simply volume: SiC substrates are so capital-intensive and hard to produce that their leader Wolfspeed went bankrupt building them. The path from design win to volume shipment is 1–2 years, and qualifying a SiC socket with Nvidia is deep co-development. Chinese suppliers (Innoscience, StarPower) press prices on commodity GaN and SiC, but do not penetrate qualified AI sockets. Both the 200 mm scale-up and the move to 800 V itself are 2027–2028 events.
wbg.problems.items.0.problem: From 2027 racks move to 800 V DC (800VDC, the Kyber architecture, Rubin Ultra), because at the old 48 V the current becomes so large that the copper overheats and its weight gets out of hand. Silicon can no longer switch 800 V — that needs silicon carbide chips (SiC, which withstands high voltage across a thin layer). The scarcest link in this whole new layer is not the chip but the SiC substrate (wafer) beneath it: it is hard to grow, capital-intensive, and 200 mm capacity is limited. How hard it is shows in the fact that the substrate leader Wolfspeed went through bankruptcy (Chapter 11 — reorganisation under creditor protection, 2025). Power chip content per rack is growing faster than anything else in the AI chain — from ~$11,200 (B200) to ~$191,000 (Feynman), nearly 17x across four generations (a Morgan Stanley estimate).
wbg.problems.items.0.solution: The main lever is moving substrates from 150 to 200 mm: a 200 mm wafer yields roughly 1.7x the dies, so scaling it relieves the shortage directly (Wolfspeed leads here, and after bankruptcy its debt is down 70%, to ~$2B). The manufacturers with their own fabs are building their own SiC lines (Infineon, onsemi, STMicro). In parallel, gallium nitride (GaN, which switches at a higher frequency still) takes on the high-frequency conversion and lifts part of the load off SiC: Innoscience is expanding its 8-inch line from 13,000 to 20,000 wafers a month, and Infineon had its first 300 mm GaN samples at the end of 2025. The first 800 V shipments come from 2027.
wbg.problems.items.0.winners: STMicro (EPA: STM) — no. 1 in SiC (~33–36%) and an Nvidia partner on 800 V; onsemi (NASDAQ: ON) — no. 2 in SiC, with a full 0.8 to 800 V power stack, AI revenue doubling year on year, and also an Nvidia partner; Infineon (ETR: IFX) — no. 1 in power chips overall, with demand already exceeding capacity, plus the scale and the €5B Dresden fab. Wolfspeed (NYSE: WOLF) holds the technology lead in 200 mm substrates, but it is a speculative bet on emerging from crisis. Navitas (NASDAQ: NVTS) is Nvidia's only partner on both GaN and SiC from grid to processor, but its revenue is tiny ($8.6M).
wbg.problems.takeaway: Relieving this binding constraint rewards the large companies with their own fabs (STMicro, onsemi, Infineon), which can fund capital-intensive SiC capacity and are already qualified as Nvidia's 800 V partners. But the move to 800 V itself creates an entirely new layer that racks did not have — and that gives GaN newcomers (Navitas) a genuine, if binary, chance to capture value the incumbent silicon-regulator leaders cannot defend.

wbg.roadmap.generations.0.name: The 800VDC architecture (Nvidia Kyber)
wbg.roadmap.generations.0.note: 13.8 kV AC → 800 V HVDC through a solid-state transformer; it removes several AC/DC stages; ~1 MW racks; Nvidia has named 14+ silicon partners

wbg.roadmap.takeaway: 800VDC (2027) is a transformational shift: a new market for SiC/GaN, new players, a new architecture. Vertical power delivery and power-on-package are the long-term threat to discrete VRMs. GaN and SiC scaling (300 mm/200 mm) lowers unit costs. Power integrated into the GPU is the worst case for MPS and Vicor.
wbg.scenarios.cases.0.name: Bear

wbg.scenarios.cases.1.name: Base
wbg.scenarios.cases.1.note: content grows, 800VDC starts in 2027, MPS holds ~60–70% of the socket, and Infineon drives AI revenue toward €2.5B. Part of the growth is eaten by the de-rating of high multiples
wbg.scenarios.cases.2.name: Bull
wbg.scenarios.cases.2.note: 800VDC accelerates, the wide-bandgap market materialises (SiC ~$10B, GaN ~$3B by 2030), Navitas and onsemi convert design wins into revenue, and Feynman confirms $191K of content per rack
wbg.scenarios.expectedReturn: ~+5…+10%/yr (probability-weighted) — with a very wide spread; the wide-bandgap names (Navitas, Wolfspeed) are several times more volatile
wbg.scenarios.takeaway: The asymmetry depends on the name. At Infineon and onsemi the downside is capped by scale and a low valuation, with the upside coming from 800VDC landing. At MPS and Vicor the upside is played out while the downside is amplified by multi-sourcing and integration risk. Navitas is an option with large upside and a genuine risk of going to zero. Bet on the combination, not on one name.

wbg.thesis.bigIdea: Power chips are a fraction of a percent of a rack's cost, but without them a GPU simply does not switch on: they carry electricity from the grid down to the current the die runs on. Their content per rack is exploding — roughly 17x from Blackwell to Feynman — as racks move to 800 volts and megawatt power. The market read that as «17x more content means everyone wins» and re-rated the whole layer. But that is a mistake: inside the layer the value is dispersing — the most valuable spot (the voltage regulator right beside the GPU) is being lost by its leader, while the pure plays on the new materials (Navitas) are loss-making and represent an all-or-nothing bet on 2027. The theme is better owned through broad, supply-constrained manufacturers (Infineon, onsemi) than through re-rated single names.
wbg.thesis.stream.0.t: The tiny part without which a GPU is dead
wbg.thesis.stream.1.t: Power chips are ~0.5–1% of a [[rack|rack's|borrows to buy GPUs]] cost, but the [[asic|accelerator|earns on every chip]] without them is a dead piece of silicon. They are the final stretch of [[power|electricity's|not generation, but connection]] journey: they bring the voltage down from the grid to around 1 volt, which is what a GPU runs on, and deliver hundreds of amps to the die. And their content per rack is exploding as racks move to 800 volts and megawatt power.

And it re-rated the whole complex: MPS at ~50x earnings, Navitas +780% (on revenue of just $8.6M), Vicor +145–179% year to date.

wbg.thesis.stream.19.t: The content growth is real — but «everyone wins» is wrong, because inside the layer the value migrates and disperses. Three cracks: MPS, the leader of the most valuable spot, is actually LOSING share to multi-sourcing (up to 15% of revenue at risk — the shares fell 25% in a day on that news). The pure plays on the new materials (Navitas) are loss-making and represent an all-or-nothing bet on the move to 800 volts, which only starts in 2027 (revenue of $8.6M, a beta of 3.6). And the base market is cyclical — it contracted in 2024, and automotive and industrial are still weak.

wbg.thesis.stream.20.t: And the most structural risk: Nvidia could build power directly into the GPU package — at which point the open market for this chip, on which the whole bet rests, collapses. «Content per rack» says nothing about who keeps it.
wbg.thesis.stream.21.t: «Content grows 17x» is not «everyone wins». Inside the layer the shares are being redealt, and the most valuable spot is being lost by its leader.
wbg.thesis.stream.22.t: What is already in the price
wbg.thesis.stream.23.t: MPS at ~50x embeds flawlessly holding a share it is already beginning to lose. Navitas embeds a successful move to 800 volts on top of $8.6M of revenue and a loss. Vicor at +145% is already paid for production revenue that only arrives in 2027. Meanwhile the broad, supply-constrained manufacturers — Infineon (a ~17.5% segment margin, targeting 20%, with AI power heading to €2.5B) and onsemi (margins expanding toward a 60–70% analogue target) — are valued far more modestly for a position that wins regardless of how any single chip is redealt.
wbg.thesis.stream.24.t: Our read: Infineon and onsemi are fair; MPS, Vicor and Navitas are expensive.
wbg.thesis.stream.25.t: Where the technology is going — and where the money is going
wbg.thesis.stream.26.t: The direction is set: the whole data centre moves to 800 volt power distribution (Nvidia Kyber/Rubin Ultra), which replaces the conversion chain with a few higher-voltage stages and forces a move from silicon to SiC/GaN. Content per rack keeps rising — toward ~$191K at Feynman. Beyond that, power moves physically closer to the GPU (vertical delivery, backside power on the die) to cut losses — and that redeals once again who owns the spot next to the chip.
wbg.thesis.stream.27.t: Where the money is going: Nvidia is pulling the whole industry toward 800 volts and naming partners (Navitas is its «grid-to-GPU» partner on GaN+SiC), which is why a $3B company with $8.6M of revenue costs so much. The full-cycle manufacturers (Infineon, onsemi, STMicro) are investing in silicon carbide capacity — but SiC is short and cyclical (the pure substrate maker Wolfspeed came close to bankruptcy). And the analogue leaders (TI, MPS) are expanding capacity ($6B at MPS) to defend the high-margin spot beside the GPU.

wbg.thesis.stream.29.t: What the players are betting on: Nvidia — on 800 volts and the new materials for the energy savings at megawatt scale (and on multi-sourcing, so as not to depend on one supplier). The full-cycle manufacturers — on breadth and SiC capacity: they win whoever gets any particular spot. The single-chip leaders (MPS, Vicor) — on defending their high-margin spot from multi-sourcing and from power being built into the GPU package. The pure plays on the new materials are betting everything on the 2027 move to 800 volts. The next battlefield is vertical power delivery and whether the spot beside the GPU stays an open market.

wbg.thesis.stream.32.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
wbg.thesis.stream.33.t: Power chips are a tiny but critical part of a rack, and their content really is exploding ~17x as the move to 800 volts arrives. But the market's error is reading «content is growing» as «everyone wins»: inside the layer the value disperses, the leader of the most valuable spot (MPS) is losing share, and the pure plays on the new materials are all-or-nothing bets on 2027.
wbg.thesis.stream.34.t: The conclusion: own the theme through broad, supply-constrained manufacturers (Infineon, onsemi) that win regardless of how any single chip is redealt. And treat the single-spot leaders (MPS, Vicor) and the new-materials pure plays (Navitas) as expensive, riskier bets priced as though content growth guaranteed them the win.
wbg.thesis.stream.4.t: How it works. A power chip steps the voltage down from the grid to ~1 volt and delivers hundreds of amps to the die. In essence it is a fast switch: a transistor opens and closes thousands of times a second, chopping the current into portions, and a filter smooths them into a steady voltage. Every switching event loses some energy as heat — and the higher the voltage and frequency, the more those losses matter. So the industry is moving from ordinary silicon to «wide-bandgap» materials — silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN): they switch faster and with lower losses. At megawatt scale, saving even a few percent is worth billions.

wbg.thesis.stream.5.items.1.n: at gigawatt scale, that is billions
wbg.thesis.stream.6.t: Why the content is growing — the move to 800 volts
wbg.thesis.stream.7.t: The ~17x growth runs along two axes. Volume — more racks. And content per rack: when a rack moves to 800 volt DC power distribution and megawatt capacity, a whole new SiC/GaN conversion layer appears, and doubling a rack's power multiplies its silicon carbide content roughly fivefold. The voltage regulator beside the GPU alone (the VRM) is ~41% of the cost of all the power chips in a Feynman rack.
wbg.thesis.stream.8.t: Where the margin sits — and where the shares are being redealt
wbg.thesis.stream.9.t: The money is distributed unevenly. The highest and most durable margins are in the analogue layer and in intellectual property: TI 58%, MPS 55%, Vicor 55% (targeting 70%). Discrete chips on the new materials (onsemi 38%, Navitas 39% and only on a non-GAAP basis — on GAAP it is a loss) earn less, even though they are growing. And the most valuable spot — the voltage regulator (VRM) beside the GPU, where MPS holds ~70% of the Rubin chip — is exactly where the share redistribution begins.
wbg.tldr.0: Power chip content per rack grows ~17x: $11,200 (B200) → $17,800 (GB300) → >$33,000 (Rubin) → ~$95,000 (Rubin Ultra) → ~$191,000 (Feynman). This is the fastest content growth in the entire AI chain.
wbg.tldr.1: MPS leads in VRMs (the voltage regulators closest to the accelerator processor): Enterprise Data +98% y/y, ~33% of revenue. But Nvidia is actively bringing in second sources (Infineon, Renesas) — MPS fell 24.9% in a session in November 2024 on those fears.
wbg.tldr.2: Infineon is the world's no. 1 in power semiconductors: AI revenue of €250M (FY24) → €1.5B (FY26) → €2.5B (FY27). The best combination of product breadth and scale. It opened a €5B fab in Dresden.
wbg.tldr.3: The move to 800 V DC (800VDC, from 2027, Nvidia Kyber) creates a new $3–10B market by 2030 for silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) chips. Navitas is Nvidia's only partner with both materials (GaN+SiC), but revenue is $8.6M and it is loss-making. A bet with two outcomes.
wbg.unitEconomics.costCurve: Silicon VRMs are cheaper to produce (MPS is fabless). SiC and GaN cost more but save energy: 800VDC plus wide-bandgap delivers up to 5% end-to-end savings plus a ~3x reduction in copper cabling cost (Vicor: $14/ft → $5/ft). At gigawatt scale: ~100 W per accelerator × millions = terawatts and billions of dollars.
wbg.unitEconomics.grossMargin: TI: 58%. MPS: 55%. Vicor: 55% (targeting 70%). onsemi: 38.5% (expanding; a 60–70% Treo target). Navitas: 39% non-GAAP (negative on GAAP). Infineon: a ~17.5% segment margin (targeting 20%).
wbg.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: VRM content: $11.2k (B200) → $191k (Feynman) per rack. onsemi: $15k (a 120 kW rack) → $115k (600 kW–1 MW). Doubling a rack's power means ~5x the SiC content.
wbg.unitEconomics.takeaway: The best economics belong to the analogue and IP companies (TI 58%, MPS 55%, Vicor 55% → 70%). SiC and GaN are lower for now but growing, and they pay for themselves through energy efficiency. Operating leverage is high: a rising AI mix improves margins quickly.

wbg.unitEconomics.yields.1.note: operating profit growth at ~2x revenue growth
wbg.update.bottomLine: Power chip content per rack is growing ~17x — the fastest growth in the AI chain. Infineon (the ballast core) + MPS (the aggressive VRM play) + onsemi (overlooked value) are the trio for covering it. 800VDC/Kyber (2027) is the next catalyst. Dual-sourcing and integration are permanent risks, but demand is confirmed by records.

Content per rack keeps rising: the Vera Rubin BOM is +233% on PCB at $7.8M a rack.
wbg.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: 800VDC conversion (from 2027): solid-state transformers plus SiC/GaN DC-DC conversion from grid voltage down to the GPU. An entirely new layer that does not exist in today's racks. Navitas, Infineon, onsemi and Power Integrations are the main contenders.
wbg.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: The VRM / point of load (closest to the GPU): ~41% of the power chip cost in a Feynman rack (26% for the second-stage VPD plus 15% for the lateral VRM). MPS dominates thanks to its monolithic analogue design. This is the highest-margin and hardest layer.
wbg.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Medium for the fabless players (MPS, Navitas); high for the IDMs (Infineon: €2.7B of FY26 capex, Dresden at €5B; onsemi's SiC fabs). SiC substrates are capital-intensive (Wolfspeed went through bankruptcy).

wbg.valueCapture.takeaway: Value concentrates in the VRM/point of load (MPS at a ~55% gross margin) and broad analogue (TI at ~58%). 800VDC opens a new high-value layer for SiC/GaN. Margins are best at the analogue and IP companies; discretes and wide-bandgap are lower but growing.
wbg.verdict.bear.0: Multi-sourcing at MPS: −24.9% in a day (November 2024), ~−37% (October 2025). Infineon takes 60–70% of Blackwell (per analysts). The cloud giants buy voltage regulators directly, bypassing the server makers. Deutsche Bank: «up to 15% of MPS's revenue is at risk».
wbg.verdict.bear.1: Integration: Nvidia and TSMC could pull power into the GPU package (backside power delivery), destroying the market for separate voltage regulators. A structural multi-year risk.
wbg.verdict.bear.2: Cyclicality plus valuations: the base market contracted in 2024. Automotive and industrial are still weak. MPS at ~50x forward, Vicor +179% year to date, Navitas +780%. A perfect future is priced in.
wbg.verdict.bull.0: Content per rack is exploding: $11.2k → $191k (B200 → Feynman). Every 1% of energy saved at gigawatt scale is worth billions. Power chips are a mandatory cost.
wbg.verdict.bull.1: The move to 800 V DC (800VDC) plus silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) chips from 2027 opens a new market: GaN at ~$3B by 2030 (42% a year), SiC at ~$10B. Nvidia is organising the ecosystem (14+ silicon partners). Every new rack above 200 kW requires 800 V power.
wbg.verdict.bull.2: MPS's dominance in voltage regulators (VRMs) + Infineon's product breadth + Vicor's patents (an ITC ban on importing infringing devices) = several ways to win.
wbg.verdict.horizon: 3–5 years — the move to 800 V power and SiC/GaN chips, plus growing power content per rack.
wbg.verdict.keyQuestion: Will voltage conversion for GPUs stay a protected market — or will Nvidia and TSMC integrate power into the chip package?
wbg.verdict.sizing: The total power semiconductor market: ~$46–55B (2025, depending on the definition). The AI subsegment grows at a >40% CAGR: onsemi's TAM is ~$12.2B by 2029. GaN: $355M (2024) → ~$3B (2030, Yole). SiC: up to $10.3B by 2030.
wbg.verdict.summary: Power chip content per rack grows ~17x across 4 accelerator generations — the fastest content growth in the AI chain. MPS (the VRM leader — the voltage regulators beside the processor, at a ~55% margin) and Infineon (no. 1, with a broad range) are proven leaders. But the move to 800 V DC (800VDC) plus silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) chips in 2027 redistributes the value, and Nvidia is actively bringing in second sources for voltage regulators (MPS −24.9% in a day). Valuations are high: MPS at ~50x forward, Vicor +145–179% year to date, Navitas +780%. The base market (~$46–55B) is cyclical and actually contracted in 2024.
wbg.whatIsIt: The chips that manage electricity inside a data centre: they step the voltage down from the grid to around one volt, which is what the accelerator processor itself runs on, and deliver hundreds of amps to it. In essence they are very fast switches — thousands of times a second they chop the current into portions, and a filter smooths them into a steady voltage. Without working power even the most expensive accelerator is simply dead weight.
